title: Transfusion Science
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: Histopathology is the study of cellular abnormalities and disease processes in human tissues through the application of various histopathological techniques. This course will introduce the application of special staining procedures, cryotomy, immunohistochemistry, and gross anatomical pathology specimen handling.
title: Histopathology
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: Hydrology is the study of the occurrence, distribution and movement of water on and beneath the Earth's surface. This course develops an understanding of hydrological processes and their application to engineering design and water resources management. Topics include rainfall, evaporation, infiltration, surface runoff, groundwater, and hydrological extremes such as floods and droughts. Students develop practical skills in analysing hydrological data, estimating design rainfall and floods, and modelling catchment responses to rainfall. Particular emphasis is placed on rainfall losses, rainfall-runoff transformation, and flood routing. Lectures and workshops connect hydrological theory with engineering applications, including the use of HEC-HMS to build, calibrate and evaluate catchment models. The course also considers how climate change and land-use change influence hydrological behaviour and the implications for flood risk and sustainable water management.
title: Hydrology
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This sequence of courses involves the identification of a research topic, the development of a research proposal to address that topic, the undertaking of the proposed research project, and its reporting in a dissertation. Where relevant, candidates will also obtain ethical clearance for the proposed project.
title: Dissertation 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course focuses on the application of biochemistry to medicine. We will examine existing and newly developed diagnostic tests that are being used in the diagnosis of human diseases. Students completing this course are equipped to understand the central role of the clinical biochemistry laboratory in medicine.
title: Clinical Biochemistry
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course is divided into two independent modules. One module provides students with an understanding of the complex design issues encountered in computer systems. While this module is mostly hardware oriented, the implications on operating system are also covered. The other module is a special topic, chosen from specialist areas of computer system design. Advised Prerequisite: 3302ENG Computer Systems Incompatible: 6305ENG Advanced Computer Systems
title: Advanced Computer Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: Students are required to complete 560 hours of placement across courses 4001MSC and 4002MSC. The course consists of 14 weeks of laboratory placement. The schedule of activities to be undertaken by the student will be determined by the placement laboratory and designed to allow achievement each of the learning outcomes and competencies.
title: Clinical Placement II
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: A major objective of this course is the generation of retirement planning strategies. Assessment items reflect the challenging demands of an industry which seeks to ensure all Australians enjoy a comfortable and self-funded retirement. Therefore, it is expected that students are knowledgeable of technical and regulatory issues, skillful in strategic thinking and analysis and aware of contemporary issues in the superannuation and retirement context.
title: Superannuation and Retirement
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: Students are required to complete 560 hours of placement across courses 4001MSC and 4002MSC. The schedule of activities to be undertaken in 4001MSC by the student will be determined by the placement laboratory and designed to allow the achievement of each of the learning outcomes and competencies. The evidence of this attainment will be found in the student's weekly journal of activities and in the training records or training booklet of the laboratory. 4001MSC aims to provide students with supervised practical experience in a workplace setting such as a hospital, private medical laboratory, or research laboratory to educate and train future diagnostic or medical research scientists. It is designed to develop in students the skills and competencies appropriate for a professional entry-level medical (clinical) laboratory scientist. After this course, students are expected to be competent at a basic level with the operations and functions of the diagnostic laboratory under-skilled and supportive supervision.
title: Clinical Placement I
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: The 7009CSR_P1 to P4 courses are designed for Master of Suicidology (Dissertation pathway) students to carry out a research project under supervision of a member of staff with substantial research experience. The courses will allow the student to implement research skills obtained from the course work component of the Master of Suicidology (Dissertation pathway) program and to learn and develop additional research skills under supervision. The student will need to prepare a dissertation which is a coherent exposition of a research study that follows an ordered sequence in which the research objectives, relationship to other scholarly work, methodology and strategies employed, and the results obtained are identified, analysed and evaluated. Through the dissertation a student establishes her/his capacity for independent research and knowledge of the topic and the discipline. Specifically, the student needs to develop an argument which demonstrates an ability to initialise and frame a question, respond to and represent a variety of viewpoints, provide balanced evidence for positions adopted, develop appropriate methodologies and methods, collect data in an ethical manner, and interpret and generalise data in a defensible way. Students will develop dissertations in suicide research through a guided approach encompassing academic liaison. Students will be given individual feedback and supervision on the development of a hypothesis, techniques for research design and appropriate statistical methods. Assessment will require a written report and seminar presentation of the research.
title: Dissertation
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course will equip graduates with the knowledge and skills to competently undertake haematological investigations by problem-solving exercises examining the clinical presentation and laboratory investigation of a range of blood cell disorders and acquired or inherited disorders of haemostasis. The course material is aligned with AIMS and IBMS accreditation bodies learning objectives. Students knowledge will be assessed by both theory and practical exams with Mandatory Pass requirememt.
title: Haematology II
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: You will learn about the role of scientific data gathering in psychology which underpins all evidence-based practice, including both qualitative and quantitative approaches. Basic research approaches will be described and the manner in which research is communicated will be practised. You will gain skills in the description of quantitative data using basic graphical (e.g., histograms) and numerical (e.g., mean and standard deviation) methods. The association between variables through scatterplots and correlations is examined and you will learn how to calculate and interpret the confidence interval of the mean and make inferences using t-tests. You will learn to create and interpret output from the statistical software package SPSS for these statistical techniques. Prerequisites: Nil Co-requisites: Nil. Incompatible: Students must not have completed 1 of 1002MSC Introduction to Biomedical Data Analysis/1014SCG Statistics/1305AFE Business Data Analysis/2009CCJ Quantitative Methods for Social Research/2013AHS Research Methods and Statistics/2022MSC Introduction to Biostatistics
title: Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This is the third of four Advanced Topics in Information Technology courses. Each of these courses embraces subject matter close to the current state-of-the-art. Students select a topic from the list. Students are strongly advised to consult the academic offering their selected topic well before the course starts. Any topic studied in one Advanced Topics in Information Technology course cannot be studied in any of the other three Advanced Topics in Information Technology courses. Students must submit a Departmental Consent Form prior to enrolment in this Advanced Topic course.
title: Advanced Topics in Information Technology C
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: This course extends students' programming skills through the introduction of alternative programming languages, the study of data structures, algorithms, and concurrency, and the use of software development tools and environments. This course builds on the concepts of object-oriented programming as well as data structures and algorithms introduced in 7001ICT Programming Principles 1 and 7005ICT Programming Principles 2, broadening the theoretical knowledge and practical programming experience through the introduction of a programming language different from Programming Principles 1 and 2. Assumed background: This course assumes fundamental knowledge in object-oriented concepts and an object-oriented programming language such as Java.
title: Mobile Device Software Development
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: Geographical information systems are essential tools for the management, analysis and presentation of spatially referenced data. This course addresses methodological concepts of GIS, technical and organisational issues as well as practical applications in environmental sciences and planning. Earth resource satellites provide vast geospatial datasets for GIS and underpin our capacity for environmental monitoring and management. The course also include basic concepts in remote sensing and how to access and retrieve satellite remote sensing data for GIS applications. Different approaches, including the use of remote sensing metrics and indicators to extract important information from satellite data will also be delivered.
title: Geographic Information Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: The main aim of this course is to provide sound knowledge of the principles and practices of digital systems, both at the device and circuit level. The course covers topics in digital electronics including: Number Theory, Boolean Algebra, Logic Circuits, Logic Minimisation Techniques, Multiplexers, Adders, Flip-Flops, Counters, Registers, State Machines, Memory Circuits, Digital / Analog Conversion, Programable Logic Circuits and Microcomputer Bus Architecture.
title: Digital Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course introduces the basic semiconductor concepts, the principles of diodes and transistor operation, and the fundamental transistor circuits. The physical operation and the current--voltage characteristics of the two most common transistors, metal--oxide--semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) and bipolar-junction transistor (BJT), are introduced. The fundamental amplifier and digital (inverter) circuits are introduced with MOSFETs, whereas the amplifier topologies and the small-signal analysis by equivalent circuits is introduced with BJT circuits. Circuit simulation (SPICE) and laboratory exercises complement the teaching approach in this course. Assumed or recommended prior knowledge of 2319ENG Introduction to Electronics.
title: Semiconductor Devices and Circuits
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course introduces students to the programming and interfacing of a modern microcontroller. The course outlines the theory behind microcontrollers, with a focus on architecture, memory structures, and peripheral interfacing. The course also involves an insight into programming methodologies in C and illustrates ways of successfully debugging embedded systems. The course will give the student the background knowledge to successfully develop an embedded system using any microprocessor. The course is highly practical in approach and covers such areas as data acquisition, sensor interfacing, electronic control, and microprocessor communication protocols. Incompatible: 3323ENG Microcontroller Techniques
title: Embedded Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course covers aspects of a computer system from the hardware level to the software level. The hardware covers the basic components of a computer system, CPU architectures, the I/O subsystem, and common Buses. The software covers common data structures and algorithms, parallel programming techniques and an in-depth look at the low-level design of a Real Time Operating System. Throughout the course, the assignments and laboratories will be used to further develop the practical skills of the students.
title: Computer Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: The supply of good quality water, together with the removal of subsequent wastewater, is essential for modern communities. This course deals with the theory, methods, processes and design principles involved in treating and managing water and wastewater, including reticulation systems. The main focus is on municipal use of water and municipal wastewater production. This course concentrates on providing a solid understanding of conventional practice. Incompatible: 7345EVE Water and Wastewater Treatment Fundamentals
title: Water and Wastewater Treatment Fundamentals
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: The supply of good quality water, together with the removal of subsequent wastewater, is essential for modern communities and for maintaining water quality in the environment. This course concentrates on providing a solid understanding of the more advanced aspects of the treatment processes. The content of this course goes beyond conventional practice and deals with a number of more specific, specialised or advanced aspects, theories, methods, processes, design principles and associated trends in treating water and wastewater to the required quality. The main focus is on municipal water and wastewater treatment. Prerequisites: Sound knowledge of conventional water and wastewater engineering. Incompatible: must have completed 3201ENG Water and Wastewater Treatment Fundamentals OR must have completed 7411ENG Water and Wastewater Treatment Fundamentals.
title: Advanced Water and Wastewater Engineering
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: The main aim of this course is to provide the student with an opportunity to pursue an in-depth study of a single topic, bringing together the wide range of skills developed in the program courses. Students will conduct research on a topic agreed between the student and the supervisor(s), to be carried over two trimesters. Assessment is based on oral presentations as well as a final dissertation. Students will be required to analyse a problem, develop solutions and make necessary decisions regarding the problem under investigation.
title: Dissertation Part 2
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course introduces fundamental structural concepts and provides students with an understanding of structural behaviour and design. Topics include equilibrium, internal forces, stress, structural elements and systems, design actions, load transfer, and the stiffness and strength of structural members. The course is delivered through weekly lectures and workshops, supported by hands-on experiments.
title: Introduction to Structures
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course examines issues involved in the management of energy resources and the strategies required to develop sustainable energy systems. The course will be taught principally by specialist professional engineers from industry. The exact topics covered may vary from year to year and may include: estimation and evaluation of energy resources, energy reserves, forecasting, modelling and simulation of renewable energy systems, energy management in relation to sustainable development, energy demand management, resource management in relation to power infrastructure, power infrastructure planning and energy distribution, organisational challenges in sustainable energy management. Incompatible 6311ENG Energy Resources Management.
title: Real World Energy
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course explores the link between the environment, development, and the quality of life. It considers some of the key issues faced by both developing and developed states, and examines various proposals for achieving sustainability. Students use the concepts derived from these explorations to analyse a range of case studies.
title: Environment and Development
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: Engineers working in air pollution control have many responsibilities. One of the most demanding, yet most satisfying, of these is the design of air pollution control system. This course provides with the philosophy and procedures for the design of such systems. In addition to design work, the responsibility of air pollution engineers can include monitoring, permitting, performance testing, maintenance scheduling, and operational troubleshooting. The two main objectives of this course are to present essential basic information about air pollution and its control and to provide formal design training of engineering students. This subject provides detailed knowledge of theoretical and practical aspects of industrial air pollution control and monitoring. It covers main processes and devices widely used in the area air pollution control, particularly filtration and separation, chemical and mechanical methods of air purification, absorption, adsorption, precipitation, etc. The subject also covers main technologies and protocols used for air pollution monitoring.
title: Air Quality Monitoring and Control
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: As the final course in the Professional Pharmacy Practice series, 7010PHM is designed to further enhance student skills in providing patient-centred care, promoting quality use of medicines, developing individualised strategies to support people with medication adherence and lifestyle change, and communicating recommendations to health professionals. In 7010PHM, students will cover the following therapeutic areas: geriatrics, palliative care, paediatrics, mental health, immunisation and travel health. Advanced topics will be provided on medication management, professional services and risk management in practice. Pharmacy speciality areas include medication management reviews and this course provides students with an introduction to some of the core skills related to this professional service. This course has a significant emphasis on the development of life-long learning skills through an evidence-based approach.
title: Professional Pharmacy Practice III
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course requires all students to undertake placement in community and hospital settings over a period of 4-weeks. This course will begin to develop your ability to bridge the gap between your academic learning and the professional practice under the guidance and supervision of a preceptor. You will experience a semi-structured learning environment during your placement, in which you will observe practice in this environment, become an active participant (where possible) and synthesise your learning. Activities undertaken during placement are designed to allow achievement of the course learning outcomes and competencies.
title: Placements
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course explores approaches and issues in contemporary global security, aiming to extend skills in the critical analysis of international relations. The first part examines theoretical approaches to the study of the topic and then how states and non-state actors have sought to establish and maintain global security since the end of the Second World War. The remainder of the course assesses a range of security challenges, from nuclear weapons and missile proliferation to terrorism and the protection of human rights in civil conflicts. It explores perennial and novel challenges to global security, from power transitions between major powers to the use of economic heft for strategic purposes, as well as the impact of information technology on the conduct of war and the use of political warfare and propaganda in an age of social media.
title: Global Security
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

description: This course offers an overview of Australia's foreign relations. It covers economic, social, political and diplomatic relations, with a particular focus on the Asia-Pacific region. The course covers: the history of Australia's foreign relations; the foreign policies of the Coalition and Labor governments; defence policy and new security issues; foreign aid and the environment; Australia's foreign economic relations; relations with Asia and the United States; and the concept of national interest. This course is offered at Nathan in even years, and Gold Coast in odd years.
title: Australia's Foreign Relations
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

description: This course provides students with a broad introduction to the study of international relations. It examines the theory, history and relationships that inform our understanding of global politics. Throughout the course students will be introduced to a range of concepts, such as power, gender, anarchy, order, justice, peace and diplomacy. They will also consider a series of case studies that illustrate the importance and relevance of these concepts to the world we live in today. Students will have the opportunity to engage with classical and contemporary scholars of International Relations and to explore the different research methods they use to explain how the world operates.
title: International Relations: Ideas and Issues
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

description: This course provides a graduate-level introduction to the major approaches to global security. It examines the nature of security threats and societal vulnerabilities as well as approaches to conflict resolution and security planning. It also examines in some detail various aspects of global security challenges and responses, from terrorism and environmental degradation to borders and health governance.
title: Global Security
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

description: This course examines the relationship between the brain, cognition, and behaviour. You will learn about various cognitive functions and dysfunctions, as well as how knowledge of brain and cognitive dysfunction can be used to develop models of human cognition. Examples of the topic areas which may be covered are object and face recognition, language and reading problems, delusions, attention and video game training, and semantic processing. Inter-relationships between theory, research and practice are identified, and you will be exposed to applied problems in cognitive neuropsychology.
title: Cognitive Neuropsychology
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course provides a set of frameworks for examining and understanding human behaviour in a social and cultural context. It integrates the social and the cultural, with the overriding aim to develop an understanding of how the individual's thoughts, feelings, and behaviours can be shaped by the people around them, and the culture of which they are a part.
title: Social and Cultural Psychology
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: Students taking this course will gain knowledge of theoretical and empirical bases underpinning the construction, implementation and interpretation of some widely used cognitive and personality assessments. They will also gain knowledge of the theoretical and empirical bases underpinning evidence-based psychological interventions.
title: Professional Psychology A
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: Intellectual property law, which is the generic term for various areas of law which protect creativity, is increasing in importance. The main areas likely to be covered in the course include copyright, patents, design, trade marks and plant variety protection. The syllabus will be based on Australian law as well as relevant international developments (such as GATT/TRIPS) and the laws of the European Union. Intellectual property applies to a wide range of activities from property rights in DNA and genetically modified animals through to protection of artistic works and digital sampling. Given the breadth of the subject matter with which intellectual property law concerns itself, the course lends itself to integration with all relevant disciplines. No prior technical knowledge is required.
title: Principles of Intellectual Property Law
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: The Vis International Commercial Arbitration Moot is an annual competition involving teams representing law schools throughout the world. The Moot is designed as a clinical tool to train law students in the writing of memoranda of argument and the oral presentation of those arguments. The first component of the moot - which is the subject matter of this course - is a written exercise, which concerns issues of international contracting relating to the sale or purchase of goods under the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods and other uniform international commercial law, in the context of an arbitration of a dispute under specified Arbitration Rules. Information on application process is available at the Griffith Law School Organisation site on Learning@Griffith.
title: Vis International Commercial Arbitration Moot (Written Competition)
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course continues comprehensive training in music theory, aural studies and keyboard musicianship for music theatre students. This course sequence is exclusively for students enrolled in the Music Theatre program.
title: Materials of Music (Musical Theatre) 3
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course continues the work begun in Musical Theatre 1. The acquisition and development of Acting, Speech, Singing and Dance techniques are interdependent elements in a process that culminates in a Performance Project, a learning opportunity consisting of a short '20th Century Drama' performance presented simply to an audience of tutors and fellow students. This course continues the development of the student's potential as a musical theatre performer as fully as possible, through individual tuition in singing and class tuition in acting, dance, voice and speech and through master classes, workshops, seminars and public performances.
title: Musical Theatre 2
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course continues the work begun in Musical Theatre 1, 2 and 3. The acquisition and development of Acting, Speech, Singing and Dance techniques are interdependent elements in a process that culminates in a Performance Project, a learning opportunity consisting of a short 'Modern Book Musical' performance presented simply to an audience of tutors and fellow students. This course continues the development of the student's potential as a musical theatre performer as fully as possible, through individual tuition in singing and class tuition in acting, dance, voice and speech and through master classes, workshops, seminars and public performances.
title: Musical Theatre 4
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course continues comprehensive training in music theory, aural studies and keyboard musicianship for music theatre students. This course sequence is exclusively for students enrolled in the Music Theatre program.
title: Materials of Music (Musical Theatre) 2
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course will challenge both the students' musical and technical skills and help prepare them for the rigorous demands of the profession. This course provides an opportunity for students to select an ensemble or collaborative activity to participate in for credit, depending on their specialisation and interests.
title: Ensemble and Collaborative Activity 4A
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course will challenge both the students' musical and technical skills and help prepare them for the rigorous demands of the profession. This course provides an opportunity for students to select an ensemble or collaborative activity to participate in for credit, depending on their specialisation and interests.
title: Ensemble and Collaborative Activity 3C
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: Honours Research Project constitutes a 40CP honours research commitment within the Bachelor of Design with Honours program. Each of the four components of the course combine to introduce students to the rigors of research and engage them in an advanced level of study within visual practice. The expectation is that the research project undertaken will be based within the visual and incorporates high levels of visual literacy. Assessment of the four courses will culminate in one assessment item. Co-requisite/Pre-requisite: 6511QCA Design Research Methods.
title: Honours Research Project
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: Dissertation Project constitutes a 40CP research commitment. The course is divided into four 10CP components. Each component combines to introduce students to the rigors of research and engage them in an advanced level of study within visual practice. The Dissertation will consist of a major research project accompanied by an exegesis of 5000 words (min). The expectation is that the research project will be based within the visual and incorporates high levels of visual literacy. Assessment of the four courses will culminate in a single submission for examination.
title: Dissertation Project
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This is the first of two final-year courses in the Photography Major. The course assists students in developing a significant body of work for submission to the Graduation Exhibition, emphasising experimental and preparatory aspects of studio practice. This course should be undertaken during the same trimester and year as 3378QCA 'Studio Thinking' and in the same year as the final Major 4 course leading into the Graduate exhibition. Pre-requisite: Must be undertaking 1651 Bachelor of Visual Arts OR must be undertaking 1652 Bachelor of Visual Arts/Bachelor of Business OR must be undertaking 1187 Bachelor of Contemporary Australian Indigenous Art AND must have completed 2017QCA Photography Studio 1 OR must have completed 2801QCA Photo Studio 1 AND must have completed 2802QCA Photography Studio 2 AND must have completed 2439QCA Memory and Trauma in Visual Culture OR must have completed 3426QCA Art of Portraiture: History and Theory OR must have completed 2440QCA Abstraction OR must have completed 3403QCA Australian Art OR must have completed 2431QCA Art, Gender, Sexuality and the Body OR must have completed 2916QCA The Art of Resistance
title: Photography Studio 3
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: The Honours Research Project courses constitute a 40CP honours research commitment within the Honours program. Each of its four courses combine to introduce students to the rigours of research and engage them in an advanced level of study within visual/screen production practice. The expectation is that the artefacts and production practices arising from this research project will operate synergistically with the theoretical work to result in a project that is cohesive in all respects and which demonstrates high levels of visual and textual literacy. Assessment of the four courses will culminate in one assessment item at the end of the program, which is to be presented with the Exegesis (completed in 6012GFS) for assessment in a professional context at the completion of all four courses.
title: Honours Research Project
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Film School

description: This course focuses on the role and potential of participatory processes in the planning of neighbourhoods, cities and regions. Different approaches to public involvement and community development will be explored, with an emphasis on underlying assumptions. The historical context of different approaches will also be considered. Contemporary practices will be examined in the light of recent debates in social and political theory about civil society, governance, "the public", community and difference. Knowledge of techniques and development of practical skills will be also achieved through participation in workshops and assessment of "real-life" situations.
title: Public Involvement and Community Development
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course examines aspects of managerial accounting for planning, control and decision-making within organisations. In particular, understanding and managerial applications of technical, conceptual, behavioural and judgemental aspects of managerial accounting in planning, decision-making and performance management are emphasised. It also introduces students to the major field of accounting which emphasises accounting concepts, systems and techniques that provide information for use in the planning, controlling and decision-making activities at all levels of management within an organisation.
title: Management Accounting and Strategy
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course critically examines the theoretical framework of financial reporting and its regulation. It is therefore assumed that students have the necessary technical skills and understanding of accounting following the successful completion of the required prerequisite. The course covers the historical development of accounting and its role in society, standard setting and institutional arrangements, politicisation of accounting, international accounting trends and harmonisation, a range of theoretical perspectives and the links between accounting theory, research and practice.
title: Financial Accounting Theory and Practice
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: Successful marketing decisions require a sound understanding of consumer behaviour, whether in the context of commercial firms, non-profit organisations, or government departments. This course provides you with a thorough appreciation of the complexities of consumer decision-making to ensure that your future marketing decisions achieve your objectives in your target market.
title: Consumer Psychology
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This course concerns the identification, analysis, evaluation and treatment of risk. It highlights practical applications of general and life insurance products in developing and implementing personal and small business risk management strategies. In addition to investigating the insurance products available in the market, the course will cover the structure of the insurance industry, its regulation, insurance law and the skills necessary to provide risk management and insurance advice to clients.
title: Risk Management and Insurance
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: The Corporate Finance course involves three broad aspects: The financial management of companies; financial institutions and markets; and investments. These three aspects are interrelated and complementary. In Corporate Finance the central questions are: (a) What investments should you take on (b) Where will you get the financing to pay for your investment (c) When the business is successful, how will you share in the rewards. The role of the financial manager is to answer these questions. In order to acquire funds, a financial manager needs some knowledge of the operations of financial institutions and markets. Investments involve the allocation of funds once they have been acquired. Since the three aspects are so closely related, it is impossible to study any one of them in isolation.
title: Corporate Finance
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course is for students enrolled full-time in the Doctor of Visual Arts (6009). Course content is to be determined in consultation with the nominated supervisors.
title: Studio Practice and Research
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course requires execution, analysis and presentation of a research thesis. This involves development of a project, analysis of literature and execution of experimentation. Results and conclusions are presented in oral and written forms.
title: Dissertation Thesis
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course will enable the acquisition and development of knowledge and practical skills to process clinical specimens, assess pathological states, understand the aetiology of infections, and subsequently identify, diagnose, and report infectious diseases caused by bacteria, fungi, viruses, and parasites.
title: Clinical Microbiology
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course describes the general principles of pharmacology from a contemporary viewpoint. Topics include receptor theory, mechanisms of drug action, absorption and distribution, metabolism and excretion of drugs, pharmacokinetics, drug delivery systems, toxicology and clinical testing for drugs. Drug classes are illustrated using prototypical drugs.
title: Pharmacology
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course describes the general principles of pharmacology from a contemporary viewpoint. It will cover the pharmacology of inflammation and immunology, respiratory pharmacology, cancer, including chemotherapy, infectious disease and endocrine and reproductive pharmacology. Sound knowledge and understanding of tertiary-level physiology and pharmacology is expected.
title: Human Pharmacology II
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: With a focus on Precision Medicine (diagnostics and treatment), in this course students examine the molecular bases for pathogenesis of major diseases, focusing on cell signalling pathways and their modulation. The major idea is that understanding these pathways makes it possible to design efficient diagnostics and treatments for prevention or suppression of a particular pathology.
title: Precision Medicine
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course introduces students to a sequence of topics in health sciences at the Honours and Masters level. This will complement their knowledge of corresponding topics at the postgraduate level and may aid in the construction of a research strategy for their own Honours or Masters research project.
title: Advanced Studies in Health Sciences
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course covers carbohydrate metabolism; oxidation and synthesis of fatty acids, acylglycerides and phospholipids, nucleic acid and amino acid metabolism and regulation and the influence of hormones on metabolism.
title: Metabolism
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: The recruitment and selection of the best employees is central to organisational success. Recruitment and selection policies and practices are core processes within all organisations, across all industries and irrespective of country. Success and failure of organisations can often be attributed to strengths and weaknesses with the recruitment and selection process. However, these activities need to be carried out within a legislative framework that increasingly influences our practice. This course will provide you with an understanding of the activities involved in the more complex and difficult areas of recruitment and selection, from the viewpoint of a human resource practitioner and/or business manager.
title: Recruitment and Selection
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: This course aims to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills in training and development processes. It covers learning theories and principles, design and evaluation of learning experiences, and individual, group and organisational development within particular contexts. The course focus is on the critical issues of training and skills development within society, and today's organisations as they strive to meet the changing needs of their competitive environments.
title: Developing Talent
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: Business operations have been facing several ethical and sustainable issues, impacting people and the planet around the world. As a manager, it is essential that you have a grounding in the key economic, social and environmental impacts of business and its implications for management practice and decision making. As a part of this course, you will explore ethical and sustainable business, by referring to the concepts and theories of business ethics and sustainability. You will be able to identity, analyse and resolve ethical, social and environmental issues impacting various stakeholders, such as employees, shareholders, customers, government and civil societies.
title: Creating Ethical and Sustainable Business
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: This course provides students with a framework for critical understanding the contextual, strategic and operational issues of export management. It covers the operational aspects of international trading and enhance students' ability to apply integrated discipline knowledge to formulate an export plan and to deal with practical challenges such as exporting documentation, payment methods, financing options and legal considerations. As a result, students' employability in the field of international business will be greatly improved. Whenever applicable, industry engagement, such as a field trip to the Port of Brisbane, company visit, and guest presentation will be incorporated in the course to offer students opportunities to understand the dynamic nature of international trade.
title: Export Management
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: Management Employee Relations aims to provide you with an understanding of industrial relations. It includes the roles of trade unions, the industrial tribunal system and employer associations. It places these in an historical and theoretical context that explains their present structures, activities and limitations. It will also address the contemporary approaches to workplace relations between managers, employees and unions. You will become acquainted with critical approaches to the practice of industrial relations.
title: Management Employee Relations
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: This course focuses on human behaviour within organisational contexts. It highlights the relationships among people and organisations through relevant theories and concepts that are important in obtaining critical insight into current organisational behaviour issues.
title: Organisational Behaviour and Wellbeing
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: The course is intended to provide an overview of the main issues involved in performance management, including rationales for conducting it, the costs and benefits of performance management, alternatives to it and expected as well as unintended outcomes that may emerge from it. The history of performance management is examined. Different techniques for conducting performance evaluations are critically examined, as are the links between performance evaluation and systems of remuneration and opportunities for training and promotion. Finally the role of performance evaluation in different industries and occupations is examined.
title: Managing Performance and Rewards
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: Soils and Geomorphology develops concepts and information on: geology, geomorphology and pedology introduced in the first-year course, Earth Sciences. This interdisciplinary approach provides an introduction to Australian soils and landforms and their formative process. Prior Assumed: 1044SCG Earth Systems
title: Soils and Geomorphology
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: Pedagogy Practicum is a course that addresses the development of practical skills for studio teaching. It will endeavour to respond to the stage of development and particular experience of each student. The core activity of the course is dual: teaching and observation with reflection on the pedagogical practice contained in both these activities. The program will incorporate skills and approaches for both individual and group teaching. These activities will be supervised and pedagogical communication and skills analysed and synthesised within a two hour weekly conferences.
title: Pedagogy Practicum 2
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course considers some of the chemical processes involved in water pollution. It covers topics such as toxicology, risk assessment, kinetics, sorption, biotransformation, phototransformation, redox processes, the use of stable isotopes and chemodynamics of pollutants together with potable water and wastewater treatment processes. Chemical aspects of water pollution problems of local and contemporary interest such as cyanobacteria and acid sulfate soils are examined. Chemical groups such as nutrients, PAHs and dioxins are considered with emphasis on their behaviour and mode of action. Assessment involves write up of lab work, a mid-trimester exam and an end of trimester exam. Prerequisite: Completion of 130CP and 2209ENV Environmental Chemistry. Incompatible: 3201ENV Aquatic Chemistry and Pollution.
title: Water Pollution Chemistry
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course introduces the basic chemical principles that underlie biological systems. Students will benefit from a basic understanding of mathematical and scientific concepts. Success in this course will be supported by a willingness to engage with the material, apply logical reasoning, and develop problem-solving skills. The foundation provided in this course will enable students to be able to further develop their chemistry knowledge and skills relevant to health and medical sciences in later years.
title: Chemistry of Biological Systems I
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: It is conservatively estimated that 70% of forensic mental health (FMH) clients in Australia are males of functioning intelligence who have English as their preferred language and who align themselves with the dominant Australian culture. As they comprise such a large proportion of the FMH client group, the majority of resources and interventions are targeted towards them. This then means that there are a number of minority populations within FMH, who without our intentional investment and understanding would not receive effective assessment, intervention and management. This course examines the special needs of these minority FMH groups, namely the specific needs of the elderly, adolescents, women, people with an intellectual disability, people of a different culture or language, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
title: Minority Populations in Forensic Mental Health
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course identifies, examines, and evaluates current and emerging policies and structures of the criminal justice system. It focuses on debates and problematic issues in the provision of criminal justice. Components of the system are examined in terms of fairness, justice and effectiveness. The extent to which the Australian system is effective in maintaining maximum levels of social harmony is explored. Alternative models of criminal justice are critically examined within the context of liberal-democratic society.
title: Making Sense of the Criminal Justice System
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course will examine the wider social and cultural dimensions of suicidal behaviour by introducing the topics of voluntary assisted dying, and the laws and ethics surrounding the expression of suicidal behaviour in society. It will build upon the general suicide and suicide research content delivered in 7002CSR and 7004CSR (courses located in the Graduate Certificate in Suicidology, 3382 and Master of Suicidology, 5666). In particular 7007CSR will enable students to undertake a closer examination of the wider social, legal and cultural perspectives that surround suicide and suicidal behaviour. This course will be compulsory for all students enrolled in the Master of Suicidology program and will contribute to their overall understanding of suicide as a human phenomenon.
title: Ethical and Cultural Dimensions of Suicidal Behaviour
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: Professionals work daily in interdisciplinary settings to provide care and support to clients. Each discipline has its own ethics code and regulatory frameworks, and individuals may have different ways of interpreting them. To guide professionals, this course introduces the concept of interprofessional ethics for the social, health and human services and explores its foundations in human rights, moral philosophy and ethical theory. You will confront a range of ethical dilemmas that face practitioners, including privacy, confidentiality, boundary issues, accountability, activism and social media and gain the ability to make informed and appropriate decisions in relation to these challenges, using decision-making models to take justifiable action. You will also be capable of identifying the code of ethics and regulation that governs various professional disciplines, as well as their founding principles, and then analyse and critique these codes in relation to their reliability and applicability to professional integrity. You will engage in active communication and dialogue with fellow students and others from different professional disciplines to promote a shared understanding of values and ethical perspectives. You will also explore your personal value positions and understand how they can influence your professional practice.
title: Interdisciplinary Professional Ethics
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course develops an understanding of the unique needs of youth and the roles, responsibilities and needs of those who work with them in a range of settings. Various structural and personal issues impacting on the lives of youth will be examined, as well as an analysis of current definitions, roles and functions of services for youth will be undertaken. Principles and practices underpinning program outcomes are discussed. Consideration will be given to future organisational models for the provision of services for youth.
title: Children and Youth
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: Disability inclusion is grounded in the principles of social inclusion, human rights and social justice and has an applied focus on addressing issues of inclusion. In this course, students will explore and critically analyse some of the challenges in working responsively and effectively alongside people with disabilities and their families within the context of government and community sector service delivery Some of the policy, program and service issues that students will consider include the National Disability Strategy as one of the Australian government's political/policy responses to disability, evidence-based approaches such as positive behaviour support, and examining disability equity and access issues in work, education, and housing. Through their reflections, research, analysis and scholarship, students are expected to translate and apply their learning into new knowledge and skills to assist people to "live a life worth living". Incompatible: 7006HSV Disability Process and Practice, 7006HSV Disability: The Inclusion Project.
title: Disability Inclusion
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: Workplace psychology is a component of psychology that applies psychological principles within the workplace. This course introduces psychological theories and models relevant to understanding individual and small group behaviour within an organisational context. In this course you will learn about topics such as motivation, leadership, job satisfaction, stress, organisational culture and climate, occupational safety, organisational change and teams, particularly as they relate to people within workplace settings. In this course students will develop an understanding of the field of organisational behaviour along with the application of theories, models and techniques relevant to the work environment. Prerequisites must be completed prior to enrolling in this course. It is the students' responsibility to ensure these requirements have been fulfilled.
title: Workplace Psychology
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course covers the structure and function of three major classes of biological macromolecules (carbohydrates, fats and proteins) and the metabolic pathways used for the biosynthesis and degradation of these macromolecules, including the mechanisms used for integration and regulation of these pathways. Enzymes are also covered. Note: Dual enrolment in 2005MSC and 2008MSC is ONLY permitted with approval by your Program Director
title: Biochemistry
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: Five body systems: Skeletal, Muscle, Nervous, Endocrine and Reproductive Systems are studied in this course, which integrates anatomy with physiology. The theory presented in this course is supported by practical laboratory experiences, which include the study of human cadaveric material.
title: Anatomy and Physiology Systems I
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This intermediate course will introduce students to experimental design and analysis in psychology. Building on basic experimental research and statistical concepts, material on statistical hypothesis testing (especially in the ANOVA tradition) is integrated with new material on the design of more complex experiments and on issues concerning measurement, reliability, and manipulation. Topics include: between subjects designs; between subjects analyses including confidence intervals and multiple comparisons up to factorial ANOVA; within subjects designs and analyses up to within subjects factorial ANOVA; and mixed designs and analysis using ANOVA. Prerequisites: 1003PSY Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology OR 1305AFE Business Data Analysis
Competence in using SPSS statistical software
title: Experimental Design and Analysis
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course examines strategies for changing criminal behaviour available within the correctional system, drawing particularly on psychological principles and research. The implications of the various theories of crime causation for correctional programming are considered. A review of specific rehabilitation programs, in institution and community settings, is presented. A critical assessment of the rehabilitation ideal, in terms of ethical, theoretical and practical concerns, is undertaken.
title: Rehabilitating Offenders
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: Students enrolled in the Bachelor of Information Technology or Bachelor of Computer Science with Honours undertake a detailed study, literature survey, analysis, solution, and evaluation of a selected research problem relevant to their degree. Students present the details of their work in a dissertation, seminar and if applicable, an academically assessable implemented system. Students choose a research problem in consultation with academic staff members. Prior to being admitted to an Honours program, students negotiate the supervisory arrangement with the Program Director. Students should complete 6190ICT_P1, 6190ICT_P2, 6190ICT_P3 and 6190ICT_P4 in sequential order. A grade will be assigned upon successful completion of 6190ICT_P4. This course is part one of a set of four courses. Students must submit a Department Consent Form applicable to Honours Thesis courses prior to enrolment in 6190ICT_P1.
title: Honours Thesis
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: Students enrolled in the Bachelor of Information Technology or Bachelor of Computer Science with Honours undertake a detailed study, literature survey, analysis, solution, and evaluation of a selected research problem relevant to their degree. Students present the details of their work in a dissertation, seminar and if applicable, an academically assessable implemented system. Students choose a research problem in consultation with academic staff members. Prior to being admitted to an Honours program, students negotiate the supervisory arrangement with the Program Director. Students should complete 6190ICT_P1, 6190ICT_P2, 6190ICT_P3 and 6190ICT_P4 in sequential order. A grade will be assigned upon successful completion of 6190ICT_P4. This is the final part of a set of four courses. Students must submit a Department Consent Form applicable to Honours Thesis courses prior to enrolment in 6190ICT_P4. Access form here: https://forms.office.com/r/hDnDttRWzz. The submission deadline is Friday of Week 13.
title: Honours Thesis
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: The course introduces students to the theory and practice of control systems. It discusses the basic (introductory) methods of control systems analysis and design, with emphasis on the principle of negative feedback which is the essence of operation of control systems. Engineering examples are used to introduce and illustrate the usefulness of the control systems theory and to make the students aware of this important engineering area. Assessment is by lab preliminaries and experiments, lab tests, and a final examination.
title: Control Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: The main aim of this course is to provide the student with an opportunity to pursue an in-depth study of a single topic, bringing together the wide range of skills developed in the program courses. Students will conduct research on a topic agreed between the student and the supervisor(s), to be carried over two trimesters. Assessment is based on oral presentations as well as a final dissertation. Students will be required to analyse a problem, develop solutions and make necessary decisions regarding the problem under investigation.
title: Dissertation Part 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course develops the advanced knowledge and professional judgement required to manage and lead complex projects across engineering disciplines. It draws on contemporary international standards, methods and frameworks, including the PMBOK Guide, PRINCE2, ISO 21502/ISO 31000, Agile and Scrum, and the GPM PRiSM methodology and P5 Standard for sustainability in project management. Students examine how these approaches are selected, applied and adapted in Australian practice. Across the project lifecycle (from project selection and initiation through to closeout), students critically apply and evaluate techniques for scope definition, stakeholder engagement, scheduling and resource planning, cost estimation and budgeting, risk management, and earned value performance measurement. These techniques are considered across predictive, agile and hybrid delivery approaches and from the perspectives of clients, contractors, consultants and engineers. The course emphasises the leadership, ethical, governance and sustainability responsibilities of project managers. Learning is grounded in Australian and international case studies and applied problem-solving that reflects professional project practice.
title: Project Management
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

Students will conduct research on a topic agreed between the student and the supervisor(s), to be carried over two trimesters. Assessment is based on oral presentations as well as a final dissertation. Students will be required to analyse a problem, develop solutions and make necessary decisions regarding the problem under investigation.

description: This course introduces students to the process of structural design including: dealing with a client and defining a design brief, load estimation, elementary structural analysis and the design of timber and steel members and connections using the relevant Australian Standard design codes.
title: Structural Design
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course mainly covers the analysis and design of reinforced and prestressed concrete structural elements. Both strength and serviceability design requirements are covered. Problem solving exercises based on actual design situations are utilised extensively in this course. After completing this course students will be able to analyse and design structural concrete elements and structures. Assessment is by, tutorial and design assignments, and examinations.
title: Concrete Structures
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: Safe, reliable, and sustainable access to energy technology is a crucial element of modern society - one we can no longer take for granted. The world must find new ways to reduce energy wastage, and energy use in general, through the development and application of sophisticated electrical engineering technology. This course will build on your existing knowledge of electromagnetic fields and propagating systems, as well as electric circuits, to explore theory underlying a variety of energy technologies and the ways in which they can be harnessed and utilised to improve efficiency and adaptability of energy systems at the domestic and industrial level. These lessons include laboratory experiences, giving you a hands-on introduction to various energy topics including utilisation and energy harvesting. You will also build your research and analytical thinking skills with a state-of-the-art review paper, which will help you to improve your academic writing abilities and teamwork capabilities, while examining current and future trends in energy efficiency. At the conclusion of the course, you'll be prepared to implement each of the energy efficiency solutions explored during your classes, as well as having the knowledge, confidence, and problem-solving skills to optimise a business that utilises such technologies.
title: Efficient Energy Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course covers fundamental topics in power transmission and distribution, including distributed energy generation, transmission lines, voltage control, power factor correction and energy storage systems. It also includes various high voltage equipment used in substations, and future distributed power systems, such as smart grid technology and renewable energy systems. It is strongly recommended that students have prior knowledge of 1301ENG (Electric Circuits). Historical evidence indicates that students who lack this foundational understanding, specifically in Circuit Theory, Thevenin Equivalent networks, superposition theorem, often struggle to pass the course. Incompatible: 3319ENG Power Transmission and Distribution AND 3314ENG Power Distribution and Storage.
title: Energy Storage and Power Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course provides an overview of major natural and synthetic pollutants existing in the environment and a practical foundation in environmental monitoring and assessment (with a focus on water quality). The sources, fate and effects of key pollutants on environmental and human health will be covered, including important physicochemical and physical processes that influence chemical speciation, transport and toxicity. Finally, the principles of toxicological risk assessment and its contribution to the establishment of water quality guidelines will provide the necessary background to effectively design, interpret and report on chemical monitoring data.
title: Environmental Pollution
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: 7001PHM Pharmacotherapeutics I provides an introduction to the role of the pharmacist in the management of gastrointestinal, ophthalmic, respiratory and cardiac conditions. The course outlines the clinical context and therapeutic management of these conditions, and overviews relevant laboratory tests and their interpretation. Furthermore, the course introduces principles of Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM). Case-based workshops serve to develop students' practical clinical skills for the promotion of and contribution to optimal use of medicines in relation to the therapeutic areas covered.
title: Pharmacotherapeutics I
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: Specialised Dosage Forms II (7007PHM) builds on the knowledge gained in the pharmaceutical studies in MPharm and BPharmTox. The course covers aseptic technique, sterile products, cytotoxics and specialised delivery systems in human and veterinary applications. The course utilises didactic, practical, tutorial, self-directed learning and on-line resources for content delivery.
title: Specialised Dosage Forms II
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: The dissertation is the culmination of students' training in the fundamental sciences and professional practice of pharmacy. Qualitative and quantitative research projects serve to address topical issues relating to the practice of pharmacy (e.g. quality use of medicines; pharmacoeconomics; pharmacy management; social aspects of pharmacy; rational prescribing; drug utilisation etc.) and specific research topics within the health sciences (pharmacology; pharmaceutics; pharmacogenomics; medicinal chemistry; pharmacognosy; molecular biology etc). Students work with an experienced academic supervisor/s within and external to the School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences who maintains regular contact and provides support and direction in the design and execution of the dissertation.
title: Dissertation
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

Students work with an experienced academic supervisor/s within and external to the School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences who maintains regular contact and provides support and direction in the design and execution of the dissertation.
title: Dissertation
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course introduces students to the principles and practice of policy evaluation. How do we know if public policies are working as intended? How can we distinguish policy success from policy failure? How can we capture unintended consequences? This course addresses these questions and more by exploring a range of approaches to policy evaluation. Students have the opportunity to develop an understanding of key tools including program logic models, evaluation methods, and approaches for determining causality. The course considers the important distinctions between policy outputs and outcomes, and how to measure these outcomes. Evaluation is situated within a democratic context, by engaging with theories on citizen engagement, democratic values and trust in public institutions. As part of the course, students design, plan and conduct a program evaluation, developing skills in research, communication and critical analysis. The course provides a toolkit for evidence-based policymaking and highlights the important role of evaluation within the broader policy process.
title: Evaluating Policy and Measuring Performance
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

title: Exchange Studies - Undergraduate
academicOrgDescription: Griffith International

description: This sequence of courses involves the identification of a research topic, the development of a research proposal to address that topic, the undertaking of the proposed research project, and its reporting in a dissertation. Where relevant, candidates will also obtain ethical clearance for the proposed project.
title: Dissertation 4
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course is an applied skills-oriented course. The aim of this course is to provide you with the opportunity to develop your mastery of the generic interpersonal communication skills necessary for building and maintaining effective working and personal relationships, and managing interpersonal interactions and change. In addition, you will be introduced to skills which are the "building blocks" for more advanced skills that you may use in future professional roles such as Consultant, Counsellor, Lawyer, Manager, Psychologist, Public Health practitioner or Social Worker.
title: Interpersonal Skills
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course will assist students to identify how their values and beliefs impact on their ability to recognise and assist individual and family issues. Students will have the opportunity to revise and utilise their microskills and to plan some preliminary intervention strategies. This course requires compulsory attendance during a one-week intensive for the Gold Coast offering (intended for students enrolled in the external/distance offerings of Human Services and Social Work programs)
title: Counselling Individuals and Families
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: Engaging social justice and human rights perspectives, this course critically analyses the various historical, political, institutional and social forces that have shaped welfare and health policies and practices for Indigenous Australian peoples.
title: First Peoples and Social Justice
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This Honours level core course examines professional, ethical, and legal issues in psychology. It is workshop based and designed to introduce key competencies required in the profession. Workshops provide opportunities to examine research based applications of the core content to a selected area of psychology.
title: Professional Psychology B
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: Griffith University Innocence Project students, acting under the supervision of the Director and Convenor of the Project, and on instructions from the associated lawyers, review cases where a person is claiming to have been wrongly convicted of a criminal offence. Students may also undertake research activities associated with the case review. All professional case-management decisions are the responsibility of the lawyers involved. NOTE: Information on application process is available at the LLB and JD Organisation sites on Learning@Griffith. Preference will be given to Juris Doctor and Bachelor of Laws students who have completed: 7719LAW Crime 1 OR 2019LAW Crime 1 OR 4032LAW The Principles of Criminal Law; 7720LAW Crime 2 OR 2020LAW Crime 2 OR 4031LAW Criminal Procedure and Sentencing; and who have completed or are currently undertaking, 7794LAW Evidence OR 5194LAW Evidence OR 4022LAW Evidence.
title: Innocence Project Clinic
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course continues the work begun in Musical Theatre 1 and 2. The acquisition and development of Acting, Speech, Singing and Dance techniques are interdependent elements in a process that culminates in a Performance Project, a learning opportunity consisting of a short 'Classical Book Musical' performance presented simply, to an audience of tutors and fellow students. This course continues the development of the student's potential as a musical theatre performer as fully as possible, through individual tuition in singing and class tuition in acting, dance, voice and speech and through master classes, workshops, seminars and public performances.
title: Musical Theatre 3
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course covers a range of projects in studio and live pre-production, recording and postproduction, including contexts for games, film and on-air broadcast. This course Includes Work Integrated Learning (WIL) engagements as part of the core learning and teaching. Coverage includes advanced mic and recording techniques not done elsewhere (for studio and for live), post-production and mix workflows, and more advanced work with EQ, compression and reverb with awareness of film, TV, radio, online and other generalist post-graduation employment opportunities. This is all done with emphasis on live-capture of events in conjunction with "clients", where client-based contact is mentored and guided. The course leverages Con events as well as special events that may occur during a semester, and learning is done in-situ as well as in the classroom. The course is intended to provide invaluable experience in working outside the confines of a studio for event-based contexts. While Con events cover a range of genres, content covered in the course is equally pertinent for pop, electronic, experimental, film, games, and acoustic music contexts.
title: Concert Recording
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course will challenge both the students' musical and technical skills and help prepare them for the rigorous demands of the profession. This course provides an opportunity for students to extend themselves in the ensembles space by selecting extended ensemble/collaborative activities to participate in beyond 3551QCM (Ensembles and Collaborative Activity 3C), depending on their specialisation and interests.
title: Ensemble and Collaborative Activity 3D
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: Honours Research Project constitutes a 40CP honours research commitment within the Honours Programs. Each of the four components of the course combine to introduce students to the rigors of research and engage them in an advanced level of study within visual practice. The expectation is that the research project undertaken will be based within the visual and incorporates high levels of visual literacy. Assessment of the four courses will culminate in one assessment item. Honours Research Project is presented for assessment in a professional context at the completion of all four courses. PRE-REQUISITE: 6301QCA_P1, 6301QCA_P3. CO-REQUISITIE: 6301QCA_P3 (this course can be completed prior to or at the same time as completing 6301QCA_P4).
title: Honours Research Project
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: Dissertation Project constitutes a 40CP research commitment. The course is divided into four 10CP components. Each component combines to introduce students to the rigors of research and engage them in an advanced level of study within visual practice. The Dissertation will consist of a major research project accompanied by an exegesis of 5000 words (min). The expectation is that the research project will be based within the visual and incorporates high levels of visual literacy. Assessment of the four courses will culminate in a single submission for examination.
title: Dissertation Project
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course in stop-motion animation covers both fabrication (puppets and sets) and character animation, informed by a critical evaluation of the technique's unique attributes: tactility, space and performance.
title: Stop Motion
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Film School

description: This course provides an introduction to art practices from a range of cultures and periods. Students will gain an understanding of key art historical and theoretical concepts as well as the social, cultural, political and religious contexts for art.
title: Visual Analysis and Critical Reflection
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: In Constructional Systems, students develop an architectural proposition of medium scale and a high degree of complexity where formal composition and layout are developed in concertation with structural and technological requirements. Students are guided through the process of critically exploring construction as an expressive and creative tool. A holistic view of the built design process is put forth. Students will research architectural exemplars to inform design decisions, encompassing their proposals' conceptual and compositional aspects. Prerequisite: 7009ENG - Research by Practice Workshop 2.
title: Advanced Architecture Studio 1 - Construction Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment
