Prerequisite: Student must have completed 80CP and have gained a GPA of 4.5 or higher. Enquiries are to be directed to the Course Convenor.
title: Work Integrated Learning Special Topic
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course explores how and why theory is used in the humanities. Students are introduced to a range of classical and contemporary social and cultural theories and the debates that surround them via a focus on some of the key concerns and facets related to the production of knowledge and identity.
title: Thinking with Theory
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: GLEAM Internship offers students Work Integrated Learning experiences centered in Galleries, Libraries, Visual Arts Events, Archives and Museums. Students will work closely with professional organisations and individuals to learn new skills in gallery management, administration and communications. This course is particularly suited to those students wishing to develop careers in arts administration, curatorship, and management.
title: Galleries, Libraries, Events. Archives and Museums Internships
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course considers how public international law applies to state-sponsored cyber operations in peacetime. Students should have a basic understanding of what public international law is. Students will analyse and apply the law in relation to case studies and hypothetical problems involving cyber operations, but no prior technical knowledge about cyber operations is required.
title: Cyber International Law
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course focusses on the application of innovative new technologies across the supply chain network. Currently, for-profit and non-for-profit businesses are increasingly using new technologies to simultaneously improve efficiency and deliver flexibility across supply chains. Specifically, this unit discusses the application of artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, automation, big data and internet of things (IoT), as well as the use and result interpretation of optimisation packages for supply chain management.
title: Supply Chain Innovation and Optimisation
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: This course includes placement activities, within the practice of Psychology, external to Griffith University. External placements are selected and designed to provide students with rich and varied learning opportunities and experiences in clinical psychology. As part of each external placement students will complete a minimum of 120-140 hours of client contact and 40 hours of clinical supervision. Prior to completing an external placement, students are required to have successfully completed the Practicums 1A/B and 2A/B, which provide intensive training and supervision within the Psychology Clinics at Griffith University. Incompatibilities: 8183PSY_P1, 8183PSY_P2, 8183PSY.
title: Practicum 3
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course aims to supplement and support students' learning from external placements to further develop students' professional identity and deepen their understanding of professional and ethical conduct. Through participation in practicum classes, students will relate their knowledge to broader practice of clinical psychology.
title: Advanced Professional Practice
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: Advancing technologies, including AI and augmented/extended reality, ethical and regulatory issues such as data privacy and protection, and increased expectations on corporate brands in social leadership and sustainability require marketers to be responsive to rapid change. Designed to introduce marketing professionals to emergent areas of importance, Marketing Futures aims to inspire students to develop future-focused marketing ideas and strategies.
title: Marketing Futures
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: Domestic and family violence is a pressing social issue with significant implications for individuals, couples, families, communities and societies. It makes up a large portion of cases in justice, health, and social systems in Australia and around the world. This course provides students with a critical understanding of the dynamics, distribution, outcomes, and responses to domestic and family violence. Students will learn about key topics such as coercive control, how children are involved in domestic and family violence, and gender and intersectional social categories and domestic violence. Students will gain critical research literacy skills to interpret key data sources on domestic and family violence. Students will practice skills to effectively and accurately communicate complex information about domestic and family violence. WARNING: The content of this course could be triggering for some students. If this is the case, please contact your Program Director to organise an alternative course.
title: Understanding Domestic and Family Violence
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course will survey Hollywood cinema from its beginnings through the present, considering Hollywood in terms of its industrial, technological and economic development; its aesthetic priorities and influences; its social and cultural contexts. Students must have completed 40CP of any UGRD subjects.
title: Hollywood: From the Nickelodeon to Netflix
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: The Integrated Brain examines how neural systems work together to support human cognition, behaviour, and health, drawing on contemporary neuroscience concepts such as the connectome and circuit-level integration. Students engage with interactive digital resources, case-based workshops, and emerging technologies including AI to explore how brain architecture shapes function and how disruptions lead to neurological disease. The course develops a cohesive, future-focused understanding of the brain that aligns with Griffith's commitment to innovation, translational learning, and real-world application.
title: The Integrated Brain
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: Students will engage in professional development on various contemporary topics in higher education, including the scholarship of learning and teaching. Informed by a skills audit and environmental analysis, students will identify an L&T project appropriate to their context.
title: Contemporary Issues in Higher Education 1
academicOrgDescription: Centre for Collaborative Educational Excellence

description: This capstone course provides a work-integrated learning opportunity to apply knowledge and skills garnered throughout the program to develop projects and media outputs that focus on communication solutions to address social, environmental, and other issues of concern. Prerequisites: 2513LHS Media Law AND must have completed 2505LHS Ethical Communication OR must have completed 2501LHS Public Relations Theory, Ethics and Professional Practice OR must have completed 2511LHS News Writing and Ethics; Incompatible: 3503LHS Communication for Social and Environmental Change Project
title: Communication for Social and Environmental Responsibility
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course provides knowledge and skills in the development of professional social media and considers theory and practice to take advantage of the opportunities of social media while navigating the risks that come with the terrain.Prerequisites: NIL; Incompatible: 3521LHS Social Media for Global Communicators
title: Social Media for Global Communication
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course introduces the fundamentals of musical improvisation across a variety of genres, including jazz, contemporary, and modern classical music. Operating as a practical musical laboratory, the class prioritizes hands-on experience through solo, small group, and large ensemble performances. Students will develop their creative skills by exploring diverse techniques, ranging from traditional chord progressions and melodic motifs to experimental methods like graphic scores and nature-based improvisation. The curriculum utilizes collaborative learning strategies such as group listening, call-and-response exercises, and improvising alongside significant recordings. Additionally, the course bridges the gap between theory and practice by examining significant historical works, encouraging students to use the traditions of the past to inform their own contemporary musical voices.
title: Topics in Improvisation
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course develops your understanding of how sustainable arts projects and enterprises are ideated and established within the current Australian and Global Arts context. Through the learning activities and assessment experience you will acquire useful industry support skills and knowledges, understand how to successfully acquit your own creative projects and enterprise, plus gain further insight to the systems and processes that exist within the music industry.
title: Music Enterprise and Professional Practice
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: Contemporary Creative Practices 2 builds on knowledge and skills from Contemporary Creative Practices 1, continuing exploration of the creation and realisation of music alongside traditional and emerging instruments/technologies. Practical teaching includes iterative demonstrations of techniques and contexts, along with mentoring, instruction, discussion, and feedback from peers and staff.
title: Contemporary Creative Practices 2
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This subject focuses on policing in Australia. It commences with its historical development, including the impact of the English tradition. This is followed by an analysis of a variety of organisational issues and an examination of a range of operational strategies of policing.
title: Introduction to Policing
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course focuses on primary teachers' professional knowledge of language, literacy, and literature as a foundation for learning across the curriculum. It begins by exploring how primary teachers use the learning and teaching cycle to make professional judgements and plan for elements of reading instruction to accommodate diverse learners including: phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, comprehension and oral language and explicit teaching of reading and writing in subjects other than English. To do this effectively, beginning teachers need to develop skills relating to the effective use of student data, including how to read, moderate, interpret and then employ this data to enhance the learning and teaching process.
title: Research Informed Teaching of Reading for Diverse Learners
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: Building on knowledge of human behaviour, basic counselling skills and processes, as well as case conceptualisation, students will be introduced to the processes and techniques of postmodern therapies including Narrative Therapy and Solution Focused Therapy. Students will participate in activities that will prepare them for counselling work with people experiencing a variety of complexities including social and personal difficulties, and will develop skills in effectively working with a diverse range of clients using narrative and solution focused strategies in their work. Corequisite: Students must be enrolled in corequisite 3015PSY
title: Counselling Development 2
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course prepares students for employment across criminology and criminal justice settings by developing professional awareness, practical insight, and reflective capacity. Students will identify the diverse skills and attributes required in roles relating to the discipline of criminology. Emphasis is placed on inclusive engagement, ethical practice, and culturally responsive approaches when working with diverse individuals and communities. Through structured reflection and applied activities, students will critically examine their own values, strengths, and areas for growth, enabling them to articulate a clear professional identity and targeted development plan aligned with contemporary criminology and criminal justice careers.
title: Developing Professionally 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course equips students with essential legal writing skills required for success in the study of law. The course introduces students to different types of legal writing including essays, legal problem-solving, client letters, and memoranda. The course focuses on building students' understanding of how to write logically and clearly, and to differentiate between different aspects of writing including descriptive content and critical analysis. The course also embeds the requirements for proper academic referencing and the acceptable use of artificial intelligence in both academic and professional contexts. Students will learn to write effectively for varied legal audiences and understand the ethical importance of precise, stakeholder-appropriate legal communication.
title: Legal Writing
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course introduces tourism and destination marketing. The course includes a broad range of topics that range from destination branding to the challenges facing national and regional destination marketing organisations.
title: Destination Marketing
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This course is a community-engaged learning opportunity exploring the importance and development of legally specific Cultural Intelligence skills, capabilities, and modes of inquiry. This is a work-integrated learning approach to respectful and informed engagement with the First Nations community, in the context of access to legal certainty and real Justice. Difference not deficit underpins every aspect of this clinical engagement. The CPP Unit covers critical inquiry of bias and conditioning, ethical lawyering, legacy relationships, positive otherness, and moral injury. The course seeks to apply trauma-informed approaches to First Nations realities (including Human Rights). First Nation's communications approaches are key components of the client collateral the CPP participants are tasked to develop over the 12-week course. Attendance, in person at each class is a mandatory requirement (and necessary to pass this unit). No classes are available or recorded for online access. Students must also attend two Field Trips to Cherbourg Aboriginal Community.
title: Culturally Principled Practice Clinic
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: The course will provide students with statistical and data-analytic tools applicable to problems in business, finance, and economics.
title: Business Analytics and Quantitative Tools
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course is a 10 Credit Point course within the Masters Qualifying Program. It introduces students to the study of Management within organisations. An integrated view of both theory and practice will be examined pointing out applications of social science and implications for management action. An analysis in which organisational performance through a better understanding of effective management of people will also be studied investigating important issues such as an increased awareness of, and sensitivity to, personal skills and employability within a context of globalisation and the need for economic, socio-cultural and environmental sustainability.
title: Managing Organisations
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: This course introduces students to the practices, techniques and forms of contemporary poetry. Students will explore a range of poetic forms and styles, will learn the core techniques of writing poetry, and will respond to a range of prompts and provocations that invite them to produce their own original poetry. In this course, students will develop their understanding of 20th and 21st century poetry and poetics through weekly readings and writing activities, and will consider the role of poetry in contemporary society. Students will develop original poems reflecting their own interests and influences in a supportive environment, responding to feedback as they enhance their skills in using poetic techniques.
title: Writing Poetry
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course facilitates student involvement in a structured Work Integrated Learning (WIL) placement related to their studies under the guidance of an academic supervisor. Students will couple their practical experience with critical reflection on industry practice and standards relevant to their degree and majors.
title: Industry Internship 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course covers advance economic theories and models in the context of a small open economy framework with topics relevant to understanding and working of open economies. The aim of the course is to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of characterization of open economies and implications of this on modern global macroeconomic outcomes/issues.
title: Open Economy Macroeconomics
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: Business and Company Law provides an introduction to the legal framework governing business activities in Australia and offers students a foundational understanding of Australian business law and company law. The course introduces the Australian legal system, with particular emphasis on the primary sources of law, the roles of courts and legislatures. It examines key areas of law relevant to business, including contract law, data protection and privacy law, Australian Consumer Law, the law of negligence and partnership law. The course also focuses on company law, corporate governance, accounts, auditing and financial reporting and corporate insolvency. Through practical examples and case studies, students will develop the ability to identify legal issues, apply relevant sections of legislation and case law and understand how the law affects business activities and commercial decision-making. The knowledge gained in this course will be invaluable throughout students' careers, particularly in fulfilling their business and professional responsibilities. Incompatible: 2105AFE Introduction to Business Law.
title: Business and Company Law
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: Students develop the basis of a working knowledge for the German language with a specific emphasis on aural comprehension and pronunciation in musical repertoire and literature.
title: German for Musicians
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This subject introduces students into the tax consequences of many investments that individuals in Australia may make. This course primarily considers the tax outcomes from the individual's perspective, such as the receipt of dividends, rental properties, sale of investment assets and superannuation.
title: Taxation Law
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course is only available to students enrolled in a Master of Science program offered through the School of Environment and Science. Students will undertake a research project relevant to their area of specialisation under the guidance of one or more supervisors within the School. The topic and nature of the Research Project will be determined through consultation and mutual agreement of the student and supervisor/s and approved by the Program Director. The project will involve original research and will be under the direct supervision of an academic staff member. Assessment will comprise a written report of the work, prepared in the form of a thesis submitted for examination and a seminar defending the work. The thesis is expected to be no longer than 60,000 words in length.
title: Dissertation
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: In this block, learners explore how young children learn and develop from birth to age 8 with a focus on early mathematical thinking, early language and literacy, and the broader developmental needs of children in the early years. Learners will engage with inclusive and developmentally appropriate practices, examine the role of play in learning, and consider how to create engaging and responsive learning environments. Learners begin to shape their teacher identity by reflecting on their values, beliefs, and approach to supporting diverse learners.
title: Early Years of Primary Education
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: Successful marketing decisions require a sound understanding of consumer behaviour, whether in the context of commercial firms, non-profit organisations, or government departments. This course provides you with a thorough appreciation of the complexities of consumer decision-making to ensure that your future marketing decisions achieve your objectives in your target market.
title: Consumer Psychology
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This introductory course to human geography explores how the places that people inhabit are filled with culturally- and ecologically-specific experiences and phenomena. We explore how global, regional and local issues influence how humans understand their relationships with the environments in which they live, and how large-scale processes such as migration and globalisation interact with regional and local framings to influence our experiences of a place. We also take a critical look at patterns of global mobility to explore how we might conceptualise through frameworks of, and place-based approaches to, justice, diversity and fairness.
title: People, Place and Diversity
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course includes placement activities, within the practice of Psychology, that may be internal and/or external to Griffith University. description: The Work Integrated Learning (WIL) course provides students unique placement and learning opportunities in contemporary healthcare facilities with health leaders and managers. The aim of WIL is to provide students with the opportunity to translate the knowledge and skills learned in the postgraduate program into practice in the context of the workplace. This translation will occur with support from an academic and a workplace supervisor. This experience will allow the student to develop further the necessary attributes, skills and competencies expected in a health service management postgraduate professional. It is available to students enrolled in the Master of Health Services Management (5586) (120CP) and the Advanced Master of Health Services Management program (5627) (160CP) programs. This course has two parts, each worth 20 credit points. Students must complete both parts in the same trimester when studying full-time or in two consecutive trimesters if pursuing part-time to complete the course. This course is offered in Trimester 1 and 2 only. Part-time option: This course is available to students enrolled part-time; however, it must be completed in two consecutive trimesters in which WIL is offered (20 credit points each trimester) if students take the part-time option. This option is only available for students starting WIL in Trimester 1. Due to individualised placement and/or Visa requirements for international students, the part-time option requires approval from the WIL course convenor and the Program Director. The WIL course convenor and the Program Director will consider student preferences, industry partner preferences, and where applicable, student Visa requirements before approving the part-time option. Students wishing to take WIL within their employing organisation may do so. However, students must complete work-based learning and a project that supports students to achieve the aims and outcomes of the WIL course. Enrolment doesn't guarantee placement. To secure placement students must contact hsmplacements@griffith.edu.au
title: Work Integrated Learning Part 2

description: Abstraction is one of the most important and original developments in twentieth-century art. This course traces the emergence of abstraction in Europe in the early part of the century (Wassily Kandinsky, Piet Mondrian, Kazimir Malevich, Katarzyna Kobro, Wladslaw Strzeminski) through to the deadpan literalism of American minimalism in the 1960s and artists such as Frank Stella, Robert Morris, Donald Judd and Carl Andre. South American abstraction will also be examined, kinetic artists from Venezuela and Argentinas such as Jesus Soto and Julio Le Parc, as well as the development of a particular form of organic geometric abstraction in Brazil in the late 1950s and 1960s Neoconcretism. We will examine artists' writings and manifestoes, where they articulate their aims and intentions, as well as considering key interpretations of abstract art by critics and art historians. Topics to be examined include: spiritual versus literal accounts of abstraction; various languages of abstraction (expressionism, constructivism, concretism, biomorphic); genres of abstract painting (the monochrome, the achrome); and historical movements centering on abstraction (Suprematism, Russian Constructivism, Group Zero, Unism, Spatialism, Kinetic Art, Abstract Expressionism, Brazilian Neo-concretism, Colour Field Painting, Minimalism).
title: Abstraction
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: Mechanical engineers need to possess sound understanding of the physics of the design and use of machine elements such as gears, cams, springs, pulleys, joints etc., that are used in engineered components. This design process is deeply enshrined in established design standards/codes that all engineers should be knowledgeable of. 3511ENG Design of Machine Elements is aimed at integrating and applying prior knowledge in fundamental design, materials sciences, statics and dynamics coupled with design strategies and knowledge of machine elements to design various machines. These skills and knowledge help engineers to design, analyse, synthesize and deliver robust engineering solutions. The main learning outcome of this unit is the students' acquisition of strong analytical knowledge of machine elements, their design and load carriage/power transmission mechanics. This course will be delivered through a combination of specially developed lectures, design problem solving methods, case studies and hands-on design assignments' all rolled together into workshops. description: This course introduces the principles and practice of distributed programming. It examines programming models used in distributed and multiprocessor systems, including processes, threads, shared memory, and message passing. Students study synchronization mechanisms such as locks, semaphores, monitors, and non-blocking techniques to coordinate concurrent activities. The course explores correctness properties of distributed programs, including safety, liveness, mutual exclusion, deadlock, and starvation. Classical algorithms and multiprocessor synchronization techniques are analyzed to understand how reliable and efficient distributed systems are designed. Through programming assignments and practical exercises, students implement and evaluate distributed programs, developing the ability to reason about correctness and performance in distributed environments.
title: Distributed Programming
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

The theory of computation is the core area of computer science that attempts to achieve deep understanding of computational processes by means of mathematical models, tools, and techniques. It is important for algorithm, compiler and VLSI design, the creation of intelligent systems, and cognitive psychology. This course aims to provide generic skills and concept tools that practitioners use in computer engineering. For instance, grammars studied in this course are useful in dealing with strong searching and pattern matching. Studying this course significantly helps in training generic abilities to think and to solve computational problems. This course was previously known as 3825ICT Theory of Computing and is incompatible with 3825ICT Theory of Computation.

academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course will examine the history and theories of portraiture. A diverse range of images will be discussed from Egyptian funerary portraits through to modern and contemporary likenesses. Alongside large oil paintings and monumental sculpture, the course will include the study of coins, miniatures, silhouettes, photographs, prints and caricatures. The major figures in the history of Western portraiture, such as Van Eyck, Hals, Velásquez, Holbein, Goya, Gainsborough, Cassatt and Kahlo will all be included. The course also utilises local collections and includes the study of Australian portraiture. A range of challenging concerns and issues will be addressed: such as likeness and authenticity; memory and commemoration; identity and the projection of self; portraiture and its relationship to class, race, sexuality and gender. We will also explore the curatorial and exhibition practices surrounding portraiture, especially the formation and role of National Portrait Galleries and the popularity of portrait prizes. Prerequisites: 1216QCA Introduction to Theory 1 AND 1217QCA Introduction to Theory 2
title: Art of Portraiture: History and Theory
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

academicOrgDescription: Griffith International

description: This course builds on 'The Emerging Journalist' to introduce students to longer forms of journalism such as news features, in-depth features and profile writing, and provides students with the skills set to package feature or profile pieces for publication.
title: Beyond Hard News: Writing for Longer Formats
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course brings public relations and strategic communications to life through focusing on three key areas: politics, government, and corporate / not-for-profit sectors. Students will be presented with advanced information about these three areas, and the central role that strategic communications takes within them. Given this is an advanced strategic communications course, students are expected to possess the knowledge and skills necessary to know the basics of communication. This course will build on their already growing skillset in strategic communications, and get them to think critically - while also design - the 'why' and 'how' behind strategy. As such, most of this course's assessment is drawn from students' practical application of acquired knowledge and skills that are then applied to either a political, government, or business case study.
title: Communication Campaigns and Strategies
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course introduces students to Australian literature as a field of study connected to and intersecting with questions of Australian national history, culture, and identity. Students will encounter a dynamic range of Australian texts, including novels, short stories, personal essays, graphic narratives, and literary criticism, that capture the vitality and direction of Australian writing and publishing more broadly. Through close engagement with these texts, students will develop and practise transferrable skills such as critical reading, comprehension, and interpretation in order to reflect on and better understand the role Australian literature plays in addressing political, social, ecological, and cultural issues and/or debates.
title: Contemporary Australian Literature
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: They say systematic desensitisation is the cure for all phobias. In this course, you will be 'desensitised' to statistics through a practical and down-to-earth approach that minimises the mathematics and maximises the applications. We will concentrate on what can be done with statistics to solve social problems and describe communities. To do so, the course describes the construction, evaluation, administration, and analysis of survey-based data. This course prepares you for many rewarding career paths: government policy, data analyst, applied researcher, customer insights and marketing professional, and community program developer/evaluator, just to name a few. Students will benefit from a wealth of learning resources, including: lectures, tutorials, online reference videos from practicing social scientists and statisticians, contemporary readings, and summary materials to review each week. The course is organised around a problem or question-centred model, with a focus on how to use statistics to solve real-world issues and discover data-driven insights.
title: Social Data Analytics
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course comprises of an 8-week project-based placement aimed at planning, implementing and/or evaluating a community nutrition program that considers the local food system to improve the health of groups and/or communities. Students will be evaluated against the Dietitians Australia National Competency Standards for Dietitians in Australia (2021).
title: Food Systems Placement
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course builds the academic and practical skills you need to succeed at university. You'll strengthen your critical thinking and problem-solving abilities while developing academic literacy skills such as research, referencing and writing. You'll also gain confidence with digital tools and everyday maths, giving you a strong foundation for further study and your future career.
title: Foundations for University Success
academicOrgDescription: EmpowerED

description: This block establishes a technical and conceptual foundation in ICT by focusing on how systems are designed, and how data is structured and managed. Students explore the principles and tools that underpin modern information systems, gaining practical experience with databases and application frameworks.
title: Designing Application Systems and Databases
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: This is a capstone course which offers students nearing graduation the opportunity to synthesise and apply learning to enhance general employability knowledge and skills. This course is relevant to a range of employment contexts including clinical, counselling, health, education, forensic, leisure, organisational, professional and community settings. In this course you will learn about key constructs, principles and processes of human behaviour change, with topics related to multi-level influences of behaviour; nonadherence and motivation; behaviour change functions and techniques; intervention design and evaluation, and ethical and cultural issues. The course covers individual-, organisational- and settings/population-level approaches to understanding and changing human behaviour. By the end of the course, you will have practical frameworks for understanding and changing behaviour, and have applied these to prepare a written proposal including a needs analysis and behaviour change intervention and evaluation plan in your area of interest. PREREQUISITES: Student must complete 160 credit points including 120 credit points of core psychology courses. Students enrolled in the Behavioural Science major in B Business and B Commerce programs, who commenced their degree prior to 2024, must have completed the Business Foundation year and are exempt from the above prerequisites.
title: Behaviour Change Skills
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course introduces students to a variety of Light Aircraft Systems, and builds on their aircraft general knowledge. This course will also assist in the practical aviation environment, by having a thorough and broad knowledge of different Light Aircraft Systems in accordance with the CASA CPL Aeronautical knowledge syllabus. Note: Incompatible with 2503BPS/2503NSC Light Aircraft Systems
title: Light Aircraft Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: In this course students in groups will undertake a research project, gather and analyse data, document the project and present the findings. Pre-requisite: Students must have successfully completed all preceding years courses to progress to year 2 (commonly known as year 5).
title: Research Project
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: Research typically involves the collection of data and subsequent statistical analysis. Good research, which enables valid conclusions, requires consideration of experimental design, data collection, data visualisation, and appropriate statistical analysis. This course presents some common approaches to these issues, as they apply in Science. Through the completion of a project, students experience all aspects of the quantitative process from question definition and initial exploratory data analysis, through formal statistical inference, its interpretation in terms of an original research question, and the implications of underlying assumptions and resulting limitations. The use of statistical software enables real experiences of data management and analysis. (This course was previously known as 2291ENV Experimental Design and Statistics and is incompatible with 2291ENV Experimental Design and Statistics)
title: Applied Data Science
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course provides the registered nurse with the knowledge and skills required to care for high acuity patients in a variety of clinical settings. The physiological, psychological and social needs of the acutely ill patient are presented.
title: Management of High Acuity Clients
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: This course is designed to enable students to develop structures and processes required to successfully design or reorientate current maternity service provision within a primary maternity care focus. Students will have the opportunity to examine and evaluate innovative models of publicly funded maternity care and private midwifery practice. Students will have the opportunity to explore drivers and barriers to the sustainability of primary maternity care in the context of their professional / discipline backgrounds and the nation in which they practice.
title: Changing Childbirth: Service Design and Implementation
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: Provide the support women and their newborns need to successfully start and sustain breastfeeding. Guided by the Baby Friendly Health Initiative Framework, you will explore factors that impact successful initiation, establishment and maintenance of the mother-infant breastfeeding relationship. Develop skills in critical analysis, evaluation of current practices and proactive strategies to support women to overcome breastfeeding challenges and achieve their goals. A key lesson is the impact of formula feeding on the infant, mother and community, including the importance of support for women who decide not to breastfeed. Additionally, you'll study anatomy, physiology, and the physical and psychological aspects of lactation to enable sustained breastfeeding relationships post birth. Whether you work in social work, public health, or as a midwife or advanced practice nurse, this course, with its focus on interprofessional education, will ensure you can provide the best care to mothers across a range of contexts. The knowledge and skills gained include empathetic communication, engagement and collaboration that will enable you to facilitate best practice healthcare and support for infants and their mothers managing breastfeeding and lactation.
title: Advanced Breastfeeding and Lactation
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: This course provides opportunities for pre-service teachers to acquire a developed understanding of the relationship between reading, language and literacy teaching in the Australian Curriculum: English with an emphasis on the needs of students with English as an additional language or dialect (AL/D).
title: Teaching Reading to students with English as an Additional Language/Dialect (AL/D)
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course will introduce students to the profession of occupational therapy and the concept of occupation. Students will begin to develop their knowledge of occupation as the organising construct of occupational therapy. Students will be introduced to occupation, its relationship to health, occupation as a vehicle for living a meaningful life and asserting identity.
title: Occupation and Occupational Therapy I
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: New business ventures typically start with no recognised brand name, no customers and no market reputation. Without a strong brand and effective promotion the new venture is likely to fail. One of the key challenges for new ventures is to create awareness of their business offering, and to build customer interest in the new business enterprise. Potential customers must be converted to actual customers by building their desire to purchase the new venture's product or service. This course provides an introductory smorgasbord of creative and cost-effective promotional techniques in the special context of new business ventures, small and family businesses. In the case of self-employed professionals, building a personal brand is imperative to differentiate your business offering to stand out from your competitors and build increased customer loyalty. This course provides students with the skills and knowledge necessary to successfully build their brand, utilise their social networks, and employ other cost-effective promotional tools to communicate with their customers.
title: Branding and Promoting New Business Ventures
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: 6000MED_P1-P5 are five, 10 Credit Point Dissertation courses that make up the research component of the School of Medicine and Dentistry Honours programs. The Dissertation courses (6000MED_P1-P5) require students to undertake a research project relevant to their area of specialisation under the guidance of a supervisor. This will involve the identification of a research question, selection of appropriate research design, data analysis and carrying out the research project. At the completion of the five Dissertation courses students will submit for examination a thesis (with an upper limit of 25,000 words) describing the research project and will deliver a seminar describing their findings.
title: Dissertation 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

Students will further explore the theoretical issues related to second language acquisition, focusing on linguistic, psycholinguistic and sociocultural theories about how second languages are learned/acquired.
title: Second Language Acquisition: Theory and Application
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course provides dental hygiene, technology and prosthetic students with knowledge of anatomy, histology and embryology of the mouth, head and neck region. It covers the macroscopic and microscopic anatomy of the dentition, jaws, oral cavity, salivary glands, tongue and temporomandibular joint.
title: Applied Oral Biology
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course aims to introduce students to human development and the concept of psychosocial changes across the lifespan. Students will gain an understanding of psychosocial development through childhood into adulthood and this will provide a conceptual foundation for clinical practice. Prerequisites : NIL Corequisites : NIL Incompatible : 1010HSV Lifespan Development
2015PSY Developmental Psychology
1973NRS Foundations of Psychosocial Care
3011PSY Lifespan Development
title: Psychosocial Development across the Lifespan
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: This course challenges students to consider the complexity of older people's health in their dynamic environment. Students will examine the role of the registered nurse in promoting evidence-based nursing care for, and the health of, older people.
title: Older Adults' Health
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: Advanced Architectural Documentation focuses on the development of design and technical documentation within the legislative framework. Students extend knowledge of the fundamental structural principles, building products and construction systems through progressively more complex activities and assignments. Ultimately, students will critically apply their knowledge through a given complex medium to large-scale architectural design project that will be developed from Development Application to Building Certification. This course is only available to students enrolled in program 5558.
title: Advanced Architectural Documentation
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course consists of readings, presentations and discussions of current ideas, theories, principles and views on 'human error,' accountability, and just culture. In most safety-critical activities, societies and organizations demand that practitioners are 'held accountable' for their mistakes. But ideas about both 'human error' and accountability vary widely, and many forms can prevent organizations from drawing lessons from the failure. This course will cover models of human error, retributive and restorative just culture and backward- and forward-looking accountability.
title: Understanding Human Error and Just Culture
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course covers the structure and chemistry of the fundamental functional groups in used in standard organic synthesis as well as the basic stereochemistry nomenclature routinely used in organic molecules. It then develops to cover basic synthetic organic mechanism and introduces methodologies for the multistep synthesis of small organic molecules.
title: Organic Chemistry
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: Teaching and learning in the digital age requires teachers to understand the relationships between content knowledge, pedagogical knowledge and technological knowledge. This course introduces preservice teachers to a range of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) tools, resources, frameworks and pedagogical approaches that can be used to support purposeful, engaging and inclusive learning across curriculum areas. Through practical learning experiences, preservice teachers develop their digital literacy and technological capabilities while exploring the pedagogical decisions that underpin effective ICT integration. The course also examines contemporary and emerging areas of educational technology, including adaptive technologies, professional learning, digital safety and cyberbullying, artificial intelligence, and virtual learning environments.
title: Educational Technologies for Teaching and Learning
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This is a core first year course and has no pre-requisite, co-requisite or prior-assumed course requirements. This course enables you to examine, understand and develop theoretical perspectives and practical applications of professional and personal communication in educational environments.
title: Communication for Teaching and Learning
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course, Research Methods and Statistics provides students with the statistical and mathematical skills used in measurement, processing and analysing of data typical of those obtained in Exercise Science. The course also provides an introduction to experimental design and academic writing appropriate to studies and publications in Exercise Science. No Prerequisites.
title: Research Methods and Statistics
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course provides students with an introduction to the entrepreneurial process, including trend analysis, opportunity discovery and creation, understanding customer needs, and product/service development. Students will explore current health and social issues and critique those issues using their unique professional perspective. In teams, students will identify a market opportunity and develop an entrepreneurial response using recognised tools and processes.
title: Contributing to the Community
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

This will involve the identification of a research question, selection of appropriate research design, data analysis and carrying out the research project.
