The dissertation courses require students to undertake a research project relevant to their area of specialisation under the guidance of a supervisor. The dissertation involves the identification of a research question, selection of any appropriate research design and data analysis. At the completion of the five dissertation courses students will submit a research report for examination. Students may have to defend their work at a research seminar. Students are advised to consult the relevant course convenor regarding appropriate word limits or expectations concerning the amount of work to be produced in their disciplines. Students should be aware that when they enrol in the final dissertation component (6001DOH_P5) they are required to submit their dissertation by Friday of the first week of June for students submitting in Trimester 1 or Friday of the last week of October for students submitting in Trimester 2.
title: Dissertation 5
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: Pharmacy is a multifaceted profession with the key goal of promoting safe, effective use of medicines through person-centred care. This course will introduce students to the pharmacy profession, person-centred pharmacy practice and managing minor ailments. Students will learn how to access, interpret and apply selected laws, professional standards and professional pharmacy and medication resources. Competency in professional communication, person-centred care, evidence-based medicine and management of minor ailments will be developed through self-directed learning, practical workshops and simulated learning. As students are adult learners and clinical practitioners-in-training, there will be significant emphasis on development of life-long learning skills, including reflective practice.
title: Introduction to Pharmacy Topics
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: Police, Courts and Corrections explains the processes that govern the way crimes are investigated, tried, and punished. The course begins with an overview of the aims and functions of the criminal justice system with consideration for the laws and justice principles that underpin it. It then examines the roles and functions of the police, courts and corrective services and the process through which a criminal case progresses through the system, concluding with some reflections on alternatives to traditional practice. Throughout this course, consideration is given to understanding the powers, responsibilities and accountabilities of key criminal justice actors as well as the application of justice principles within the system. The course particularly references the Queensland criminal justice system, however general principles are common to all Australian systems.
title: Police, Courts and Corrections
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: In this course students will be introduced to the origin and direction of paramedic care. Students will also learn the role of interpersonal communication in paramedic practice. Students will also be introduced to a safe systematic clinical approach to assessing and managing a non-complicated patient in a paramedicine setting. Co-Requisites 1014MSC Cells, Tissues, and Regulation, 1016MSC Anatomy and Physiology Systems I and 1804NRS Psychosocial Development across the Lifespan.
title: Introduction to Paramedic Practice
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This is an advanced nutrition course designed as a pre-requisite for professional applications of knowledge to various age groups and normal physical states. Students will study the role and function of food and nutrients in the various physiological states during the lifecycle, and address lifecycle nutrition issues to a comprehensive understanding of human nutrition Advised Prerequisite: SECOND YEAR LEVEL OR EQUIVALENT BIOCHEMISTRY AND PHYSIOLOGY Incompatible: 7054AHS Public Health Nutrition
title: Nutrition Through the Lifecycle
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course involves development of a research project under supervision, analysis of literature and execution of experimentation. Results and conclusions are presented in oral and written forms.
title: Dissertation 4
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course is designed to teach students the logic of research methodology in the social sciences. Students will learn how to articulate a researchable problem, formulate research hypotheses, logically determine what research methodology provides the best avenue to test these hypotheses, and carry out research. Students will also develop the necessary skills to analyse and write criminal justice policies.
title: Criminology and Criminal Justice Research Methods
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course builds on prior study of Italian - whether through 1091LHS Italian 1B at Griffith University, secondary school programs, or other learning contexts - and strengthens students' ability to understand and engage in everyday Italian communication. Students further develop their reading and writing skills through work with a range of contemporary and authentic materials, expanding their vocabulary and consolidating key grammatical structures. By integrating language learning with cultural insights into modern Italian society, the course supports students in developing greater cultural awareness.
title: Italian 2A
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course examines the interplay of linguistics with social and cultural issues, such as identity, political influence, education, literacy, workplace relations, justice systems, multilingualism and endangered languages. It develops students' capacity to use their linguistic expertise in leading social change.
title: Linguistics in the Public Sphere
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Gothic Afterlives traces the history of the Gothic genre from its origins in the ghoul-infested castles and spectralised landscapes of 18th century art and literature through to the secretive suburban blood-suckers of contemporary television drama. From its beginnings the Gothic has been a popular and controversial phenomenon that has drawn its energies from the darker regions of the imagination and the borderlands of taste. In the Gothic nothing is as it seems. The world of cheerful and comforting appearances, secure homes, grand cities, and the reassuring solidity, identity and sexuality of the body are all made vulnerable by the uncanny effects of the Gothic imagination. In this course we'll follow the development of the Gothic in selected texts, films and TV series.
title: Gothic Afterlives
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course develops the essential skills learners need to understand basic Japanese sentences, communicate in routine tasks, and describe personal and familiar topics. It helps learners gradually progress towards basic social proficiency, equivalent to B1 Threshold level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR). As a 10C course, 2040LHS comprises approximately 150 hours of work in total. Students should follow the enrolment pattern for their major.
title: Japanese 2A
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course continues to develop the essential skills learners need to understand basic Japanese sentences, communicate in routine tasks, and describe personal and familiar topics. It helps learners gradually progress towards basic social proficiency, equivalent to B1 Threshold level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR). As a 10C course, 2042LHS comprises approximately 150 hours of work in total. INCOMPATIBLE: 2045LHS Japanese 2B (Enhanced). Students should follow the enrolment pattern for their major. PREREQUISITE: 2040LHS Japanese 2A OR 2043LHS Japanese 2A (Enhanced) OR Equivalent level of proficiency certified by means of a placement test administered by our Japanese teaching staff.
title: Japanese 2B
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course places the making of the modern world in a global historical perspective. Students examine themes such as trade, empire, disease, religion and human rights. The course enables students to analyse, understand and explain global historical interconnection and change.
title: Making the Modern World
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Conducted through seminars and lectures, this course considers contemporary visual arts in the context of a global cultural landscape. The course is designed to engage students directly with the histories, tensions and circumstances of global visual arts practice. An investigation of the nuances, sensitivities, protocols and complexities of specific practitioners, movements and events will enable the student to apply a sophisticated and critical knowledge to global contexts with an understanding of a diversity of perspectives. Students will also develop communication skills that reflect contextual awareness and responsiveness to rich and complex intercultural dynamics. This is a third year course. Students must have completed all second year art theory and second year visual arts major courses prior to enrolment. Prerequisites: 1216QCA AND 1217QCA AND 20CP of 2nd year level Art Theory courses
title: Global Visual Culture
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course prepares students for life and work beyond graduation. Students will explore creative arts industries and design strategies for enhancing their professional practice. They will learn skills including CV building, writing artist statements, grant writing, networking and proposal development. In conjunction with seminars led by professional practitioners, students will also investigate arts law, finance, business models, entrepreneurship, copyright law, professional protocols and the attitudes and dispositions of professional visual arts practitioners. Prerequisites: Students must have successfully completed at least 160CP of Bachelor of Visual Arts (1st year and 2nd year level courses).
title: Professional Practices in the Visual Arts
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: The course provides the opportunity to develop professional HR skills through the examination and application of learning theories and HRD frameworks to individual, group and organisational development needs and challenges. Content includes the development of skills in needs assessment, design, delivery and evaluation of training and development, reflection and analysis, the HRD professional role, application to organisational cases and current issues. This course emphasises both theoretical and practical aspects in the understanding and integration of learning theories, models and processes of HRD, sustainable organisational development, and professional L&D/ HRD practices. The course is designed to encourage students to examine 'real world' issues through critical thinking and the application of their learning to organisational challenges. This course encourages the learner to evaluate their own L&D/ HRD competencies and apply them to their future career development plans.
title: Human Resource Development
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: This third year course builds on previous courses to develop an advanced level of theoretical knowledge and practical understanding of typographic design. Curriculum departs from the traditional typographic discourse of form and function and encourages students to consider their work through the lens of form and content. Engaging with experimental and rhetorical approaches to typography, students explore their own position and practice in relation to the overall context of intended (and unintended) audiences, subject matters, social environments, and available media.
title: Typography and Context
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course will teach you the fundamental principles of developing brand strategies and identities and how to redirect visual communication towards social critique. Through studio-based projects, you will engage with essential concepts such as the impact of branding on contemporary society, brand auditing and brand personalities. You will work with a range of core design methods including sketching, iterative visual exploration alongside the considered use of AI tools for idea generation, developing brand strategies, creating brand marks, incorporating motion, and designing brand identity systems. By the end of the course, you will be able to develop a brand strategy, apply it to a contemporary brand identity system, and articulate your ethical framework within a global brand design context.
title: Design and Branding
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course is an introduction to creating screen-based interfaces across multiple platforms. Students learn the conceptual underpinning of user's experience and visual interface design and enact those ideas in prototyping software such as Adobe XD or Figma.
title: Interactive Design
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course involves the execution of the research proposal, including experimentation, and analysis of research results, under the guidance of two or more supervisors. It also involves the preparation of the completed Masters Thesis including research aims, hypotheses, significance, literature review, experimental design, methods, results and conclusions.
title: Research Thesis
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course focuses on developing skills to engage with clients in a real-world context and is delivered by experienced industry professionals via online learning over twelve weeks. This course maps to a number of National Financial Adviser Curriculum core knowledge areas. In particular, we focus on client relationships and consumer behaviour, which includes coverage of the following: Communication in a professional context, providing information about services to clients (FSG, PDS), collecting information from clients and setting goals, understanding self and others, interpersonal communication skills, the importance of client cues and prompts such as body language, tone of voice, how to create and build trust, fiduciary duty, ethical and professional conduct, legislated 'client best interests' requirement, risk profiling vs investment behaviour, managing the ongoing relationship and conflict resolution.
title: Financial Planning Skills
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: Students will be allocated a four (4) week clinical placement at the end of their First Year of the Bachelor of Paramedicine Program. Students will be assigned to an Operational Ambulance Station as a third officer, rotating through a roster with an operational Ambulance Paramedic crew. Whilst immersed within the prehospital environment, students will be required to complete associated assessment tasks to further scaffold and foster learning.
title: Work Integrated Learning 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course introduces cardiovascular conditions that are likely to be encountered in the out-of-hospital setting. Students will develop specific theoretical knowledge and clinical skills to assess and manage sub-acute, acute and chronic cardiovascular conditions encountered in the out-of-hospital setting. Students will apply a systematic approach, demonstrate clinical reasoning and evidence-based management of out-of-hospital cardiovascular conditions. 12 lead ECG acquisition and interpretation knowledge will be developed and integrated into clinical reasoning and practice.
title: Cardiac Conditions in Paramedic Practice
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course is designed to provide you with the opportunity to consolidate the knowledge, skills and attributes from your degree which are required for safe, competent and professional practice in a healthcare setting as a graduate paramedic. This course aims to make sure you are "work ready" and eligible to be registered with Australian Health Practitioner Registration Agency. Prerequisites: 3801MED Work Integrated Learning 3 , 3810MED Mental Health Conditions in Paramedic Practice and 3811MED Major Incident Management in Paramedic Practice. Co requisite 3820MED Maternal and Neonatal Conditions in Paramedic Practice and 3830MED Introduction to Community Paramedicine.
title: Transition to Paramedic Practice (Capstone)
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: The reality of work has changed radically, and human resource management practices have evolved with these changes. The rise of the knowledge economy means intellectual capital management is crucial. In this course you will apply theoretical perspectives to interpret and critically evaluate the changing nature of work and work arrangements and the implications these changes pose for managers. Critical issues revolving around the impact of technological augmentation and disruptions will also be examined. With thorough knowledge of policies and strategies to manage organizations human, social and structural intellectual resources in a dynamic working environment, you will be able to create frameworks for building relevant future-focused competencies and innovations in the workplace.
title: The Purpose and Future of Work
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: Data Mining and analysis: Data mining algorithms, Associative and sequential patterns, Market basket analysis, Bayesian modeling and maximum likelihood estimation techniques. Application of supervised learning methods, correlation analysis, linear regression, modeling spatial and temporal data such as via hidden Markov models, data visualisation. Pre-requisites: Must have completed 1808ICT Discrete Structures AND must have completed EITHER 2802ICT Intelligent Systems OR 2030ICT Introduction to Big Data Analytics.
title: Data Mining
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: This course will cover the design criteria for UAV with rotary, fixed wings and hybrid craft. Topics covered will include mechanical structures, motors and control systems, energy management, communications and stability.
title: UAV Design
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: From navigating natural disasters and a global pandemic to managing financial crises and growing political instability at home and abroad, the need for Australia's organisations to be skilled in communicating response and recovery planning is greater than ever. In this course, you'll gain an understanding of the principles of crisis communication and the vital role it plays in business, government, not-for-profit organisations and public relations. As you learn through a series of case studies, theory and practice, you'll develop your skills in communication, problem solving, critical thinking and strategic thinking. You'll be prepared to build an effective crisis communication response plan and team that can identify and manage a range of communication-related issues that may face an organisation. On completion, you'll be equipped to apply your knowledge of risk, issue identification and crisis communication planning to advise organisational leaders from across the social, corporate and political spectrum on communication strategies during crises and disasters of all kinds.
title: Communication in Crises and Disasters
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course explores processes and approaches used for managing society's impacts on the environment. Topics include: environmental protection, ecological impact assessment, ecosystem management plans, environmental monitoring, climate change adaptation and the interactions between environment, economy and society. Where possible, fieldwork activities will be used to demonstrate how environmental problems cause impacts and how environmental management and sustainability practices can be implemented to mitigate risks.
title: Environmental Management
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course explores narrative-driven processes to designing interior spaces and environments. Students will learn the fundamentals of designing spatial experiences and identities, demonstrating design development through sketching, physical model making and prototyping. The course also includes learning how to interpret and refine designs through 3D software and architectural drafting.
title: Interior Identities
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: Interior Technologies introduces students to the fundamental principles, methods and technologies underpinning interior fitout construction and documentation. Through a combination of lectures, demonstrations and studio-based exercises, students will explore how interiors are assembled, how building codes and Australian Standards inform design decisions, and how to represent this information accurately using both manual and digital drafting conventions. The course emphasises industry-standard practices for producing coordinated documentation sets in Autodesk Revit, enabling students to translate design intent into clear, buildable documentation suitable for communication with clients, consultants and contractors.
title: Interior Technologies
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: Jewellery and Small Objects introduces students to the lost wax casting process including technical considerations, design, materials handling, bench skill development, and materials knowledge. The course will cover the history of the technique and the current contemporary applications. Wax working techniques, investing, burnout and centrifugal casting procedures will be covered. Students will cast their works in either bronze or sterling silver. Studio projects will be theme or concept driven and intentionally designed to pose challenges to engage students to develop their understanding of issues of contemporary practice incorporating concepts developed referencing historical and or contemporary sources. Prerequisites: 1320QCA Jewellery and Small Objects Foundations
title: Small Objects Lost Wax Casting
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course examines risk management concepts and strategies, and disaster management frameworks within the context of the event and tourism industries. It firstly establishes a theoretical foundation which focuses on organisational and operational safeguards followed by consideration of a variety of risk management issues such as natural disasters, terrorism, public health, crowd control and pyrotechnics.
title: Tourism Disruption, Risk and Resilience
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This course introduces tourism and destination marketing. The course includes a broad range of topics that range from destination branding to the challenges facing national and regional destination marketing organisations.
title: Destination Marketing
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: As the largest industry in Australia, generating more economic activity than any other sector, and creating approximately 25% of all employment the property industry creates prosperity, jobs and strong communities. This course presents property principles for students entering the real estate and property development sectors.
title: Real Estate and Property Development Principles
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: Culinary tourism is one of the growing niche areas of special interest tourism which reflects changing lifestyles, and the role that some goods and services play as status symbols and identity formation, together with the recognition of the business opportunities in this area. Together, food and wine have become an integral part of the visitor experience to many destinations around the world, and this Course explores the development of food and wine tourism enterprises, food and wine tourism marketing, and trends and opportunities. Whilst the Course has a global perspective, students will focus on domestic examples.
title: Culinary Tourism
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This course provides an introduction to the basic concepts and practices of data analysis and inferential statistics. It will provide and understanding of several techniques including testing one or more means from sampled populations (t-Tests and ANOVAs), relationships between scale variables (correlations and regressions), and contingency table analysis (Chi-square tests). The course places emphasis on understanding the use of appropriate data for these tests, the use of exploratory data analysis and the underlying distributions and assumptions associated with these tests. Students will learn how to carry out these tests by hand, via the use of statistical software (R), check assumptions, interpret results and report findings in plain English. Assumed prior knowledge: Grade 12 Maths A or B or equivalent. Incompatible: 1003ENV Statistics, 2012MSC Biostatistics, 2012HSC, Intro to Biomedical Data Analysis, Bioinformatics, 1003PSY Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology, 1002MSC Introduction to Biomedical Data Analysis NOTE: this course is only offered on-campus, and students are expected to attend exams and weekly classes on campus, in person.
title: Statistics
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: Nutrition Education will provide students with the knowledge and skills necessary to plan, deliver and evaluate communication and education programs aimed at improving the dietary intake of groups and communities. The theory of behaviour change will form the basis for the course, and the main models will be covered. Students will participate in workshops to develop and implement nutrition education programs to the community and compile resources for use on Professional Placement and in their professional careers. The course prepares students to deliver education programs in their final year professional placements.
title: Nutrition Education
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course provides an essential set of foundational drawing skills. The focus of the course is visual thinking and concept development including: sketching, mapping, diagramming and reflective/responsive processes. The students will develop and deliver complex and clear visual communication strategies in response to specific ideation tasks. The course introduces students to the use of fundamental drawing methods to develop flexible and agile thinking, and to extend and enhance disciplinary and transdisciplinary knowledge and production. The knowledge and skills developed in this class will be applied in all of the students' major and minor courses of study. Prerequisites: Nil
title: Drawing Foundations
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course will equip students with essential, practical skills for communicating information about health and science issues and will help them to critically evaluate and interpret health and science information and adapt that for a range of purposes.
title: Health, Science and Risk Communication
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This is the second part of the course. Students will undertake a 10,000 - 12,000 word research paper over the course of one year, as part of a staged process and under supervision.
title: Thesis Completion
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This is the final theoretical course within the Bachelor of Midwifery program. The course aims to prepare students for graduation as a competent, capable and caring midwifery practitioner.
title: Transition to Professional Midwifery Practice
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: You will be introduced to the theory and practice of Positive Psychology. You will be able to describe the development, philosophy, major models, content areas and empirical foundation of Positive Psychology, and how these can be applied in professional settings. Practically, the course will assist you to develop skills in reflective practice and the application of skills such as mindfulness, through self-assessment and the application of a Positive Psychology intervention within your own life. Prerequisites: Nil Co-requisites: Nil Incompatible: Nil
title: Positive Psychology
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course introduces the principles and practices of designing rigorous, ethically responsible research. Students will explore quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods approaches, examine their alignment with research paradigms and research questions, and evaluate their strengths and limitations in addressing complex business research problems. The course guides students through the development of a research proposal, including literature review, research design, data collection and analysis planning, and ethical considerations. Students will also develop the skills required to present, write and defend their research proposal. For students undertaking dissertation studies, it is expected that you have nominated a supervisor for your dissertation and have discussed a research topic with your supervisor prior to enrolling in this course.
title: Research Design
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

description: This course introduces students to fundamental elements of the law of property providing the basis for further study in the core course 3015LAW Property 2. This course critically assesses the justifications for property and considers the delineation of property using a variety of examples such as land, chattels and intangibles (intellectual property), illustrating how property is defined and limited through the legal concepts of "ownership", "title" and "possession". A significant focus of this course is a critical assessment of the legal justifications for property and the manner in which particular groups have used conceptual tools to secure their property rights. THIS COURSE IS ONLY OPEN TO LAW STUDENTS.
title: Property 1
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: In the context of an introduction to civil obligations, this course provides a broad introduction to legal processes, the legal system and legal theory. The emphasis in this course is on contract law, but it also introduces related areas of civil obligations, particularly negligence and restitution. Students must be enrolled in a Law program. THIS COURSE IS ONLY OPEN TO LAW STUDENTS.
title: Contracts 2
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course involves the execution of the research proposal, including experimentation, and analysis of research results under the guidance of two or more supervisors. It also involves the preparation and presentation of the completed Master of Medical Research thesis, including research aims, hypotheses, significance, rationale, literature background, experimental design, methods, results, discussions and conclusions. The thesis would normally be expected to be approximately 40,000 words. Enrolment depends on availability of research topic and supervisors.6001HLS Dissertation preparation, research proposal and ethical application (needs to be completed during 6001HLS course) and availability of a supervisor. Prerequisite: 6001HLS Dissertation preparation, research proposal and ethical application (needs to be completed during 6001HLS course) and availability of a supervisor.
title: Research Thesis
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This capstone course is the culmination of the Sport Development program, designed to provide students with practical industry exposure through an 80-hour internship. It also allows students to integrate and apply their academic knowledge to real-world scenarios, emphasising creativity and problem-solving. Through the development of an innovative project, students tackle global challenges in alignment with the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), showcasing their ability to connect theoretical insights with meaningful, impactful action.
title: Sport Development Practicum
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course introduces students to the calculus of complex functions and its use in various applications including real integration, Fourier and Laplace transforms, the theory of analytic functions and Laplace's equation, and number theory. It also introduces some key concepts in the mathematical field of analysis. Prerequisites: 2205NSC Calculus II or 2203NSC/2203BPS Mathematics 2A. Advised prerequisite: 2201NSC Linear Algebra and Differential Equations.
title: Complex Analysis and Applications
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: Each of these courses will examine an area or areas of Applied Mathematics at an advanced level. The areas selected will depend on the expertise and availability of staff and will be relevant for the student's area of applied mathematics. The specialised mathematics studied will allow students to hone their technical, analytical, problem solving and communication skills. Students undertaking multiple Topics in Applied Mathematics courses will undertake a different topic for each separate course.
title: Topics in Applied Mathematics 4
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: In this course students will study basic physio-pathological aspects of the interaction between humans and their most common pathogens. It considers basic aspects of the immune defense against pathogens as well as infectious diseases caused by bacteria, viruses and parasites. The course covers general principles and paradigms of human-pathogen interaction and an overview of knowledge in various disciplines including epidemics, public health, and infectious disease control. The course also covers key aspects of therapeutic approaches against infectious agents.
title: Infectious Disease
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course covers the anatomy and physiology of the cardiac, vascular, respiratory and renal systems. This content is then extended to explore derangements of structure and function in these systems, covering principles of pathophysiology. In addition, this course provides an introduction to the diagnostic testing methods associated with evaluation of disorders and disease processes of the cardiac and respiratory systems.
title: Advanced Physiology
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course will cover the nomenclature of major anatomical landmarks, directional references, and anatomical terminology integrated with physiology. Six body systems: Skeletal, Muscle, Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Digestive, and Nervous are studied in detail within this course. The lecture content presented in this course is supported by in-person lectorial sessions and practical laboratory experiences which include the study of human cadaveric material.
title: Human Anatomy and Physiology 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course describes in detail the techniques of performing the commonly used clinical measurements, the information which may be obtained from specific tests, and the diagnostic and prognostic significance of the data obtained. The course will be taught by a combination of lectures, tutorials and practical clinical laboratory activities.
title: Evaluation of Organ Function by Physical Means
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course provides students with the opportunity to gain professional experience in a clinical physiology discipline under the supervision of a clinical physiologist (clinical measurement scientist). This professional experience will occur in the format of a Work Integrated Learning (WIL) experience, in which a student will shadow a mentor and participate in diagnostic testing and the aspects and tasks involved in the daily practice of a clinical physiologist. Students will also be required to attend classes on campus so as to support learning whilst on placement. Performance in the course is based on maintenance of suitable work records in the form of a log book, as well as written assessment items as described on the L@G course site, in addition to evaluation of performance by the clinical supervisor(s). Students must have passed (achieved a grade of 4) both 7213NSC and 7215NSC and have met all placement requirements relating to immunisations and placement documentation (example, Blue Card, Federal Police Check, etc) before being permitted to attend placement. This Course is only available to students enrolled in the Graduate Diploma of Clinical Physiology. Full-time students enrol in both 7208NSC and 7211NSC in the same trimester. Part-time students should enrol in 7208NSC for their initial professional placement. In a subsequent trimester part-time students then enrol in 7211NSC. NOTE: The scheduling of the clinical placements may need to occur outside of the published trimester timetable due to the availability of placements.
title: Physiology Clinical Placement A
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course provides students with the opportunity to gain professional experience in a clinical physiology discipline under the supervision of a clinical physiologist (clinical measurement scientist). This professional experience will occur in the format of a Work Integrated Learning (WIL) experience, in which a student will shadow a mentor and participate in diagnostic testing and the aspects and tasks involved in the daily practice of a clinical physiologist. Students will also be required to attend classes on campus so as to support learning whilst on placement. Performance in the course is based on maintenance of suitable work records in the form of a log book, as well as written assessment items as described on the L@G course site, in addition to evaluation of performance by the clinical supervisor(s). Students must have passed (achieved a grade of 4) 7208NSC and have met all placement requirements relating to immunisations and placement documentation (example, Blue Card, Federal Police Check, etc) before being permitted to attend placement. This Course is only available to students enrolled in the Graduate Diploma of Clinical Physiology. NOTE: A discipline other than the one which was completed for 7208NSC must be chosen to undertake the placement in for 7211NSC; alterations can only occur by negotiation with the Program Director.
title: Physiology Clinical Placement B
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course typically involves a study tour to a partner organisation or university in the Asia-Pacific Region. The field tour has a pre-arranged schedule agreed by Griffith International, the course convenor/s and the in-country partner organisation/university. The aim of the course is to enable students to develop their understanding of public health issues and practices in the Asia-Pacific region by directly hearing about, seeing and experiencing such issues and practices in-country. Participants will take part in a pre-arranged schedule of activities including country specific briefing and discussion sessions on public health issues coupled with site visits to see the issues first hand. The delivery of this course is dependent upon sufficient student interest.
title: Asia-Pacific Public Health Field Tour
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: In this course, students will engage with complex principles of water resources engineering design, developing a comprehensive and specialized skill set applicable across various engineering disciplines. Through sophisticated, hands-on problem-solving, they will address real-world challenges, such as advanced flood management techniques and the design of efficient hydraulic structures. The course offers an in-depth exploration of current engineering tools, methodologies, and numerical modeling, enabling students to critically analyze and design systems in accordance with the latest industry standards and practices. While water resources engineering is the central focus of this course, the advanced design techniques and high-level problem-solving approaches developed are transferable to other specialized areas of environmental and civil engineering. By the end of the course, students will be fully prepared to apply their knowledge in professional or research environments, making informed, innovative, and sustainable engineering design decisions.
title: Design for Civil Engineers
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: Modern scientists employ a range of spectroscopic and spectrometric techniques to probe specific properties of molecules and materials. In this course we mostly consider the interactions of electromagnetic radiation such as light and radio waves with matter and further consider how these interactions can be exploited spectroscopically to provide scientists with interpretable data. Data that can be derived from mass spectroscopy analysis will also be presented. The course is split into three modules: one module considers the interactions of light with matter, particularly in a biological context; one module uses the way radio waves interact with small organic molecules to solve structures; and the third module is a laboratory component in which students will undertake hands-on training in the use of IR, fluorescence, UV/Vis, and ICP-OES instrumentation. Prerequisites: Nathan Campus Courses: (1021SCG Chemistry 1A OR 1411ESC Chemistry I) AND (1022SCG Chemistry 1B OR 1422ESC Chemistry II). Gold Coast Campus Courses: 1015MSC Chemistry in Biological Systems 2 OR (1023SCG Chemistry I OR 1411ESC Chemistry I) AND (1024SCG Chemistry II OR 1422ESC Chemistry II). Prior assumed knowledge: 2103NSC Organic Chemistry OR 2014MSC Organic Chemistry.
title: Spectroscopic and Molecular Analysis
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: The course has been designed to provide graduates with a strong theoretical foundation in Integrated Water Management (IWM) and Catchment Science (CS) good practice, strengthened by a practical applied research skill set developed through the final project experience. In the course students design and undertake self-directed project work to consolidate and apply concepts, principles and methodologies learned in the coursework components of the Masters Programs. Students are encouraged to base their final project on a focal issue that is of personal or professional development interest, which they will explore under the guidance of dedicated professional and academic supervisory expertise. Professional placements with NGOs, research institutes, water industry service providers, private consultants, or natural resources management organisations are encouraged. Where possible, students will be linked with IWC partners and associates.
title: Final Project
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This 10 credit point course forms one part of the 50 credit point dissertation/project completed by all Honours students. It provides the individually supervised context in which a student may complete written and (where appropriate) practical work for a dissertation/project at one-year Honours level in the humanities, languages and social sciences. Assessment is by Dissertation (100% weighting, between 15,000- 18,000 words) or by Creative or Professional product (60% weighting) with a minor dissertation/exegesis (40% weighting, between 5,500 and 7,500 words). Incompatible: 6005ART_P1 Project/Dissertation, 6005LHS_P1 Project/Dissertation
title: Dissertation/Project
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course introduces and applies Information Communication Technologies (ICT) and Building Information Modelling (BIM) in the construction management discipline. The course offers knowledge and skills essential for successful adoption of ICT and BIM in construction planning, construction cost management, design coordination and modelling. ICT and BIM competencies are becoming core requirements for design and construction professionals; this course covers the challenges and case studies of the adoption of ICT and BIM in the construction industry.
title: Construction Informatics
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: Medical Nutrition Therapy 2 uses the nutrition care process framework introduced in Medical Nutrition Therapy 1 to consider disease states that require dietary modification in individuals. The content will include gastrointestinal disorders, renal disease, cancer, and paediatric nutrition and the material through lectures, case studies and other applied activities. This course forms part of the knowledge base for the medical nutrition therapy placement in year 4.
title: Medical Nutrition Therapy 2
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: The course content covers the key areas of; aerodromes and aeroplane landing areas, takeoff, climb, enroute, descent and landing performance; pre-flight, and in-flight operational considerations; aeroplane loading; airworthiness and equipment requirements; flight rules and procedures. The course is covered in sufficient depth to enable students with limited flying experience or aviation industry exposure to grasp the fundamentals of aeroplane operation, performance and planning in accordance with the CASA CPL Operations, Performance and Planning syllabus.
title: Aircraft Operations, Performance and Planning
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: Forensic mental health is an area of specialisation that involves the assessment and treatment of client's who are both mentally disordered and whose behaviour has led to or could possibly lead to offending. Forensic mental health as a field therefore represents the interface between community safety and client centred practice. The two key intervention targets in FMH are mental disorders and problem behaviours. This course will address the first of these targets by providing students with knowledge of general mental health interventions and components of recovery/recovery processes. Students will also be provided with skills in the delivery of specific intervention strategies targeting the most common mental health presentations in FMH. Students will also be provided with the opportunity to practice the skill of treatment plan development and role play delivery of specific strategies.
title: Interventions and Recovery in Forensic Mental Health (Clinical)
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course is a foundation course for the development of an understanding of core concepts and basic competencies necessary for effective counselling practice, especially those essential to establishing and maintaining the client-practitioner relationship, and supporting the therapeutic process. You will also be introduced to the foundations of developing an understanding of the client as a unique person, also termed 'case conceptualisation' and the concept of diversity. The skills you will learn include micro-skills such as listening, attending fully to the client, and creating a safe therapeutic relationship; self-and-other awareness; and self-reflection. Practical exercises allow you to integrate knowledge development with skills application. You will also be given opportunities to reflect on how counselling skills will fit within your future career and how you might prepare for further professional education. Prerequisites: Nil
title: Counselling Skills
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: Urban Environmental Systems introduces urban areas as living ecosystems with unique physical characteristics. As urbanisation accelerates globally, cities are emerging as the primary 'habitat' for humans as well as a diverse array of plants and animals. Unlike other ecosystems, urban environments are dominated by hard, impermeable surfaces that shape their microclimates, hydrology, and spatial structure, often resulting in fragmented landscapes. This course explores these dynamics, examining how urban systems function within broader land-use patterns and highlighting their ecological significance in an increasingly urbanised world. It also addresses the impacts of climate change and pollution on urban systems, emphasising sustainable solutions for creating resilient cities.
title: Urban Environmental Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: Video games are often the first virtual environments people engage with, whether these are 2D platformers, 3D shooters, puzzlers or eXtended Reality (including virtual and augmented reality) environments. Building these environments requires a diverse skill set, including creativity, human-centered design, modelling knowledge, and development knowledge including object-oriented principles, mobile design, gamification best practice, technical frameworks and graphics engines. This course utilizes advanced techniques and frameworks to engage students with key ideas in game/XR design, programming, architecture and the reuse of game engines, to develop a fundamental knowledge and skills required to create interactive digital environments that engage users.
title: XR and Games Development
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: A foundational principle and practice for professional educators is engaging with the planning-teaching-assessing-reflecting cycle. Within the current environment that emphasises evidence informed approaches to teaching and learning, the value and import of practitioner research will be explored in this course.
title: Practitioner researchers and the teaching and learning cycle
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course provides information from a range of theoretical perspectives to enable students to gain insight into the developmental characteristics and competencies of children birth to twelve years of age. The course has a focus on observational processes and theoretical analysis for understanding children's development for the purpose of providing opportunities and supports for children across various child and family services. Knowledge and skills for building relationships with children, families and the wider community will also be provided for purpose of co-designing programs that support children and their families.
title: Engagement with Children
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course will provide students with knowledge, understanding and skills in clinical reasoning and evidence-based practice within physiotherapy. Students will learn to formulate clinically-relevant questions regarding assessment or treatment. They will learn to source, critically appraise and interpret scientific literature to guide and inform decision making in clinical practice across core areas of physiotherapy.
title: Clinical Reasoning and Evidence
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: The Work Based Project is a self-directed course that applies 'project based learning' principles: it places importance on the design process of the project and highlights the role of group dynamics through immersion in team activities over an extended period. The unit begins with a half day Introductory Workshop as orientation to the subject. Individual students are then supported in their research processes by a peer team, a project advisor, an agency sponsor and the WBP e-learning site. A Face Time Session is scheduled mid-way as an opportunity for face-to-face team interaction and informal consultation with course instructors. The course concludes with a two day Capstone Residential during which the team oral presentations are delivered and assessed. Teams are self-managed and students are responsible for developing strategies to overcome the challenges of working collaboratively in teams spanning jurisdictions and work backgrounds.
title: Work-Based Research Project
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

description: Musculoskeletal Biomechanics is the science that examines the internal and external forces acting on a body and the effects produced by these forces. This course builds upon knowledge and skills gained in Introductory Biomechanics. Topics covered include gait analysis, tissue mechanics, musculoskeletal biomechanics, with application to sport, work and the clinical and rehabilitation settings.
title: Musculoskeletal Biomechanics
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: Exercise Science Practicum is a mandatory course in the Bachelor of Exercise Science program. The rationale for including this course is to make students aware of the requirements of the industry they wish to enter and the working environment of various organisations in which they may seek employment. The course is designed to link and complement the student's program of study by introducing them to the work environment. The main purposes of this course are: a) to provide students with work experience within the industry they may seek to be employed; (b) to introduce students to various topics concerning the work environment and field of exercise science; and (c) to outline career planning procedures.
title: Exercise Science Practicum
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: Governments in many ways create the world within which business operates, for example through regulation, taxes, policies, specialized programs. This course explores the business-government nexus, giving students comprehensive and practical insights on ways in which governments and businesses influence, respond to and engage with one another. It includes exercises and engagement designed to give students a deeper understanding of the roles that various political and business actors play in real-life business and government settings.
title: The Government Business Nexus: Intervening, Lobbying and Responding
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

description: Introductory Aviation Studies is an entry-level university course combining classes related to academic skills and aviation. This combination starts the process of critical thinking, referencing and writing competence required throughout university study and even the aviation industry. This is not an introduction to aviation course; rather, the classes will explore various topics relevant to the aviation industry. Incompatible with: 1106AVN Introductory Aviation Studies & 1501BPS Introductory Aviation Studies.
title: Introductory Aviation Studies
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course investigates the range of curricula, frameworks and guidelines that teachers draw on to inform their pedagogies, teaching approaches, methods and strategies in early childhood education and care. It is assumed that preservice teachers have completed 3235EDN, 3401EDN, 3402EDN and 2024HSV.
title: Programs and Pedagogies in Early Childhood Education
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course is designed for registered nurses looking to gain systematic, evidence-based advanced health assessment skills. As a student, you will critically analyse health assessment findings, including diagnostic data. Effective communication of your evaluations, findings and priorities to a diversity of audiences is also a key part of this course. You'll have the opportunity during this course to reflect critically on your own professional development, or your contribution to the professional development of others, in relation to advanced heath assessment. By completing this course, you will be better able to critically analyse patient data to inform patient health and wellbeing, applying advanced problem-solving skills to key health issues that impact patient health and wellbeing while working in collaboration with peers. These skills are an integral feature of effective clinical practice for healthcare professionals, especially for people aspiring to leadership positions.
title: Advanced Health Assessment
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: This unit of competency specifies the outcomes required to develop expertise in forensic crime scene investigation, maintain discipline expertise and conduct related research.
title: Develop Forensic Crime Scene Expertise
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

title: Develop Forensic Crime Scene Expertise
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: Within this course PSTs will examine literacy and numeracy demands within and across the curriculum, developing the skills and understanding necessary to support all learners including those with specific vulnerabilities. In addition, PSTs will develop knowledge and understanding of literacy and numeracy teaching strategies (including the explicit teaching of reading and writing in subjects) so they can offer responsive teaching sequences to meet the strengths and needs of diverse learners in areas of the curriculum other than English or Mathematics.
title: Supporting Literacy and Numeracy within and across the Curriculum
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course provides a range of activities that will further develop inquiry and problem-solving skills and put the professional responsibilities of science students into practice. A range of authentic learning experiences will see students conduct investigations (open investigations, experiments, field assessments, application of theory) as individuals, occasionally working in small teams if necessary, in which data is collected, recorded and interpreted using appropriate discipline specific approaches. Conclusions will be drawn and questions for future investigation highlighted. Assessment will be by the combination of a high-quality written report and an oral defence of this report.
title: Science Capstone
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course is centred on a substantial experience in an early years' context (0-8 years) that includes observation, decision-making, planning, practice, and critical reflection. It is framed around the seven quality areas of the National Quality Standard and consists of field-based experience (60 days) in relation to Belonging, Being and Becoming: The Early Years Learning Framework (EYLF) for Australia, the Queensland Kindergarten Learning Guideline (QKLG). Note: 10 days in Birth - under 3 years; 40 days in 3-5 years; 10 days in 5-8 years. Credit may apply for working and professional experience (within undergraduate programs).
title: Professional Experience and Practice Early Childhood Education and Care

description: This course introduces forensic techniques and procedures required to investigate, detect and prevent digital crimes. description: Learn how to design and progress change initiatives at the individual, team and structural levels and achieve successful organisational transformation. You will discover and apply proven theories and philosophies, such as the plan-do-act cycle, so you can design and implement mechanisms to drive change while managing risks. The leadership skills required to successfully guide people through these processes are also an important focus of this course. You will analyse elements of successful change leadership and reflect on how you can use these in your own change leadership style. With these tools at your disposal, you will be capable of professionally presenting on the topic of change management and prepared to drive innovation at your organisation, guided by strong governance practices.

description: This subject focuses on developing skills to engage with clients in a real-world context and is delivered by experienced industry professionals via online learning over twelve weeks. This subject maps to a number of National Financial Adviser Curriculum core knowledge areas. In particular, we focus on client relationships and consumer behaviour, which includes coverage of the following: Communication in a professional context, providing information about services to clients (FSG, PDS), collecting information from clients and setting goals, understanding self and others, interpersonal communication skills, the importance of client cues and prompts such as body language, tone of voice, how to create and build trust, fiduciary duty, ethical and professional conduct, legislated 'client best interests' requirement, risk profiling vs investment behaviour, managing the ongoing relationship and conflict resolution.
title: Financial Planning Skills
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

Students will gain critical knowledge that supports professional practice. academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course covers advanced topics in classical mechanics, including Newton's path to universal gravitation, the three body problem, chaos versus integrability. It derives Langrangian mechanics from the least action principle, and Noether's theorem, and applies these to motion of a rigid body. It further develops the formalism of Hamiltonian mechanics. This provides the theoretical background to see various relationships between classical mechanics and quantum mechanics. In the second (larger) part of the course, on quantum physics, we cover formal quantum theory, quantum measurement, entanglement, time evolution, angular momentum theory, and quantum computing.
title: Honours Classical and Quantum Mechanics
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course is conducted primarily as individual student placement, or small teams of students within an industrial or research environment and emphasizes academic and vocational aspects of modern industry practice. Students consolidate their technical knowledge by undertaking a project in a professional workplace whilst simultaneously managing their learning and course assessment. The project provides students with the opportunity to undertake a substantial project that usually has an industry application. Students work in close liaison with their industry and university supervisor throughout the project and are expected to demonstrate a good understanding of their project. The course also emphasizes that competence in management, business and social responsibilities are essential components in all fields within the aviation profession and the key attributes of a contemporary industry or research environment. The entry criteria for this course is a minimum of 80 credit points and a minimum average grade point of 5. Students may apply for a new position or may bring existing positions into this course. Students bringing their existing positions into this course need to submit a brief statement explaining the difference between their existing position and planned WIL project. These cases then need to be reviewed and approved by the convenor on a case-by-case basis.
title: Aviation Work Integrated Learning Placement
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This 10 credit point internship course is an elective which is open to penultimate or final year JD and LLB students who are selected by an application process. Less frequently, there are also opportunities for students in earlier years. Opportunities are advertised by student email each Trimester for the following Trimester. Each opportunity sets out the partner's requirements for each internship, including the required year of study. This is a competitive process, but we have opportunities for students at all levels, so apply! The course is a law elective available to all JD and LLB students who have: -completed at least 120 CP in law subjects (unless the advertisement allows fewer credit points) -have a minimum GPA of 4, although some partners require a higher GPA, which will be stated. The course provides students with an opportunity to complete unpaid work in a Law firm, government department or other legal work environment. Students complete an internship for two days per week with one of our partners/hosts, such as law firms, 'in house' legal units, community legal centres, barristers, law reform agencies, and government legal units. Students will build on their University learning to develop new insights into how law works in practice. It offers students the opportunity to develop a range of professional skills, enhance their discipline knowledge, and build their research capabilities, which will enhance employability. The practical and academic components of the course are designed to build students': -capacity to make informed decisions, both personally and professionally -capacity to reflect on the impact of the law on individuals and society -ethical awareness, sense of social justice and professional responsibility -multi-disciplinary and cross-cultural awareness and competence -graduate skills, professional identity, career direction, confidence, and employability -practical and technical skills, including dealing with unstructured situations, written and oral communication, collaboration, teamwork and time management. Students report that work integrated learning (WIL) makes them more employable, and employers back this up, reporting that WIL favourably influences their perception of students' abilities. Students say WIL helps them assess their career direction, complements their learning, increases their networks, increases their motivation to study and helps them prepare for future employment.
title: Internship Clinic
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: As a student in this course, you will explore the role of physiotherapy in assessing and treating individuals across the lifespan, with an equitable focus on adult clients and populations. description: At its core, pharmacy is the discipline of pharmaceutics, which studies drug formulations and the processes by which they are designed, manufactured, and delivered to the body. Simply stated, pharmaceutics converts drug substances into medicines - delivery systems capable of administering drugs to the body safely, efficiently, reproducibly and conveniently. This course provides in-depth pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical knowledge of foundational drug delivery technologies utilised in medicine. The course provides essential skills and knowledge required for 4012PHM Specialised Delivery Systems II.

academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course is an introduction to the field of transportation engineering, including contemporary transportation engineering challenges and sustainable transport solutions. Having successfully completed this course, a student will be prepared for a position as a graduate-level transport engineer or planner.

description: This course aims to develop knowledge in current approaches toward engineering desired properties and functionalities into selected proteins. Students will explore state-of-the-art techniques used in protein engineering through a 'journal club' strategy and present reports on the techniques.

description: River catchments are fundamentally controlled by geomorphic processes and thus understanding the principles of geomorphic form, function and evolution of catchments and soil landscapes and applying them to conceptualise the landscape is fundamental to catchment science. In this course students will be introduced to the concepts of soil and geomorphological environments in the context of catchment dynamics, and how they apply to management and modelling. The course provides the necessary background to modelling water, sediment, and nutrient fluxes through catchments. It also explores how understanding catchment geomorphology and soils is fundamental to constructing conceptual models of the catchment to plan for, and manage, the impacts of land-use change, climate change, and other direct catchment disturbances on water quality and river dynamics. There are no pre-requisite courses, but 7304ESC should be undertaken after or with 7301ESC Introduction to Catchment Processes
title: Soils and Geomorphology in Catchment Science
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

The course also investigates contemporary challenges and changes facing the legal profession such as diversity in legal practice, technology and the law, social justice concerns and globalisation. As a capstone, this course offers students nearing graduation the opportunity to summarise, evaluate and integrate learning from across a range of learning experiences to engage with authentic ethical dilemmas and real contemporary issues. THIS COURSE IS ONLY OPEN TO LAW STUDENTS.

description: The course will explore how historical and cultural contexts influence education and the role of teachers. It will look into how beliefs about being a 'good student' and 'good teacher' have evolved over time. The course will also analyse how social beliefs and attitudes impact the design and delivery of various educational forms and how they influence students' educational experiences and outcomes. Special emphasis will be placed on understanding cultural responsiveness within the education of Australia's diverse student population. Educators will be encouraged to have a well-informed knowledge base about diversity and social justice, and ongoing intercultural development and the importance of self-reflection and reflexivity as ever-evolving career practice which they can utilise to meet their students' needs. Reflective practice will be highlighted as crucial for educators to understand their attitudes.

academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

Preservice teachers will develop expertise in the effective teaching of literacy, including the explicit teaching of phonics in age-appropriate interventions and the explicit teaching of reading and writing in subjects other than English. They will develop a repertoire of analytical processes and strategies for effective teaching of numeracy including the explicit teaching of relevant skills in mathematics within their teaching area, to enable and build fluency, understanding, problem solving and reasoning so mathematics knowledge and skills can be applied in other curriculum areas.

description: This course focuses on drama curriculum and pedagogy within the junior years of schooling (Years 7-10). Students participating in this course will gain an understanding of the key syllabus documents that inform drama education at this level, as well as the current trends in education that have an impact upon drama in schools and the broader field of Arts Education. The developmental needs of middle years' learners and the socio-cultural context within which these learners operate will also be a focus. Students will be supported to develop appropriate assessment procedures and the skills to confidently plan and design drama lessons, unit plans and work programs. They will also be given opportunities to work practically to develop their pedagogical skills. Course participants will be expected to read widely and reflect on their evolving understanding of the role of drama education in the development of the aesthetic dimension in young people.

academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course prepares students for the transition to clinical placements. Students will develop advanced communication, leadership, legal, ethical, and reflective practice skills within increasingly complex clinical contexts. Through workshops, tutorials, online learning, and reflective activities, students will strengthen their capacity for person-centred care, professional decision-making, self-awareness, and compassionate practice, supporting their ongoing development as future medical practitioners. Clinical practice courses emphasise hands-on learning and supervised skill development, which cannot be fully achieved through independent study. Attendance is therefore mandatory for all scheduled sessions. Students must meet both of the following minimum attendance requirements: Attendance at a minimum of 80% of all scheduled course sessions; and Attendance at a minimum of 70% of sessions within each module. The number of scheduled sessions may vary across teaching sites. Attendance requirements will be adjusted proportionally where required. Permissible absences (up to 20% across the course and up to 30% within an individual module) apply only in exceptional circumstances, such as illness, emergencies, or other valid reasons. These absences must be reported promptly using the Student Absence Form (available in Course Essentials) and supported by appropriate documentation (e.g., a medical certificate). Where appropriate, the Module Lead may assist students with approved absences by offering alternative learning opportunities, subject to availability and class capacity. Such opportunities are provided to support skill development and do not contribute to attendance requirements. No alternative arrangements will be made for unapproved absences, and individual remediation sessions cannot be provided. Monitoring and recording attendance is the responsibility of the student. No warnings will be issued when a student approaches or exceeds the allowable absence threshold. Students who have concerns regarding their attendance are encouraged to contact the Course Convenor as early as possible. Learning and skill development within this course are cumulative and scaffolded, with knowledge, clinical skills, and professional behaviours progressively developed throughout the semester. As a result, absence from clinical and field-based learning activities may adversely affect a student's ability to achieve subsequent learning outcomes. Students who do not meet the minimum attendance requirements may be required to undertake additional assessment to demonstrate attainment of the course learning outcomes. The nature and format of any additional assessment will be determined by the Course Convenor and the Module Lead/s and may include written, oral, reflective, and/or practical assessment tasks. Such assessment may evaluate learning outcomes and competencies from across the course, rather than solely those associated with missed sessions. Failure to

description: This course introduces students to a perspective on the purpose of business that incorporates values such as responsible leadership, integrity, ethical behaviour, respect for others, trust, and sustainable enterprise. The relevance of these values and their impact on behaviour and outcomes in a business context are illustrated through case studies and real-world examples. Building on this discussion, the course examines how businesses develop solutions to meet growing demands for sustainability, transparency, and good governance. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) framework is introduced and used to explore the alignment between business practices and sustainable solutions to real-life challenges. The course also considers the role and responsibilities of professionals and the importance of professional standards in today's society.
