description: This subject provides an overview of the various areas within the criminal justice system in which frontline workers come across people with mental disorders. It examines the way in which the criminal justice system (including police, court, and correctional staff) deals with individuals with mental disorders. In particular, the subject focuses on the identification and treatment of individuals with mental disorders; relevant processes and decision-making in different elements of the criminal justice system; examining contemporary approaches to definitions, diagnostic tools, notions of criminal responsibility and fitness to stand trial; and the use of psychological knowledge, theory, and research to guide reflective practice and build personal, professional resilience.
title: Mental Health, Psychology and the Criminal Justice System
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course examines the relationship between popular genres and popular culture since the late 19th century. By focusing on three of the most popular genres in the world: crime, romance and speculative fiction the course examines how the style and focus of popular texts reflects shifting attitudes and tastes in society and culture. These popular genres are examined in a range of modes including fiction, television, film and a variety of screen based cultures. The course develops a range of skills and knowledge that explore the relationship between written and screen-based texts and publishing in popular genres. Students should note that content referred to in this course can be challenging or explicit when exploring genre intent, parameters and innovations. Students will be provided with learning options and context in relation to this material.
title: Popular Genres
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course introduces students to public interest news-writing through text based news production for contemporary news media.
title: The Emerging Journalist
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This placement course allows students to explore a relevant field of interest after they have successfully completed their capstone placement courses. Students will spend 20 working days in a dietetic workplace, completing a project and tasks relevant to the placement site. Relevant placement opportunities are established collaboratively between the student and course convenor and are designed to enhance graduate employability in non-traditional fields. Students will engage in work-readiness activities, including preparing job applications and undertaking a simulated job interview.
title: Transition to Employment
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course supports students to develop a comprehensive approach to career planning through critical self-reflection and proactive career management. Students will assess their personal values, skills, and professional goals to create and implement a strategic career development plan that adapts to changing workplace environments.
title: Career Readiness for Professional Success
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

description: This course examines psychological and social models of behaviour in the context of individual and group decision making. It provides insights into the approaches and perspectives that can be taken to more deeply understand the client-adviser relationship, the advice process and design of financial strategies. Incompatible and co-taught: AFE327 Behavioural Insights Incompatible: 3218AFE Behavioural Finance; AFE328 Behavioural Finance
title: Behavioural Insights
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course constitutes Part 2 and 20CP of a 30CP individually supervised project in which a student may complete written work on an approved topic. The research project undertaken will be relevant to the music discipline and incorporate high levels of competence and academic excellence. Assessment will be by dissertation. This will be delivered by a supervisory team, which will be tailored to the needs of each student's project (this might include a combination of a practical study teacher and research supervisor or a research supervisor only).
title: Dissertation Part 2
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course lifts the curtain on the intriguing, frightening, and sometimes amusing world of modern dictatorships. The topics covered aim to familiarise students with the most pertinent issues in comparative authoritarianism: What is a dictatorship? What are the different types of dictatorship? How do dictators come to power? How do they consolidate power? How do they maintain power? How do they lose power? What happens to the regime after they leave office? In answering these questions, the course deliberately draws attention to the varying reasons why some authoritarian regimes collapse very quickly and others endure for decades. Given recent and ongoing increases in the number of dictatorships around the world, the course is particularly timely for students.
title: The Way of the Dictator
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

description: This course introduces the specialist skills of 3D computer based modelling and design using digital technology to create complex 3D computer based parametric models. Students will use industry standard 3D computer modelling software to develop proficiency in designing for 3D solid modelling, building 3D virtual objects and 2D drafting techniques and photo rendering for documentation. Main assessments will be project based, including reverse engineering and 3D modelling of a design concept to be ready for production, with a focus on preparing designs for 3D printing.
title: Digital Modelling: 3D Objects
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: 7409EDN explores the nature of teaching in culturally diverse classrooms. Within this course, pre-service teachers will develop an understanding of the importance of valuing cultural diversity and will consider how cultural identities influence and impact upon the learning of students in schools. At the heart of this course is a particular concern with young Indigenous people and the importance of teachers developing cross-cultural understandings in their curricular and pedagogical approaches to working with Indigenous youth. In that endeavour, it is vital that pre-service teachers deepen their engagement with the rich sources of cultural and pedagogical support that reside in Indigenous communities. In order to work effectively with Communities, pre-service teachers need to extend their knowledge of cultural protocols and appropriate ways of working with Indigenous Elders and others in their local areas.
title: First Australians, Education and Communities
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: In this course students will evaluate the diagnostic experiences and practical implications for autistic individuals and their families. This will take into consideration family culture, values, and personal perspectives. Students will evaluate current sources of information available for families. Using their understanding and knowledge of autism they will develop support resources for individuals on the autism spectrum and their families to navigate the post diagnostic period. They will apply a strengths-based approach to communicating the characteristics of autism and the implications, the collaborative planning process, and information on resources pertinent to support the autistic individual and their family.
title: Diagnosis and Supports
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course focuses on enabling students to demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the impact of culture and cultural identity on the diverse learning needs of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students, particularly those for whom English is a second language. The course also requires students to demonstrate a broad knowledge, understanding and respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories, cultures and languages and its application in the schooling context by engaging with the diversity within and across First Nations people including culture, perspective, language, history and varied impact of colonisation on different groups. An inherent feature of the course is the ability to understand school-community/parental partnerships in Indigenous communities to which graduating teachers will be sent, engaging with communities and families to drive successful outcomes.
title: First Australians and the Education System
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This subject is designed to illustrate to students the ongoing, constantly changing nature of knowledge through an examination of contemporary issues in health-related science. Students must become practiced in the skills of critically evaluating information (research), integrating the findings into their knowledge base, and communicating such information to their peers. Students must also be provided with a social context for their research by examining the relationship between their research topic and the wider community.
title: Advanced Studies in Exercise Science
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: Students wishing to enrol in 3615QCA Creative Internships must first organise an internship placement with a host organisation that aligns with their skills, discipline area, and career goals. This course is not timetabled and has no classes or on campus requirements. Students may enrol at any time during the year. The schedule for the internship, including days and hours per week, is negotiated directly between the student and their host, as long as a total of 100 hours is completed. To enrol, students must confirm the details of their proposed placement and then make an application to enrol by contacting the course convenor.
title: Creative Internships
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course examines the nature of language learning with reference to theories of human learning and applied linguistics. In doing so, it investigates a host of variables pertaining to linguistic, cognitive, metacognitive and social-cognitive aspects of language learners. It also facilitates the knowledge of research methods and analytical tools used for the study of these aspects in relation to language learning and acquisition. Students will be given opportunities to examine and analyse published and/or authentic data that demonstrate their knowledge in terms of the content areas covered in the course. This course is a core course in 3016 GCert in TESOL program, and a foundation course in 5756 and 5757 MTESOL/ MTESOL & Leadership. As such, this course does not assume students have any prior knowledge or experience in the content area. However, students with prior teaching experience or education will find many opportunities to draw on and extend their existing knowledge.
title: Understanding the Language Learner
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Managing Learning develops knowledge, skills, practices and strategies for planning effective teaching and learning experiences, including knowledge of and skill in explicit teaching, modelling and scaffolding practices that support how a student's brain learns; and creating and maintaining safe, supportive learning environments with a focus on managing classrooms and challenging behaviour, with an understanding of the role of rules and routines in establishing a structured, safe, and positive classroom environment. The course consolidates understandings of learning, learners, planning and curriculum; and introduces contemporary approaches in positive behaviour management, including family engagement that includes demonstrating knowledge and understanding of strategies for differentiating teaching to respond to the strengths and meet the needs of students from diverse backgrounds, with diverse learning needs, including students with disability, and applying the principles of inclusive education and criteria for pedagogical choices across the full range of abilities. PST will have an opportunity to practise and apply proactive practices, including setting high expectations, building positive relationships, providing structure, and setting ambitious, achievable and personalised goals. A 15-day professional experience placement is embedded in the course, in either Years Prep - 6 (for students in the Primary major) or Years 7 - 9/Junior Secondary (for students in the Secondary major). The placement provides an opportunity for professional learning of teacher practice and knowledge in these key areas at the classroom level.
title: Managing Learning
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: Evidencing Impact in the Bachelor of Education program entails both course work on campus and a professional experience placement in schools. This course will develop professional knowledge and practices for supporting student participation in learning, including planning and sequencing content and tasks that are increasingly challenging and incorporate spacing and retrieval practice, strategies that are responsive to the learning strengths and needs of students from diverse backgrounds, and students with disabilities; foundational understanding of common whole-school behaviour frameworks; knowledge of theory of an MTSS framework, the direct relationship to evidence-based teaching practices and skill in how to practically implement tier 1 in the classroom; practise in applying techniques that positively and effectively managing behaviour in classroom contexts; and the reinforcement of understandings about teaching and assessment practices that respond to, and are informed by, evidence of impact on student learning in which they effectively select a range of evidence-based assessment practices to evaluate progress, adjust instruction, and provide targeted feedback, to support learning. Students will be placed in schools for a total of 25 days. This professional experience placement (appropriate to the major pathway) will provide the pre-service teachers with the opportunity for further development of knowledge and practices using evidence of the impact their teaching has on student learning.
title: Evidencing Impact
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: Traditional IT project management approaches work well under stable conditions, when intended project outcomes are well understood. Yet, under conditions of delivering value to clients early, in innovation projects, or new product development, traditional methods of software development are often restrictive and inflexible. This course offers an alternative approach to software development that values flexibility, time-to-market and self-organisation over rigorous planning and processes. This course is primarily based on the IIBA's Agile Extension to the BABOK with limited inclusion of PMBOK and Agile Program Management Framework.
title: Agile Methodologies
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: The Ethical Hacking course will provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the principles, techniques, and tools used in ethical hacking, also known as penetration testing or vulnerability assessment. This course aims to equip students with the knowledge and skills needed to identify and assess vulnerabilities in information systems and networks, and to understand the ethical and legal considerations associated with conducting authorized security testing. This course was previously known as 3809ICT Applied Network Security and is incompatible with 3809ICT Applied Network Security.
title: Ethical Hacking
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: This course covers the postulates of Quantum Mechanics and bra/ket Dirac notation and perturbation theory. This knowledge is then applied to fundamentally important physical systems including one electron atoms, multielectron atoms, magnetic dipole moments, selection rules, optical transitions, Einstein A and B coefficients, simple laser theory, line broadening mechanisms, nuclear models and nuclear decay (alpha, beta and gamma decay).
title: Quantum Physics III
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course examines the relationships between land use, water resources and food security, using agricultural systems as key case studies. It emphasises sustainable water management from farm to catchment scales, including efficient irrigation, water conservation, alternative water sources and adaptation to changing environmental and social conditions. The course also considers emerging contaminants, including microplastics, in irrigation water, soils, organic amendments and recycled-water systems, and their potential implications for soil function, crop production, water quality, ecosystem health and food safety. Students will explore how peri-urban expansion affects agricultural land and water use, including the management of alternative water sources. They will develop nexus-thinking skills to analyse competing water demands and contaminant risks across agriculture, communities, ecosystems and other sectors. The course builds students' capacity to connect local and global perspectives and apply multidisciplinary and transdisciplinary approaches to current and emerging water, land-use, contaminant and food-security challenges.
title: Water, Agricultural Landscapes and Food Security
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: The importance of managing for safety has been re-emphasised in recent years by the ICAO recommendation for aviation operators to implement a Safety Management System (SMS) based on the published ICAO SMS framework. This course will examine the key elements of a safety management system and the associated systems, processes and procedures used in achieving high safety standards in aviation organisations. There will be a strong emphasis on the importance of leadership and sound management principles and their important contribution to achieving high safety standards. Prior Assumed: Nil Incompatible: AVN3005 Flight Safety, 3005AVN Safety Management, 2511BPS Safety Management
title: Safety Management
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course introduces a framework for understanding the many dimensions that influence the work of teachers, including research, policy and legislation. Placing the student at the centre of the framework, preservice teachers consider how they influence learning as the student progresses from novice to expert through pedagogical choices related to process such as efficient and effective process of knowledge acquisition, the function of memory and the concept of cognitive overload. This framework will inform and support all other courses in the Program and will serve as a reflective tool within the capstone trimester. Please be aware that this course may not follow the standard academic calendar. Please check your timetable on myGriffith for details of when classes commence and the duration of professional experience placements.
title: Griffith Dimensions of Learning and Teaching
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: In this course, you will complete coursework and clinical activities which constitute a practical internship within the Psychology Clinic of the university. Full time students complete two internships (Internship 1 - 8181PSY in T1, and Internship 2 - 8180PSY_P1 in T2, and 8180PSY_P2 in T3). You will be an intern in the clinic and work as a provisionally registered clinical psychologist under close clinical supervision. Intensive pre-practicum training provides you with a minimum standard of clinical skills before commencing with clients in the Psychology Clinic. The applied focus of this internship is designed to increase your competence in managing a therapeutic caseload, utilising both face-to-face and online delivery of psychological services. You are trained to have a sense of 'ethical mindedness' and will have the opportunity to practice applying your ethical decision-making skills with a range of ethical dilemmas and problems. By the end of the internship, you are expected to have an established repertoire of core psychological competencies, including a thorough understanding of professional and ethical issues in psychological practice. You are expected to be familiar with the Psychology Board of Australia Code of Conduct, as well as the National Mental Health Practice Standards, and the Requirements of the Psychologists registration with Psychology Board of Australia. This course is a non-graded course and students who pass the course will receive a non-graded pass (NGP) on their transcript. You must have satisfactory performance on all assessment tasks to receive a non-graded pass in the course.
title: Practicum 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: Musculoskeletal Anatomy course has been designed to consolidate knowledge of structure and function of the musculoskeletal system. A thorough understanding of musculoskeletal anatomy is imperative to the practice of physiotherapists, exercise physiologists and other health professionals. Students will build on theoretical knowledge and practical skills obtained in prerequisite courses through a series of online lectures, specialised laboratory sessions and a weekly online tutorial.
title: Musculoskeletal Anatomy
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: The Environmental Engineering Research Project is a research-based project related to a topic in environmental engineering. The project is to involve a time commitment and report length equivalent to that involved in a 10 CP course. The report length will normally be around 5000 words in length depending upon the nature of the problem investigated. The scholarly integrity of the project is paramount. The aim of this course to provide an opportunity to students to undertake supervised, but independent, study of a topic of individual interest and to apply the knowledge and skills gained in their coursework studies in an extended project relevant to their future career and/or study plans.
title: Environmental Engineering Research Project
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: Students will examine how interpretive, critical, and Indigenous research approaches develop knowledge and contribute to health and human services. This course will prepare students to conduct qualitative research and evaluate the integration of qualitative evidence in their practice.
title: Qualitative Research
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: Exercise and Sports Science is a multidisciplinary field encompassing physiology, biomechanics, nutrition and the psychosocial aspects of human movement. This course provides foundational knowledge that is key to developing a sound base for understanding the health and wellness continuum between performance athletes and chronic disease patients. Theoretical and practical learning in the biophysical knowledge domains (biochemistry and energetics as well as biophysics) will be combined with professional awareness and career pathways in the exercise and sports science industry.
title: Foundations of Exercise and Sports Science I
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: Concepts of recovery have emerged due to the advocacy work of people with lived experience of the mental health system. Consumers and community-led responses have transformed care and set the platform for what exists today. As part of this course, you will explore the historical and theoretical constructs related to the development of the consumer and carer movements and the recovery paradigm they championed. Central to this is insight into the lived experience of consumers, including those from a diversity of cultural and social groups. These unique perspectives will help you to understand and develop empathy for the needs and contributions of families and carers in mental health care. You will be able to demonstrate how the recovery focused approach guides consumer-driven mental health collaboration and how this model translates into application. Hope and empowerment are important to the recovery approach, and you'll also learn how to integrate these concepts into your own practice. By completing this course, you'll have the tools and communication skills to advocate for person-centred mental health services and improved serviced provision for those experiencing mental health concerns.
title: Consumer, Carer, and Community Engagement in Mental Health
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course focuses on policing in Australia. It commences with its historical development, including the impact of the English tradition. This is followed by an analysis of a variety of organisational issues and an examination of a range of operational strategies of policing.
title: Introduction to Policing
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course offers Griffith students a unique opportunity to undertake a transformational work integrated learning (WIL) experience. You will be supported to undertake a full-time, unpaid internship with a company in Asia. Internship destinations are chosen to offer maximum exposure to the vibrant Asian economy in businesses, government offices, or not-for profit organisations. The program offers in-country global WIL experiences in selected destinations. This course is part of the Griffith Asia Institute (GAI) initiative to offer meaningful Asia experiences to Griffith students; students are invited to be contributing members of the GAI community and experience the advantages of GAI networks throughout Asia. Students are matched with a placement that best aligns with their academic discipline and career aspirations and that advances student academic interests, experiential immersion, and vocational intentions with appropriate Asian connections. The aim of this course is to increase students' skills and experience in the workplace enhancing employability at the time of graduation. By the end of the course, we expect students to develop advanced skills in areas that are in high demand by employers, such as, problem solving, working in teams, critical analysis, time management, networking, and innovation. Thus individual reflection on personal attributes such as independence, curiosity, motivation and maturity is encouraged. All students applying for this course must meet minimum requirements and will be selected for the course in a competitive process. Please note: This course is not available for credit based on prior studies or external studies.
title: UG Global Mobility Internship II
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

description: The course provides an introduction to classical physics, based on mechanics, waves, electricity and magnetism. It will be assumed that students have the knowledge equivalent to a grade of SA over 4 semesters in Mathematical Methods (Qld high school subject) or equivalent study, or 1017SCG Foundation Mathematics (grade of 4 or higher).
title: Physics 1A
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: All electrical signals produce electromagnetic fields. Therefore, it is vital to understand the generation and manipulation of these fields. This course covers classical electrostatics, including charge and charge density in volumes, force due to charge, electric field intensity, electric potential, and electric flux density. It also explores magnetostatics, including magnetic field intensity and flux density, magnetic forces, magnetic potential, and inductance. Time-varying fields are covered, including moving conductors, transformers, displacement current, and generators. The course aims to provide an understanding of Maxwell's equations as applied to engineering problems. This fundamental theory is then used to explore the principles of plane-wave propagation in lossless and lossy media. It is highly recommended that students had completed 2205NSC (Calculus II).
title: Engineering Electromagnetics
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course involves development of a research project under supervision, analysis of literature and execution of experimentation. Results and conclusions are presented in oral and written forms.
title: Dissertation 2
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: Part 5 of Dissertation (final with grade). At the completion of the five dissertation courses students will submit a research report for examination. Students will have to defend their work at a research seminar. Students are advised to consult the Honours Adviser in the School regarding appropriate word limits or expectations concerning the amount of work to be produced in their discipline. Students enrolling in the final dissertation component (6000NRS_P5) are required to submit their dissertation by week 13 of that semester.
title: Dissertation 5
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: This course provides students with a deep understanding of the core concepts and principles that underpin contemporary criminological theories. By exploring the problems, questions and ideas that have shaped modern criminological thought, students will gain knowledge of the contexts that influence the emergence and reception of modern criminological theories and the modes of social intervention that different criminological perspectives expressly or implicitly propose. Additionally, this course will equip students with the tools to evaluate the efficacy of criminological theories in explaining crime and responses to crime. Upon completing this course, students will be able to apply criminological theories to crime prevention and criminal justice programs. Theories covered will vary from year to year but are likely to include: social process and control theories, theories of crime and place, developmental theories, and theories of criminal justice.
title: Applied Criminological Theory
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: Students in 7063HSV Critical Reflective Practice and Leadership will develop knowledge and skills about critical theory, critical thinking and critical reflection. They will learn to critically analyse their own practice and how to maintain a critical gaze/agenda. Students will consolidate and articulate their practice framework.
title: Critical Reflective Practice and Leadership
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: 1080LHS (Spanish 1A) is designed for absolute beginners. Using a communicative approach to language learning and teaching, 1080LHS provides you with an initial competence in oral and written Spanish upon which to build in 1081LHS. As a 10CP course, 1080LHS comprises approximately 150 hours of work in total. No prior knowledge is required.
title: Spanish 1A
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Chinese 2B is a second-year Chinese language course that focuses on the use of Mandarin Chinese in both Chinese and Australian contexts. The teaching materials are presented as a series of topics that are organised into thematic units consisting of dialogues, communicative activities and tasks that will be completed in introductory and tutorial sessions each week. Students will use the linguistic and cultural content and skills learnt to communicate in real-life situations. NOTE: Any student who are native/proficient speakers of Mandarin Chinese or has completed their secondary education in a Mandarin or Cantonese speaking country is NOT ELIGIBLE to enroll in this course. Prerequisites: 2010LHS / 2010LAL Modern Standard Chinese (Mandarin) 2A OR equivalent level of proficiency certified by means of a one-to-one interview administered by our Chinese teaching staff. Co-requisites: NIL Incompatible: 2063LHS Modern Standard Chinese (Mandarin) 2B, CHN22 Modern Standard Chinese (Mandarin) 2B or CHN222 Modern Standard Chinese (Mandarin) 2B.
title: Modern Standard Chinese (Mandarin) 2B Enhanced
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course follows on from 1090LHS Italian 1A. It is offered in semi-intensive (6 weeks) online mode (synchronous classes) in Trimester 3 and on-campus and online in Trimester 2. It enables students to further develop their listening comprehension skills, to increase their fluency and accuracy in speaking and to identify and apply the patterns required for writing the language. The study of a variety of written texts helps students both to expand their vocabulary and to acquire basic skills and strategies required for the reading of Italian texts. Class recordings are made available for study and revision purposes. If you have not completed Italian 1A and would like to join this course, please contact the Italian Studies Coordinator. Prerequisites: 1090LHS Italian 1A OR equivalent; Co-requisites: NIL; Incompatible: NIL.
title: Italian 1B
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Building on 2080LHS and 2082LHS, 2083LHS is a 20-credit point course which continues a broadly communicative approach to language learning to progress you towards the B2 Vantage level of proficiency of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, thereby preparing you for advanced Spanish language study. Run in conjunction with 2081LHS, 2083LHS includes an additional workshop and additional assessment which uses authentic and semi-authentic oral and written materials to further focus on listening and reading comprehension, and written expression. Prerequisites: 2080LHS or 2082LHS or admission via a placement test administered by our Spanish teaching staff. Corequisites: nil. Incompatible: 2081LHS. When a student hasn't met either prerequisite 2080LHS or 2082LHS, an equivalent level of proficiency certified by means of a placement test administered by our Spanish teaching staff will be accepted.
title: Spanish 2B (Enhanced)
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course is designed for students who have no prior knowledge of Japanese language. It leads students to a level of language proficiency necessary to engage in the most basic everyday situations. Students will become familiar with Hiragana and Katakana, and will be able to read and write 58 kanji. It satisfies prerequisites for 1033LHS Japanese 1B. It is recommended that students with prior knowledge of the Japanese language do not enrol in this course without first consulting the course convenor about their knowledge level.
title: Japanese 1A
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This is an intermediate course for students who have successfully completed Japanese 2B (2042LHS or 2045LHS) or similar, or have reached an equivalent level of proficiency (e.g. N4 in the Japanese Language Proficiency Test). It leads students to a level of proficiency necessary to engage effectively and confidently in everyday situations, with an increased use of authentic materials and digital tools in the course. NOTE: This course cannot be taken simultaneously with 1032LHS or 1033LHS or 2040LHS or 2043LHS.
title: Japanese 3A
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course provides an introduction to key aspects of contemporary Japanese culture and lifestyle, exploring social structure, family life, education, the workplace, and popular culture. No prior knowledge of the Japanese language is required, as the course is conducted entirely in English. In addition to examining these topics, students will develop essential research and communication skills, including synthesising and analysing various sources, essay writing, problem-solving, and cultivating scholarly habits of inquiry and argumentation. As a 10CP course, 2406LHS requires approximately 150 hours of total work.
title: Japanese Society and Pop Culture
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: "Youth" is a sociological construct that operates at multiple levels: an individual young person, an attitude for being in the social world, and an institution. This course explores the two main branches of sociological research into the lives of young people: youth cultures and youth transitions. The course introduces students to a range of social divisions (for example, sexuality, rurality) , social institutions (such as, education, family) and social identities (including, subcultural, digital) that frame the experience of youth and draws on local, national and international examples to illustrate young peoples' negotiations of contemporary society.
title: Youth in Society
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course will teach you the fundamental principles of communicating ideas and information effectively through typography within broader historical, social, and cultural contexts. Through studio-based projects, you will engage with essential concepts such as unrepresented voices in contemporary type, type anatomy and nomenclature, legibility and readability, type for print and digital screens, typeface semiotics and selections, visual hierarchy, and grid layout systems. By the end of the course, you will develop the ability to apply contemporary typographic practices to print and screen projects.
title: Typography and Layout
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course involves the execution of the research proposal, including experimentation, and analysis of research results, under the guidance of two or more supervisors. It also involves the preparation of the completed Masters Thesis including research aims, hypotheses, significance, literature review, experimental design, methods, results and conclusions. Pre requisites: 6001HLS Dissertation Preparation
title: Research Thesis
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course involves the execution of the research proposal, including experimentation, and analysis of research results, under the guidance of two or more supervisors. It also involves the preparation of the completed Masters Thesis including research aims, hypotheses, significance, literature review, experimental design, methods, results and conclusions.
title: Research Thesis
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: 1812MED Expanding Paramedic continues to build on this foundational knowledge built in 1811MED by expanding on the systematic clinical approach to manage the unconscious and/or cardiac arrest patient. In this course students will continue to build professional identity and interpersonal communication skills. Prerequisite is 1811MED Introduction to Paramedic Practice, 1014MSC Cells Tissues and Regulation, 1016MSC Anatomy and Physiology Systems, 1804NRS Psychosocial Development across the Lifespan and Co-Req 1017MSC Anatomy and Physiology Systems 11 and 1205MED Health Challenges for the 21st Century.
title: Expanding Paramedic Practice
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: Primary Maternity Care in Context enables students to investigate the theoretical aspects underpinning inter-disciplinary primary maternity care. At its core, primary maternity care views pregnancy, childbirth, postnatal transition to parenthood and breastfeeding as essentially physiological life experiences. Primary maternity carers, usually but not exclusively midwives and general practitioners, provide continuity of maternity care for healthy childbearing women across the peri-conception, antenatal, intrapartum and postnatal trajectory. The context of primary maternity care in this course is the student's own professional discipline and national / international best practice. Primary maternity care in context is framed by two complementary and overlapping constructs: the Philosophy of Primary Maternity Care, and the Principles of Primary Maternity Care.
title: Primary Maternity Care in Context
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: This course explores the future of design via experimentation with theories, strategies and practices. A basic understanding of innovation will be developed and then placed in the contexts of design, culture, futures and economy; the history of the concept; and contemporary demands for innovation methods and products, including the notion of creative leaps and the process of incremental progression.
title: Design for Social Impact
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course examines the effective management of food and beverage (F and B) operation within the hospitality industry, including international standard hotels and resorts. Students will be exposed to the application of sustainable practices applicable to F and B outlet's design as well as the development of systems and processes through Virtual Fields Trips, and other resources.
title: International Food and Beverage Management
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This course will provide students with the opportunity to apply sustainability principles to the management of various types of events, so that the environmental, socio-cultural and economic impacts of these are optimised.
title: Sustainable Event Operations and Management
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This 10 credit point elective course is available to all postgraduate Griffith Business School students. Its purpose is to allow students to explore potential career paths and apply the necessary skills for a successful transition from university to the workforce. Throughout the course, students will develop insights into the attributes that contribute to their ability to make meaningful impact. Designed to complement students' participation in internships with organisations such as small and medium enterprises, multinational corporations, government departments, and non-profits. This course offers flexibility in delivery, including face-to-face, virtual or hybrid formats. Internship opportunities extend beyond South-East Queensland, encompassing regional and remote areas of Australia as well as other capital cities. Enrolment in this course is contingent upon completion of an application process in addition to successfully securing an internship placement. Students are encouraged to take ownership of their career development and utilise support resources available through Griffith CareerHub. Students may bring their own internship experience (paid or unpaid) or apply for a range of unpaid internship opportunities sourced by Griffith Business School - though these positions are competitive and not guaranteed. To begin the application process, please contact gbsinternships@griffith.edu.au. Please note: This course is not available for credit based on prior studies or external activities. Fluency in written and spoken English is required.
title: PG Business Internship I
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

description: Environmental Planning Studio is a foundation course within the Urban and Environmental Planning programs. The course addresses discipline specific content aligned with an introduction to generic academic skills including critical thinking, written and oral communication, research skills and reflective learning practices. Learning and teaching activities within the course are designed to encourage students to develop and hone these generic academic skills. The discipline specific planning content covered in the course includes definitions of planning, history of planning, formal and informal planning frameworks, and the spatial and temporal scales through which planning occurs. Students are also introduced to notions of environment and environmental sustainability, to build an understanding of the evolution and practice of urban and environmental planning.
title: Environmental Planning Studio
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: In The Storytellers: Reading Fiction, you will read, discuss and write about some major Anglo-American literary works written over the past 200 years. This course provides a comprehensive introduction to concepts, tools and techniques required for the analysis of fiction and verse. Further, the course will explore the historical development of various genres and chart the movement from realism to Modernism. The Storytellers: Reading Fiction aims to develop the disciplinary grounding necessary for advanced literary studies, but also to introduce you to practices of individual reading and writing that lay the foundations for lifelong learning.
title: The Storytellers: Reading Fiction
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course provides an introduction to art practices from a range of cultures and periods. Students will gain an understanding of key art historical and theoretical concepts as well as the social, cultural, political and religious contexts for art. This course must be successfully completed prior to commencing 2nd year level art theory courses. Prerequisites: NIL
title: Introduction to Art Theory
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This 50 Credit Point course provides the individually supervised context in which a student may complete written and (where appropriate) practical work for a dissertation/project at one-year Honours level in the humanities, languages and social sciences. Assessment is by Dissertation (100% weighting, between 15,000- 18,000 words) or by Creative or Professional product (60% weighting) with a minor dissertation/exegesis (40% weighting, between 5,500 and 7,500 words).
title: Dissertation/Project
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course explores the basic principles of Accent Method Breathing and aims to provide students with a solid practical skill level as well as sufficient knowledge and understanding to use Accent Method effectively as a pedagogical tool. This course is designed for vocal postgraduate students, especially in vocal pedagogy but is suitable for other vocal/instrumental post graduate students.
title: Accent Method Breathing
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course explores issues, crisis and disasters communication within a range of contexts drawing on case studies, theory and practice. Students develop the skills to build a crisis communication response plan and team, and effectively manage communication during a crisis.
title: Crisis and Disaster Communication
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This postgraduate course in Digital Investigations offers an in-depth exploration of the digital forensic process, equipping students with advanced skills in uncovering and analysing digital evidence across a spectrum of devices and environments. The course delves into various digital forensic techniques, including disk forensics, network forensics, memory forensics, and mobile device forensics, enabling students to excel in the dynamic field of digital investigations. Upon completion of this course, students will possess advanced expertise in digital investigations, with a focus on various forensic analysis techniques. Graduates will be prepared to lead or contribute significantly to digital investigations, cybercrime cases, and incident response efforts in a wide range of industries and organizations.
title: Digital Investigations
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: In this course students will learn about new technologies to improve building performance, about building and site services, facilities management, and green retrofits. The subject covers building pathology from defect recognition and diagnosis to remedial works. The focus is on the project and building scale. The latest innovations and emerging technologies are also highlighted.
title: Sustainable Construction
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course is the first of eight courses that comprise the Graduate Diploma of Australian Migration Law and Practice. The Graduate Diploma of Australian Migration Law and Practice is one of the prescribed academic qualifications for registration as a migration agent in Australia. This course covers the foundation aspects of Australian migration legislation and policy and provides an introduction to legal research using LEGENDcom. This course provides students with a sound knowledge of the importance of the legislative and policy framework in the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), Migration Regulations 1994 (Cth) including fundamental visa application processes. The companion course to 7131LAW is 7231LAW (Practitioner Skills) which simultaneously builds on the practical background to immerse students in a virtual office environment. Like the other companion courses in the Graduate Diploma Program, in 7231LAW students will learn and apply practitioner skills they need to effectively integrate the legislative content they acquire in 7131LAW. 7131LAW is offered in online mode only.
title: Foundations of Australian Migration Law and Practice
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course is one of two final courses comprising the Graduate Diploma of Australian Migration Law and Practice. The Graduate Diploma of Australian Migration Law and Practice is a prescribed academic qualification for registration as a migration agent in Australia. 7134LAW is a multi-faceted project-based course that provides students with the opportunity to integrate and consolidate the skills and knowledge that they have acquired in the previous six courses and the companion course 7234LAW. Students are immersed in a virtual office in which they have sole responsibility for managing client enquiries and running a client matter from initial client contact and file creation to file closure. In addition, students also have the opportunity to organise an optional external supervised work placement with a registered migration agent or migration lawyer. 7134LAW is the companion course to 7234LAW as it builds on skills and knowledge taught in 7234LAW that focus on professional ethics and establishing and managing a migration practice. Like the other companion courses in the Graduate Diploma Program, in 7134LAW, students learn and apply the practitioner skills they need to effectively integrate the legislative content they acquire in 7234LAW (and have acquired in the previous six courses). As such, in addition to the horizontal alignment between 7234LAW & 7134LAW, both courses are also aligned with all of the courses in the Program. The deliberate alignment and capstone nature of this course allows students to progress logically through the growing complexity of both legal and practitioner skills culminating in this self-directed simulation of life as a registered migration agent.
title: Applied Migration Law and Practice
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: The course explores sociological thinking on the origins, construction and political implications of identity. It will review classical conceptualizations and then examine the shift toward contemporary understandings that view identity as dynamic, fluid and fragmentary. The main focus will be on the questions how people learn to produce and reproduce themselves through engagement in social interaction and how interactional dynamics shape their sense of who they are.
title: Sociology of Identity
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: In this course, students will engage in a comprehensive examination of the substantive law, rules, and policies governing criminal justice in Queensland. The course covers a series of related criminal procedural issues and the sentencing process in the context of criminal investigations, trials, and appeals. Each week, legal, ethical, and policy issues relevant to substantive and procedural matters will be studied, discussed, and critically reflected upon. You will be encouraged to consider the effectiveness and fairness of Australia's adversarial criminal justice system. You will learn to interpret and apply the general principles and statutory laws governing criminal procedure.
title: Crime 2
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course develops students' knowledge of, and capacity to operate in, the policy-making world. Its underlying philosophy is that a change in public policy equates to a change in society itself.
title: Public Policy for Change
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course presents a general overview of the key issues and theories in the area of intercultural communication. Using a wide variety of authentic materials, tasks and media, this course adopts a thematic approach to explore how people communicate both within and across various cultural settings. Prerequisites: NIL Co-requisites: NIL Incompatible: 3222LAL Intercultural Communication Enhanced
title: Intercultural Communication
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course gives students an application based understanding of the key management skills necessary for formulating and implementing effective strategic planning.
title: Strategic Airline and Airport Management
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course examines how marketing concepts, frameworks and techniques developed for commercial marketers are adapted to influence behaviour at a societal level. It provides the fundamental principles of social marketing, overviews key theories/models of behaviour change, and examines the role of planning and research in developing social marketing strategies to achieve positive social change. The course emphasises the importance of systematic scoping to ensure that the social issue and a range of interventional options are properly considered prior to the development of social marketing change strategies.
title: Marketing for Social Change
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This course introduces students to the scope of speech pathology practice and evidence-based practice, across the lifespan. The activities focus on developing and applying the skills, knowledge, and personal qualities required for supporting communication and/or swallowing in individuals and communities. Under the supervision of a speech pathology practice educator, students attend placement/s in student groups to develop observation, transcription, and reporting skills, along with foundation skills in assessment, interpretation, and management. Content and skill development is further addressed through participation in skills-based tutorials and a simulated learning experience. Competencies required for speech pathology practice are informed by and assessed using the Professional Standards (Speech Pathology Australia, 2020).
title: Speech Pathology Skills and Practice 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

This Trimester 3 course will be offered in intensive mode, full time, each day of Weeks 1-3 of Trimester 3.

Students are required to complete 200 hours (minimum) on-site supervised practice in a suitable rehabilitation counselling professional context. The course will focus on facilitating students' development of the skills, knowledges, attitudes and analyses necessary to enter the Rehabilitation Counselling profession. Students must complete their 200 hour professional placement in their final trimester of study to ensure maximum course work learning is applied to the placement.
title: Rehabilitation Counselling Practicum
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course examines wealth management from both individual and institutional perspectives in relation to formulating investment strategies. This includes developing an understanding of behavioural biases in individual and group decision-making, consumer psychology and market asymmetries, the role of human capital in asset portfolios, using a range of asset allocation methods, and having an awareness of the challenges facing institutional asset managers in a contemporary business environment. Institutional asset managers include pension, endowment, foundations, insurance and bank funds.
title: Behavioural Finance and Wealth Management
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This subject introduces students to the criminal justice process using the crime of homicide. Starting with a focus on the key elements of the crime event, including the current state of homicide in Australia and abroad, students will develop an understanding of serious violent offences through the lens of offenders and victims of violence. Students then learn how the criminal justice system responds to serious violence offences through an examination of the interconnectedness of the police, courts, and correctional agencies. Students will learn how serious violent offences are detected and investigated by the police and move on to an understanding of how these offences are processed in the courts, which includes the criminal trial and sentencing. Students review the various forms of custodial sentencing and will be introduced to concepts of rehabilitation and desistance. Throughout the subject students review the ways that criminological theory has informed the crime of homicide, as well as the criminal justice system and social responses to homicide.
title: Homicide
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: Medical Nutrition Therapy is the evidence-based process used by Dietitians to treat nutrition-related problems in individuals. The course starts by describing the principles of evidence-based research and how they are applied to Medical Nutrition Therapy. The course covers applications in chronic disease and malnutrition. The main areas encountered in dietetics (including adult weight management, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and malnutrition screening and assessment) are covered in the course through lectures and tutorials including case presentations. This course forms the foundation for Medical Nutrition Therapy 2, which completes the coverage of disease states encountered by dietitians, particularly in the hospital inpatient setting.
title: Medical Nutrition Therapy 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

This course is designed to sharpen students' ability to think strategically and realise effective outcomes for organisations that are responsible, sustainable and globally focused. This course is normally offered every 8 teaching periods.

It provides a foundation in the mathematical sciences for later studies in science and engineering. description: Organisations typically use many disparate technologies to achieve their business objectives. This course first gives an overview of low-level technologies such as programming with a focus on code reuse, scripting techniques and software configuration tools. description: This course will interrogate meanings of gender and the law's interplay with gender. Students will study theoretical concepts of gender, feminism, masculinities and aspects of queer theory. They will consider how the law is gendered and how gender influences law, using examples around women's issues, masculinities and transgender issues. As examples of the law's interaction with gender, the course will include aspects of health law, family law, criminal law and legal approaches to assignment of gender.
title: Gender and the Law
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

Through hands-on learning students will apply science fundamentals to the systematic investigation, interpretation, and analysis of some engineering problems. It will be assumed that students have the knowledge equivalent to a grade of SA over 4 semesters in Mathematical Methods (Qld high school subject) or equivalent study, or 1017SCG Foundation Mathematics (grade of 4 or higher). Topics covered include Newtonian mechanics and electrical principles.

academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This subject will provide a practical understanding of how risk assessment and management is utilised within forensic mental health. This will include a foundation of the key principles for evaluating risk assessment tools, management processes and professional writing in forensic mental health. This course will provide students with an understanding of how these principles apply in the assessment and management of different offender populations (violent offending, sexual offending, stalking and juvenile). Students will apply their learning to a number of client case studies across these population groups and develop practical skills in professional risk assessment report writing.
title: Advanced Risk Assessment and Management in Forensic Mental Health
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

Students will develop skills to search for and identify credible evidence and explore how quality evidence translates to clinical practice. Students will learn the basic elements of the research process that underpin how evidence-based knowledge is attained. Students will develop informatics skills foundational for clinical practice and life-long learning. Prerequisites: NIL Corequisites: NIL Incompatible: NIL

academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

This course will culminate in students submitting a written Dissertation and providing a verbal presentation of their research and associated study findings.

description: This course explores the effects of sedentary behaviour and physical inactivity on population health, and the current knowledge-base surrounding exercise as a preventative / management measure for some common lifestyle-related diseases. In compliment, the course advances some of the foundational approaches underpinning exercise assessments from pre-exercise screening requirements, through to lab- and field-based exercise testing selections, and their contextual selection based on client needs.
title: Exercise, Health and Disease
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course introduces students to key motor learning and control concepts relating to exercise and sport contexts. Upon completion of the course students will have developed the ability to interpret, contrast, and evaluate a range of motor learning and control approaches, theories and models. Students will also develop a practical appreciation of key concepts in terms of designing effective skill acquisition and performance environments for exercise and sport settings.
title: Motor Learning and Control
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: 'Youth' is a sociological construct that operates at multiple levels: an individual young person, an attitude for being in the social world, and an institution. We explore the two main branches of sociological research into the lives of young people; youth cultures and youth transitions. You are introduced to a range of social identities (for example, sexuality, rurality), social institutions (such as education, family), and social identities (including subcultural, digital) that frame the experience of youth and draws on local, national and international examples to illustrate young peoples' negotiations of contemporary society.
title: Sociology of Youth
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

Prior Assumed: Successful completion at senior level Mathematical Methods or equivalent study over four semesters of a high school subject that includes the study of calculus. description: The aviation industry today is fiercely competitive, operating in a highly dynamic and global environment. Aviation businesses require aviation professionals with the knowledge, understanding and skills to be able to deliver sustainable and competitive products and services in this challenging climate. This course builds on principles of the air transport industry, infrastructure considerations, management functions specific to the airline environment and general management functions in aviation business. While concentrating on the contemporary issues affecting the aviation industry, the course emphasizes practical managerial applications within aviation organizations.
title: Contemporary Aviation Management
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course equips students with a good knowledge of planning law with particular reference to the law in Queensland. The course involves statutory interpretation, case law analysis and a contextual critique of the Planning Act, Qld, 2016. It includes a case study of planning and climate change and a research component allowing students to focus on an aspect of planning law of particular interest to themselves.
title: Advanced Urban Planning Law
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: There has been a rapid increase in the number of practices purported to be effective in supporting people on the autism spectrum. Being able to identify whether these have scientific support and respect the autistic person's goals and aspirations are important when considering selecting a practice. This course provides students with a framework for selecting effective supports which combines respecting an individual's value and beliefs, evaluating the evidence, and applying a collaborative approach.
title: Evaluating the evidence: What counts?
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course surveys the comparative political economy of East Asia, a highly dynamic region and one of critical importance to Australia's economic prosperity and security. It examines nine countries, including China, Japan, Korea, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. Within these national settings, it focuses on government interventions in national economies and business involvement in politics, and activities that have helped to shape different rates of economic growth and political openness.
title: Business and Politics in the Asia Pacific
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

description: This course examines the relationship between religion, politics and ideological extremism from the mid-twentieth century to the present. It explores the social, political and historical contexts in which extremist ideas and movements emerge, together with related concepts including radicalisation, political violence and terrorism. Particular attention is given to extremist manifestations associated with Islamist, Zionist and Far-Right ideologies, examining their beliefs, narratives, political objectives, organisational forms and use of violence. The course also considers the factors and conditions that contribute to radicalisation and extremism, and critically examines approaches to prevention, countering violent extremism and responses to terrorism.
title: Religion, Politics, and Ideological Extremism
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course is part of a series of courses in which students plan and execute a substantial piece of research, which is reported in the form of a thesis or creative/professional product with dissertation. The thesis or dissertation will investigate a topic that is relevant to the student and would normally be expected to be approximately 30,000 words. This research is designed to build on previously studied research courses that have developed student's understandings of current social, cultural and educational theories, research methodologies and design. The main objective of the thesis or dissertation is to provide students with the opportunity to engage in a major piece of research in the Humanities within a relevant discipline. By doing this they will come to understand better the nature and dynamics of the discipline and to demonstrate the capability to work at a high level in the application of theory and research skills to a substantial piece of research and to further doctoral study.
title: Dissertation 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Universal Interiors extends students' understanding of interior and spatial design with a focus on designing for social issues, diversity and inclusion. Through a combination of lectures, readings and studio-based exercises, students will explore phenomenology, the senses, and typological studies that centre on human experience and difference. The course introduces inclusive and multi-sensory design methods, alongside relevant Australian Standards and Universal Design principles, to inform spatially and socially responsive design decisions. Students will apply this knowledge to a major project, designing an inclusive social space that responds to the needs of a chosen client or community, and communicating this design intent clearly through verbal, visual, written and digital documentation.
title: Inclusive Environments
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: Students will undertake a research project relevant to their area of specialisation under the guidance of one, two or more supervisors. The project will involve original research and will be under the direct supervision of an academic staff member.

academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This is a 10CP version of 2011LHS, a second-year course focusing on the use of Mandarin Chinese in both Chinese and Australian contexts. Students will use the linguistic and cultural content and skills learnt to communicate in real-life situations. NOTE: Any student who is native/proficient speakers of Mandarin Chinese or has completed their secondary education in a Mandarin or Cantonese speaking country is NOT ELIGIBLE to enroll in this course. Prerequisites: 2010LHS / 2010LAL Modern Standard Chinese (Mandarin) 2A OR equivalent level of proficiency certified by means of a one-to-one interview administered by our Chinese teaching staff. Co-requisites: NIL Incompatible: 2011LHS Modern Standard Chinese (Mandarin) 2B Enhanced, CHN22 Modern Standard Chinese (Mandarin) 2B or CHN222 Modern Standard Chinese (Mandarin) 2B.

academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course introduces the basic concepts and principles of accounting with special emphasis given to the use and interpretation of financial accounting information. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to read, prepare and interpret financial statements and they will have gained an appreciation of their uses and limitations in practical and applied ways.
title: Small Business Accounting
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: In this course, students will learn how to assess and measure behaviour in a scientific and clinically effective manner. Using case studies, students will learn to define, collect, and analyse behavioural data relating to behaviours that are important in people's lives.
title: Assessing and Measuring Behaviour
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: A major objective of this subject is the generation of retirement planning strategies. Assessment items reflect the challenging demands of an industry which seeks to ensure all Australians enjoy a comfortable and self-funded retirement. Therefore it is expected that students are knowledgeable of technical and regulatory issues, skilful in strategic thinking and analysis and aware of contemporary issues in the superannuation and retirement context.
title: Superannuation and Retirement
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course focuses on developing skills to engage with clients in a real-world context and is delivered by experienced industry professionals via online learning over twelve weeks. This course maps to a number of National Financial Adviser Curriculum core knowledge areas. In particular, we focus on client relationships and consumer behaviour, which includes coverage of the following: Communication in a professional context, providing information about services to clients (FSG, PDS), collecting information from clients and setting goals, understanding self and others, interpersonal communication skills, the importance of client cues and prompts such as body language, tone of voice, how to create and build trust, fiduciary duty, ethical and professional conduct, legislated 'client best interests' requirement, risk profiling vs investment behaviour, managing the ongoing relationship and conflict resolution.
title: Financial Planning Skills
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This subject provides students with a broad overview of personal financial advice and the role of financial advisers in a dynamic environment. Students apply the knowledge and skills covered in this course to discussions of contemporary issues, such as ethics, regulation, technology and government policy, and authentic financial planning tasks.
title: Financial Planning 1
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: In Social Sciences 2 students continue to develop their knowledge and skills in communication in dentistry, First Peoples health and practice, and apply previously gained concepts and knowledge to oral health promotion on both an individual and community level. title: Social Sciences 2
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course consists of two modules. - Classical Electrodynamics (5 weeks) and Quantum Electrodynamics (7 weeks). Students will gain a basic understanding of the theory and its applications, be able to communicate this understanding, and to solve simple problems. Advanced topics may vary by offering. Assumed knowledge: Students enrolled in this course are expected to have completed an undergraduate science degree with a physics major (including content covered in 2301NSC Electromagnetism and Optics and 3301NSC Quantum Physics III)
title: Classical and Quantum Electrodynamics
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: Can well-being promotion become a core focus of your leadership? This course will demonstrate the value of applied knowledge in the workplace. You will critically evaluate theories of well-being and the research that examines its value in various industries. The lessons extend to leader self-care as part of an organisational framework to well-being. Your examination of applied theory will give you the framework to conduct an evaluation of your own and others' leadership styles, strategies, and practices and how they support and sustain mental well-being and resilience in people, organisations, and institutions. These critical reflections can be applied to your own leadership style in relation to leading theories of health and well-being promotion and how you can expand these ideas in your sphere of influence. You will move from theories and models of leadership through to case study analyses and micro-policy framework development and finish with a thorough knowledge of the application of leadership strategies and frameworks that underpin and support employee well-being in a workplace.
title: Leadership for Wellbeing
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: Honours Research Project constitutes a 40CP honours research commitment within the Bachelor of Design with Honours program. Each of the four components of the course combine to introduce students to the rigors of research and engage them in an advanced level of study within visual practice. The expectation is that the research project undertaken will be based within the visual and incorporates high levels of visual literacy. Assessment of the four courses will culminate in one assessment item. Co-requisite/Pre-requisite: 6511QCA Design Research Methods.

academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design
