description: Forensic mental health is an area of specialisation that involves the assessment and treatment of client's who are both mentally disordered and whose behaviour has led to or could possibly lead to offending. Forensic mental health as a field therefore represents the interface between community safety and client centred practice. The two key intervention targets in FMH are mental disorders and problem behaviours. This course will address the first of these targets by providing students with knowledge of general mental health interventions and components of recovery/recovery processes. Students will also be provided with skills in the delivery of specific intervention strategies targeting the most common mental health presentations in FMH. Students will also be provided with the opportunity to practice the skill of treatment plan development and role play delivery of specific strategies. Incompatible: CCJ750 Interventions and Recovery in Forensic Mental Health
title: Interventions and Recovery in Forensic Mental Health
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: Public financial management is an 'applied' discipline, and one that is international in scope. It covers a range of resource management practices that underpin policy-making in contemporary government, including fiscal rules to guide government spending and borrowing, multi-year expenditure frameworks that capture the longer term impacts of current policy decisions, and performance-based budgeting to inform the level and relative priority of funding allocations. PFM practices permeate the information and systems that govern the everyday decision-making of public managers, and all of them operate at the messy intersection between bureaucratic processes and evidence, and political imperatives and risk. In this course you will get to grips with these practical realities. You will be equipped with key conceptual and practical knowledge to integrate financial and non-financial performance in the public sector, and how to apply it to generate public value. Using interactive teaching approaches you will learn from senior PFM practitioners and acquire skills to critically appraise the key institutions and practices that manage and account for public resources and public policies.
title: Public Financial Management
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

description: Chronic disease is one of our greatest health challenges, accounting for a high proportion of all deaths in Australia. Within a multi-disciplinary setting, physiotherapists improve quality of life for people living with complex or chronic conditions. The aim of this course is to enable you to successfully manage clients with complex or chronic conditions using an integrated model of care. The focus will be on using valid and reliable outcome measures for assessment and development of clinical reasoning to determine a suitable evidence-based management plan. You will be required to integrate knowledge of medico-legal, cultural, ethical and professional issues with physiotherapy knowledge and clinical skills that are necessary to function competently as a physiotherapist.
title: Integrated Case Management in Physiotherapy
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

This course will equip students with effective science communication skills to communicate key messages, as well as engage with non-scientists, including policy makers and the public. Topics covered will include streamlined writing and presentation skills, science advocacy, and media training.
title: Strategies for Effective Science Communication
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: The aim of this course is for students to develop an understanding of common psychological problems across the lifespan. Students will learn about diagnostic frameworks and assessment methods for mental health and cognitive functioning. Students will also examine the process of case conceptualisation based on psychological theory.

Throughout trimester students will refine their learning and skills through an integrated group activity in an immersive simulated serious pharmacy game, comprising numerous mini activities. Students will collaboratively run their own pharmacies and also undertake individual activities that prepare them for pharmacy internship and their pharmacy careers. Students will refine and demonstrate core practical and cognitive pharmacy skills including clinical decision making, interprofessional and person-centred communication, and application of current evidence to deliver health promotion and / or education.

title: Quality Use of Medicines in Practice

It includes aspects of cell biology, molecular biology and immunology as relevant to veterinary and human diseases. Students will explore state-of-the-art techniques used in biotechnology through a 'journal club' strategy and present reports on the techniques.

academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

One module will provide the know-how skills for acquiring intelligence on competitors, the latest products and technologies, markets and costing of new products.
title: Topics in Biotechnology
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

Students will undertake a research project relevant to their area of specialisation under the guidance of one or more supervisors appointed by the Honours Program Director (in consultation with the student). The topic and nature of the Research Project will be determined through consultation and mutual agreement of the student and supervisor and approved by the Honours Program Director. The project will involve original research and will be under the direct supervision of an academic staff member.
title: Honours Dissertation
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: Sexuality saturates modern life. Our sexual and gender identities signal our selfhood to others and define who we are, whether straight, queer, trans or gender diverse, or one of many other possibilities. Sex is everywhere, from the sheets to the streets, to the internet. How we present ourselves, who we are intimate with, what we do and how often we do it is the subject of commentary, intervention, and regulation. But who has determined what's 'unnatural' and what's 'normal' and when? What have historical actors, experts and institutions said in the past about sex? And have ordinary people always followed the rules? This unit explores histories of sexuality from antiquity to the present. Taking a chronological approach to private practices and erotic lives, we will investigate diverse topics, including prostitution, marriage, crossdressing, birth control, war, chastity, queer lives, and the internet, to identify historical change and continuity. The course focuses on practices, identities and attitudes in Europe, the US, and Australia to consider how gender, class and ethnicity inflect public narratives and intimate lives. Using primary sources and historical objects, you will investigate the meanings people and institutions attach to desire, bodies, and sexuality at different times and places and interrogate our contemporary sexual lives and their possibilities.
title: Histories of Sexuality
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: In the 500 years between 1300 and 1800 (CE), the peoples of the world came into ever closer contact with one another. Contact led to sustained engagements in commerce, war, empire, and colonisation. The effects of these complex patterns of interaction across the globe in this period gave rise to new ways of seeing the world, new ways of interpreting nature, and new ways of understanding its human inhabitants. This course will introduce you to the study of world history by focussing on salient themes in the emergence of the some of the modern world. Themes on which we will focus include: (1) Polities: tribes, nations, states and empires; (2) Trade and world history; (3) The crucible of war; (4) A world of disease; (5) The natural world; (6) Global Visions or World civilization?
title: Themes in World History
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Language Testing and Assessment develops your understanding of core language assessment concepts, particularly test design and analysis. You will learn about how language assessment fits within the broader context of language teaching. You will also gain the ability to analyse and evaluate language testing practices, and gain insight into some of the social, educational and political forces which underpin language testing.
title: Language Testing and Assessment
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course uses the Philip C. Jessup International Law Moot Competition to enable students to gain significant experience in written and oral advocacy in international law before a simulated international tribunal. As the International Law Students Association highlights, "Jessup is the world's largest moot court competition, with participants from roughly 700 law schools in 100 countries and jurisdictions. The Competition is a simulation of a fictional dispute between countries before the International Court of Justice, the judicial organ of the United Nations". Members of the Griffith Law School Jessup team are all expected to prepare the written memorials and participate in the internal Griffith practice moots. The team then participates in the Australian rounds of the Jessup Moot competition and, if the team reaches the Final of the Australian rounds, it would compete in the International Rounds. There is a maximum of 5 team members. Selection for team membership is competitive and involve consideration of an applicant's transcript, prior mooting or debating experience, and an interview. Applications for selection for the Summer Jessup Moot team close in second Trimester the year prior. Information on application process is available at the Griffith Law School Organisation site on Learning@Griffith.
title: Jessup International Moot
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course represents the main research component of the program. Students will gather and analyse data, document and present findings in the form of a dissertation which is potentially publishable in a peer-reviewed journal.
title: Master of Clinical Dentistry Research Project 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course provides a broad introduction to the law of contracts. We will examine which promises are legally binding and how contracts are formed. We will also be examining the different categorisations of contracts and the contents and effects of contracts. This course provides students with an understanding of contractual principles which will be built upon in 7730LAW Contracts 2. THIS COURSE IS ONLY OPEN TO LAW STUDENTS.
title: Contracts 1
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: Evidence Law aims to introduce students to the law governing proof in civil and criminal litigation. The subject matter of the course includes study of doctrinal rules in relation to the differentiated roles of judge and jury, evidential and persuasive burdens of proof, the standards of proof, admissibility of evidence, testimony, privilege and judicial warnings. There will also be consideration of the principles underlying particular doctrinal rules. Emphasis will be on the rules of evidence pursuant to provisions of the Evidence Act 1977 (Qld) and common law. Materials from other jurisdictions may be considered to elucidate principles relevant to practice in Queensland and elsewhere. THIS COURSE IS ONLY OPEN TO LAW STUDENTS.
title: Evidence
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course enhances the breadth and depth of students' critical understanding of safety leadership, investigating topics such as organizational culture, measurement, sense-making, complexity and resilience. Students engage critically with a varying literature that connects to their professional concerns and questions.

academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Operative Architectural History has the fundamental goal of providing students with an operative approach to architectural history. Focusing on the Twentieth Century, the course investigates influential architectural projects, theoretical writings and design practices from across the period. Parallel with analogical historical design issues are drawn and design strategies extrapolated. Economic, social, cultural, and technical aspects are reflected in the selected architectural exemplars' critical analysis. Students will work across the analysis of critical texts, the production of interpretative drawings, models and short reflective texts to unfold and develop intellectual tools to understand the recent and distant past. Finally, students will apply the knowledge and skill acquired to operatively and successfully engage with the architecture discipline's present and future challenges. Incompatible with 2903ENV.
title: Operative Architectural History
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: Design Studio 1 and Design Studio 2 are complementary studio-based courses. Design Studio 2 supports students in developing skills to investigate the nature of place. Through a series of exercises, students will look at the relationships between planning, architectural compositions and construction components. Students will investigate the integration of the architectural artefact with its surroundings and the planning frameworks that inform this. Plans and sections are not only representation tools, they are instruments to generate new ideas and concepts relevant to Architecture, Planning and Design. The course encourages students to build skills across a range of manual and digital media in order to document technical and conceptual aspects (diagrams/graphic/written).
title: Studio 2 Sectioned Spaces and Places
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: Construction Materials and Practice is designed to provide students with a basic understanding of the principal materials used in construction. The subject focuses on how design ideas are translated into built form through the process of construction. It reviews the form each of these materials takes and investigates how these materials are used in construction components, assemblies and buildings. Students learn about how construction information is communicated in technical drawings, and about the material properties that underpin the form and fabric of the built environment. Incompatible with 2914ENV.
title: Construction Material and Practice
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course examines the key areas of purchasing and supply of goods and services in a logistics and supply chain context. The critical areas of relationship management and managing information, in the context of purchasing and supply, will be themes throughout the course.
title: Procurement and Supply Management
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

Students will also consider the influence of the social context on young people's lives and learning.
title: Understanding Diverse Learners
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course is one of a series of courses in which students plan and execute a substantial piece of research, which is reported in the form of a dissertation. The dissertation will investigate a topic that is relevant to the student and would normally be expected to be approximately 60,000 - 80,000 words. The dissertation builds on previously studied research courses that have developed the student's understandings of research planning, research methodologies and research design.
title: Research Project - Part 7
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course builds on prior learning in the MD program, including CMPP2 and CMPP3, and supports the transition from understanding research evidence to designing clinically relevant research. The course develops practical research skills required for clinical and population health practice. Students will conduct a systematic literature review and develop an understanding of the principles of meta-analysis, with an emphasis on synthesising evidence to identify gaps in the literature and inform research questions. Students will also develop skills in research design, including selecting appropriate study designs, considering ethical requirements, assessing feasibility, and developing a structured research proposal within a defined budget and realistic clinical context. The course culminates in the preparation and presentation of a research proposal addressing a relevant clinical or population health problem. Through this process, students will integrate evidence, justify methodological decisions, and communicate their research in both written and oral formats, preparing them for future research engagement as evidence-informed clinicians. Attendance Requirements Workshops in this course have compulsory attendance. If you are unable to attend a session, you must formally notify the Course Convenor before the session you will miss, or as soon as possible afterwards, by submitting a Student Absence Form available in Course Essentials. Where relevant, you should also provide a medical certificate or other supporting documentation. Minimum Attendance Requirements Students must attend a minimum of 6 out of 7 workshops to meet course attendance requirements. Permissible vs Unexplained Absences Permissible absences (up to 20% of the course) apply only to exceptional circumstances such as illness, emergencies, or other valid reasons. These must be reported promptly through the Student Absence Form and supported by appropriate documentation. You may have one valid, reported absence without being required to complete additional work. If you miss a second workshop, even with a valid or medical reason, you will have exceeded the permissible absences. In this case, the Course Convenor may require you to complete an alternative learning activity (for example, a presentation or oral viva) to demonstrate your understanding of the missed content. The format, deadline, and assessment criteria will be determined by the Course Convenor. If your total absences exceed the attendance threshold (more than two workshops), you will be considered non-compliant with course requirements. Where appropriate, the Course Convenor may assist students with approved absences by offering alternative sessions, subject to availability and class capacity. These sessions are for skill development only and do not count toward attendance requirements. No provisions will be made for unexplained absences, and individual remediation sessions cannot be arranged. Student Responsibility Monitoring
title: Preparation for Research
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course increases students' 3D computer-aided design software skills, focusing on advanced assembly modelling techniques. Students develop proficiencies in complex part and assembly design and technical drawing development. Students will practice modelling methodologies that utilise the parametric abilities of 3D CAD software, enabling rapid design changes. Primary assessments are project-based, focusing on creating completed assemblies of products in CAD that are suitable for specific manufacturing processes. Students will gain practical industry-based skills for designing products for commercial production. Pre-requisite: 1508ENG Digital Design and Modelling OR 2639QCA - Digital Modelling for Design. Or equivalent course from other institution.
title: 3D Digital Modelling for Manufacture
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: Over the last decade, populists have come to power in the world's four largest democracies: India, the United States, Indonesia and Brazil, among a range of other countries. Populists have run on platforms challenging the checks and balances of liberal democracy, rejecting globalization and international institutions, and opposing free trade and movement. This course will enable students to gain a deeper understanding of the unique challenges posed by populism to democracy in the twenty-first century, including in Australia and Asia. It examines what happens when populists take power, what the impacts of populism on global politics are likely to be in the 2020s, and how political leaders can respond.
title: The Rise of Global Populism
academicOrgDescription: School of Government and International Relations

description: Programming is a foundational skill for all computing disciplines. This course develops skills and concepts that are essential to good programming practice and problem solving. It covers fundamental programming concepts, object-oriented programming, basic data structures, and algorithmic processes.

academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

academicOrgDescription: Griffith Graduate Research School

description: This capstone course will provide students with the opportunity to learn, develop, and demonstrate leadership and professional skills relevant to physiotherapy practice. Specialised and emerging areas of practice will be explored, and employability aspects emphasised.
title: Leadership and Professional Skills
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course introduces the emerging research field of neurocriminology, which integrates the disciplines of neuroscience, biology, psychology and criminology to understand criminal behaviour. Students will learn how principles and methods drawn from neuroscience (e.g., neuroimaging techniques, neuropsychological assessment) can be applied to study the neurobiological foundations of crime. Contemporary and cutting-edge findings from neurocriminology research will provide insight into how criminal behaviour can be influenced by brain structures and functioning, biochemical abnormalities, genetics and psychophysiology. The course will review the application of neurocriminology methods and findings at various levels of the criminal justice process (e.g., prevention, investigation, assessment, prosecution, intervention), including the limitations of these applications.
title: Neurocriminology
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: Business success is highly dependent on the effectiveness of the selling process, sales management and business negotiation. This course will provide the knowledge necessary for students to understand the selling process and be able to apply key principles of successful sales management. It provides an introduction to personal selling, as well as a detailed analysis of the selling process, environmental influences, business negotiation, estimating demand, account management and sales force management including the recruitment, selection, training, motivation and performance of salespeople and control of the selling effort.

academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: Students develop the basis of a working knowledge for the Italian language with a specific emphasis on aural comprehension and pronunciation in operatic and other vocal repertoire.

academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: 7411EDN is the culminating course in the capstone trimester. It requires students to undertake a reflective process in order to identify their achievements and learning within the degree, whilst also envisioning future growth towards becoming a highly accomplished professional within secondary schools. In particular, it invites students to identify strengths and weaknesses in their achievement of the APST and to plan professional learning to address gaps. They complete this course and their degree by reviewing and revising the philosophy of teaching they wrote in 7401EDN at the very start of their pre-service journey. Given the holistic nature of their reflections, this course is non-graded. It is marked on a 'MET/NOT MET' basis.

academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This Subject introduces the basic concepts and principles of accounting with special emphasis given to the use and interpretation of financial accounting information. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to read, prepare and interpret financial statements and they will have gained an appreciation of their uses and limitations in practical and applied ways.
title: Small Business Accounting
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: Research by Practice Workshop 1 provides students with a framework for critical thinking, supports intellectual independence and provides tools to develop self-learning. Students acquire a critical and holistic approach to tackle design-focused questions and are prepared for higher-degree research. The course involves research, analysis and the exploration of approaches, design ideas and alternative solutions that are evidence-informed, creative, iterative and culturally responsive in relation to a specific challenge, theme or idea. This course is supported by 7161ESC. Incompatible 7701ENV.
title: Research by Practice Workshop 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course builds on undergraduate courses such as contract law, torts, and foundations of law to explore the national and international law relevant to digital media, data and digital influence. Topics covered include the interface between the law and digital identity protections; privacy regulation; algorithms and automated decision-making systems (ADMS); online consent; social media and democracy; digitally-facilitated harms such as mis/disinformation. The course also invites a consideration of potential legal interventions. The course focuses on Australian law but will include legislation from other jurisdictions such as the European Union and United States where required to compare and contrast key differences between different jurisdictions (including any effective legal interventions).
title: Law and Digital Media
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: In the past several decades, the field of portfolio management has evolved from a descriptive process to a highly formalised and quantitative area of study. The rapidly changing financial environment and the number of new instruments available have made portfolio selection and management a task which can only be carried out by persons who have been equipped with updated skills. This course studies the controversial issues and the current advances in the analysis of international capital markets, presents an optimal portfolio design methodology, and several ongoing management strategies. This course is the logical conclusion to the courses in the finance stream as it builds on the foundations of accounting, corporate finance and investment analysis to apply these concepts to their ultimate application in the design, construction and management of investment portfolios.
title: Portfolio Management
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course will focus on the arc of relationships between Australia, Asia and the Pacific to develop students' understanding of the integration of business and political institutions across the region. Students focus on trade dealings between countries and within multilateral organisations such as ASEAN, APEC as well as other Fairtrade organisations. The purpose of this is to equip future regional business and political leaders with an essential understanding of both the role of certain organisations and the attached opportunities that can be explored through working with those trade alliances and potential partners. This is considered in terms of dealing effectively with multilateral bodies and/or with the individual countries within those bodies.
title: Partnerships in Australia, Asia and the Pacific
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: This course is tailored to address the unique challenges presented by securing critical systems, including Modbus, CAN Bus, and IoT systems, against cyber threats. Through hands-on exercises and simulations, students will gain specialized expertise in defending and safeguarding these essential components of modern critical infrastructure. On completion of this course, students will have advanced knowledge and practical skills in safeguarding critical infrastructure components, including Modbus, CAN Bus, and IoT systems, against cyber threats. Graduates will be well-prepared to assess vulnerabilities, implement robust security measures, and respond effectively to incidents, ensuring the resilience and security of these vital systems.

academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: The course is an intensive activity in the area of Opera Studies. The options available are for classical singers (operatic roles) and pianists (Repetiteur activities.) Vocal technique, musicality, language and ensemble work are combined, consolidated and refined through intensive rehearsals. New skills are integrated into the discipline of the theatre.

academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: In this course students will develop a persuasive visual communications strategy in the context of social justice in a globalised world. This involves research and the conceptual and technical development of multiple artefacts through practice-based research and design.
title: Strategic Visual Communication
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This postgraduate course teaches the practical and theoretical aspects of cloud computing, focusing specifically on Amazon Web Services (AWS). The course curriculum covers essential topics related to both cloud architecture and security. The course will also explore AWS core services, including compute, storage, databases, and other network services. In addition, the course will discuss security responsibilities for both customers and AWS, and study cloud architecture principles, design patterns, and scalability. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine the best-fit solution for projects based on cost and support structures.
title: Cloud Architecture and Administration
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: In this course, students will complete coursework and simulation-based clinical activities which constitute the first placement in the Master of Professional Psychology. The applied focus of this course is designed to prepare students for an external placement experience in 7610PSY. This course is a non-graded course and students who pass the course will receive a non-graded pass (NGP) on their transcript. Students must have satisfactory performance on all assessment tasks to receive a non-graded pass in the course. Prerequisites: Nil Co-requisites: Nil Incompatibles: Nil

academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course focuses on knowledge and skills development in psychological assessment and its application to problem formulation, or the generation and testing of hypotheses leading to a dynamic psychological understanding of a client's presentation. The course will also focus on developing skills in evaluating the progress of a single client and a program-based intervention. These are critical skills and knowledge required of psychologists.
title: Assessment and Evaluation
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course explores the principles and practices of teaching and learning in the field of English for Academic Purposes (EAP) and English for Specific Academic Purposes (ESAP). Students will consider a range of issues, research, and professional knowledge and skills associated with the teaching of English for Academic Purposes (TEAP) around three themes: academic and disciplinary discourse features and practices, understanding and producing academic texts, and ESAP course design and assessment.

academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course provides students with the opportunity to develop self-directed projects, either individually or collaboratively, including ensemble-based work. description: This subject provides a solid introduction to applied statistics for students in criminal justice and related fields. The subject covers both descriptive and inferential statistics, and students learn to use Microsoft Excel for statistical analysis.

academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: The social, political and economic contributions of education have been debated from a range of philosophical and ethical perspectives. In this course influential arguments about the purpose of education are investigated while taking into account contemporary challenges from the local into the global.
title: Philosophy and Ethics in Education Studies
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: Psychology and neuroscience have had a powerful influence on how learning and learners are understood within education and society more broadly. This course critically considers established and emerging psychological science to inform the work of educators and education leaders

description: Educational settings are increasingly diverse, requiring strength-based approaches that work with and value the cultural and linguistic wealth that students arrive with. academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course provides a broad introduction to machine learning and AI search. Topics will be selected from: supervised learning (generative/discriminative learning, parametric/non-parametric learning, neural networks); unsupervised/semi-supervised learning (clustering, association rule learning, and dimensionality reduction); learning theory (bias/variance trade-offs, practical advice); and reinforcement learning (Markov decision processes, time-difference learning, Q-learning, and Monte Carlo methods). Students will learn about basic concepts, key techniques, popular tools and platforms and how to formulate and solve a machine learning problem.
title: Computational Intelligence
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: In Year 3 of the Doctor of Medicine (MD) program, students enroll in Medicine 3 twice annually. This course encompasses four key domains of medical education: 1. Science and scholarship 2. Clinical practice 3. Professionalism and leadership 4. Health and Society Students are assigned to designated hospital(s) for the full academic year, rotating through six 6-week clinical blocks: 1.Medicine 2.Aged/Cancer Care 3.Mental Health 4.Surgery 5.Women's Health 6.Children's Health. Learning experiences occur in diverse clinical settings, including ward rounds, out-patient clinics, procedural and specialist clinics, theatre sessions, multidisciplinary team meetings, liaison rounds, community clinics (both medical and nonmedical), and on-call with junior medical staff. There is an emphasis on learning in clinical and small group environments. A variety of delivery methods are used in relation to educational resources (additional to clinical teaching), including seminars, Case-Based Learning (CBL) tutorials with an online case presentation system (OSCAR), an online lecture series covering the common conditions, and relevant journal articles/ guidelines /textbooks linked to learning items on Learning@Griffith. Students will be assessed throughout the year with a variety of assessment modalities including oral and written presentation of cases (OSCAR), mini-clinical evaluation exercises (mini-CEX), in-block training assessments (ITA), written assessments including multiple choice questions, assignments, competency-based clinical assessments, and an OSCE. A satisfactory summative ITA is required to pass each rotation.
title: Clinical Medicine Year 3
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course develops to an advanced degree student knowledge of editorial practice and its application, in particular the developmental intervention required to bring a variety of texts to publication standard in either print or digital formats. academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course offers you a basic introduction to postgraduate research to understand how evidence is used for decision making. By exploring scholarly literature you will become familiar with the objectives and importance of quality research, and the methods and processes involved in carrying it out. Understanding research and the processes involved in conducting, designing, reporting, interpreting and evaluating research is of paramount importance to success in postgraduate study. Research activities whether of a primary or secondary nature occupy a significant proportion of postgraduate students' time and effort at university both within and beyond the classroom. Through applied examples, including evidence-based policing and justice policy, students will develop the capacity to critically assess research and understand its relevance in real-world justice contexts. academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course aims to introduce the basic knowledge and necessary skills for analysis of Big Data. Big Data analytics is regarded as one of the important emerging technologies in different fields. The course is designed to stimulate interest in big data analytics in a popular scenario, i.e. social media. As such, some topics will be covered in depth while some will be covered only on an introductory level. Students will be shown how to collect data and extract information hidden in huge volumes of social media data, which can be valuable for many businesses to understand the perceptions or opinions of their services or products.

description: In the era of growing environmental concern and regulatory scrutiny, the practice of sustainability and climate reporting has become essential for businesses and organisations worldwide. Having the ability to apply principles of sustainability, climate mitigation, and carbon reporting is vital for organisations across sectors. You will explore concepts and issues related to sustainability, climate, and carbon reporting, covering both theoretical foundations, practical applications, and implications for business. description: Incorporating cyber security design in software development is essential for producing contemporary software systems. description: This course introduces students to methods for collecting and interpreting information that is relevant to the hotel and tourism industry. Students will be exposed to practical ways of developing analytical skills that will be invaluable to future employment. The course will address industry issues and problems, and students will develop skills that will enable them to make evidence based decisions to improve practice. description: This course provides students the opportunity to develop and refine their graduate employability skills as they transition out of university. description: This subject introduces students to the tax consequences of operating a business in Australia, and considers how the tax outcomes can be influenced by the business structure adopted (such as a sole trader, partnership, trust or corporation). description: This course provides an integrated introduction to the field of criminology and criminal justice, with a focus on developing foundational professional skills, critical perspectives on justice, and a nuanced understanding of crime and victimisation. Students will explore how crime is defined, measured, and theorised, while examining key justice issues such as inequality, victim rights, and serious violent offending. Through case studies and structured activities, students will build academic and professional capabilities, gain awareness of career pathways, and develop a sense of purpose and belonging within the criminology and justice community.

academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: Screen Safety Fundamentals provides students with essential knowledge and practical skills to work safely in professional screen environments. The course emphasizes health and well-being, legal and ethical responsibilities, and a strong sense of professional accountability. Students will learn to identify hazards, follow safety protocols, and respond effectively to emergencies, fostering collaborative workflows and enhancing employability through demonstrated readiness to work safely in demanding production settings.

description: This course introduces students to key professional standards and the formal recognition systems that underpin industry-specific certifications and accreditations within the screen sector. These credentials, often required for below-the-line (BTL) crew roles, validate practical skills and demonstrate readiness for real-world production environments. By obtaining these certifications, students will meet industry expectations, ensure compliance with safety regulations, strengthen collaboration and workflow practices, and build confidence in problem-solving within professional screen contexts.

academicOrgDescription: Griffith Film School

description: This course introduces key characteristics, concepts and trends in social entrepreneurship that are emerging locally, nationally and globally. Through applied practice and engagement, students will explore how innovation approaches can used for the common good and are the key success factors of delivering both commercial and societal outcomes.

description: The aim of this course is to understand the complex workings of businesses that are family-owned and run. The course explores the unique personal and interpersonal issues, as well as the business issues associated with the family-owned and managed firm.

Industry projects will see student teams working with a diverse profile of clients across industries, ranging from large Australian and multinational companies to niche agencies, start-ups and not-for-profit organisations. Supported by interactive online material, workshops with experienced academic coaches and industry mentors and a final interactive oral assessment with the industry client, this course and its assessment platform have been specifically designed to facilitate a critical reflection on your employability skills and provide you with evidence to demonstrate that you possess the attributes of a Griffith Graduate.

description: This course demonstrates the importance of the service sector, how marketing theory differs for this sector, the unique challenges faced by service businesses and the application of service theory in practice. description: This course is aimed at undergraduate students wishing to develop greater understanding of some of the complex issues facing organisations today and in the future. As innovation and technology are key drivers of organisational success, economic growth, and sustained business competitiveness, the effective management of innovation and technology should provide solutions and strategies to tackle major challenges such as climate change and responsible production and consumption from business organisations. As parts of this course, students will explore the following broad areas: competitive industry dynamics, sources and patterns of technological innovation, formulating and devising innovation strategy, and implementing strategy for technological innovation, and responsible innovation for sustainability.

Students will explore how the neurodiversity paradigm can be used to recognise and emphasize each person's individual strengths and talents while also providing support for differences and needs if required. description: Coral reefs are iconic ecosystems. Despite occupying less than 1% of the sea floor they support 25% of all marine species. Coral reefs provide valuable ecosystem services; they support commercial and artisanal fisheries, generate substantial tourism revenue and employment, protect shorelines from coastal erosion and are a source of novel chemicals. Despite their inherent ecological and societal value, cumulative anthropogenic stressors have caused 13.5% of coral reefs to be lost since 2009. 'Coral Reefs' explores the biogeography, ecology and economic importance of coral reefs. The course also discusses the anthropogenic stressors that are causing the decline of reefs, and their conservation and management.

Through investigation, experimentation and prototyping students are provided with the opportunity to successfully position themselves for future practice in the cinematic arts industries. description: This course builds upon foundational knowledge in basic statistics and research methods, offering a more advanced exploration of statistical analysis tailored to health research. There will be a strong emphasis on incorporating research design, sampling and sample size concepts into data analysis and interpretation of research results. Through consideration of a variety of statistical methods, this course will provide students with practical experience and skills focussing on analytical planning, result presentation and interpretation. In particular, emphasis will be on specifying appropriate statistical methods and their interpretation within a health research framework. A unifying theme of the course will be the relationship between descriptive statistics and inferential statistics in presenting and interpreting quantitative research data. Students will be made aware of the importance of data management in preparation for statistical analysis. Students will also be provided with substantial practical experience to foster their skills in selecting and applying inferential statistics appropriate to specific data sets. In particular, measurement issues, data type (categorical and continuous variables), test assumptions (distribution of the data, equity of variances) will be considered in deciding between parametric and non-parametric statistical approaches to research questions. Students will develop skills in formulation of experimentally testable hypotheses at the bivariate level. The primary statistical techniques to be covered in this course include Chi-square tests, correlation, t-tests, analysis of variance, multiple linear regression, logistic regression and non- parametric tests such as Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis test. Analytical strategies for modeling data are covered in this course, with a focus on multiple regression techniques. Factor analysis will also be introduced, providing students with a deeper understanding of how to identify underlying relationships between variables, reduce data dimensionality, and interpret complex data sets in health research. Students will be provided with substantial experience in the use of the widely used statistical package SPSS to analyse data. This will be achieved through data analysis and interpretation of various research data sets.
title: Quantitative Research
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry
