description: The SCADA course is designed to teach system configuration with an emphasis on hands-on, activity-based learning. Configuration techniques taught include Database Objects, Mimic Configuration, Animated Symbols, Navigation, Trends, IEC61131 Logic, Scripting, Templates and Instances, Security, Alarm Redirections, Reporting using Crystal Reports, Server Configuration and PLC/RTU Communications Architectures. Incompatible: 6323ENG SCADA Systems.
title: SCADA Systems
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This 20 credit point internship course is an elective which is open to penultimate or final year JD and LLB students who are selected by an application process. Less frequently, there are also opportunities for students in earlier years. Opportunities are advertised by student email each Trimester for the following Trimester. Each opportunity sets out the partner's requirements for each internship, including the required year of study. This is a competitive process, but we have opportunities for students at all levels, so apply! The course is a law elective available to all JD and LLB students who have: -completed at least 120 CP in law subjects (unless the advertisement allows fewer credit points) -have a minimum GPA of 4, although some partners require a higher GPA, which will be stated. The course provides students with an opportunity to complete unpaid work in a Law firm, government department or other legal work environment. Students complete an internship for two days per week with one of our partners/hosts, such as law firms, 'in house' legal units, community legal centres, barristers, law reform agencies, and government legal units. Students will build on their University learning to develop new insights into how law works in practice. It offers students the opportunity to develop a range of professional skills, enhance their discipline knowledge, and build their research capabilities, which will enhance employability. The practical and academic components of the course are designed to build students': -capacity to make informed decisions, both personally and professionally -capacity to reflect on the impact of the law on individuals and society -ethical awareness, sense of social justice and professional responsibility -multi-disciplinary and cross-cultural awareness and competence -graduate skills, professional identity, career direction, confidence, and employability -practical and technical skills, including dealing with unstructured situations, written and oral communication, collaboration, teamwork and time management. Students report that work integrated learning (WIL) makes them more employable, and employers back this up, reporting that WIL favourably influences their perception of students' abilities. Students say WIL helps them assess their career direction, complements their learning, increases their networks, increases their motivation to study and helps them prepare for future employment.
title: Extended Internship Clinic
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: Students will undertake a research project relevant to their area of specialisation under the guidance of one, two or more supervisors. The topic and nature of the Research Project will be determined through consultation and mutual agreement of the student and supervisor, and approved by the Program Convenor. The project will involve original research and will be under the direct supervision of an academic staff member.
title: Research Project
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: Global forces are rapidly changing the way we work. Globalisation, automation and digital communication have altered the way that employees engage with the workplace and provide value to employers. Career pathways have changed too. It is likely that you will have many jobs across a variety of careers and industries in your lifetime. Rapid advances in technology are enabling firms to automate processes, which is displacing or changing routine work. Simultaneously, the power of knowledge workers is rising. In parallel, new industries and new forms of collaborative and distance-based work are emerging. All of this is offering new challenges and opportunities. In this course you will explore how rapid technological advances are creating digital disruption that will impact your work in the future. It will enable you to identify opportunities to craft your own career pathway in a rapidly globalising, knowledge and service-intense economy.
title: The Future of Work
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

description: This course enables students to articulate the concept of a wicked problem and understand the importance of collaboration and inter/transdisciplinary approaches. Students learn to work collaboratively across diverse perspectives to design authentic solutions in consultation with community and industry stakeholders.
title: Wicked Problems
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course enables you to develop the knowledge required to support the woman, her baby and family during normal pregnancy, labour and birth, and the postnatal and early neonatal period, including the initiation of breastfeeding.
title: Holistic Midwifery Care
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: This course will introduce students to the field of applied behaviour analysis (ABA), creating a foundational understanding of key concepts, principles, and theoretical underpinnings as well as their application in a variety of health, education, and community settings.
title: Introduction to Applied Behaviour Analysis
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course extends first year forensic biology into a practice focused exploration of how biological evidence is used to answer forensic questions. Students develop skills in recognising and prioritising biologically relevant material (including blood, semen, saliva and trace DNA), applying presumptive and confirmatory tests, and recovering DNA via appropriate sampling and extraction strategies. These practical components are integrated with a theoretical treatment of current DNA profiling methods, the interpretation of STR profiles, and the communication of findings in formats suitable for investigative use and court. By the end of the course, students will be able to follow a biological exhibit from initial examination through to DNA profile reporting, with an appreciation of the scientific, ethical and evidentiary considerations involved.
title: Forensic Biology
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course provides you with the knowledge and understanding of new business ventures. This course is designed to put entrepreneurship into practice as you will examine the viability of the business idea you have through the development of a business plan.
title: Building the New Venture
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: Archaeology offers a unique deep time perspective on the human experience. In this course you will discover: the diverse approaches archaeologists use to interpret the material traces of the past; the long, non-linear, and complicated trajectories of humanity; and how archaeology contributes to our understanding of societies on the Australian continent and globally. In the tutorial component of the course, students will practice archaeological analysis and interpretation.
title: Archaeology: Discovering the Human Past
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This subject concerns the identification, analysis, evaluation and treatment of risk. It highlights practical applications of general and life insurance products in developing and implementing personal and small business risk management strategies. In addition to investigating the insurance products available in the market, the course will cover the structure of the insurance industry, its regulation, insurance law and the skills necessary to provide risk management and insurance advice to clients.
title: Risk Management and Insurance
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course is conducted primarily as individual placements, or small teams of students, within an industry or research environment and emphasizes academic and vocational aspects of modern scientific practice. Students consolidate their technical knowledge by undertaking a work placement in a professional workplace while simultaneously managing their learning and course assessment. Students work in close liaison with their industry supervisor throughout the project and are expected to demonstrate a good understanding of their duties and responsibilities. The course also emphasizes that competence in management, business and social responsibilities are essential components in all fields within science professions and the key attributes of a contemporary industry or research environment. Students should be in the third or final year of study and must have completed the online registration form which can be followed by clicking on the red 'Access Learning@Griffith' link provided here: www.griffith.edu.au/griffith-sciences/partnerships/student. To be eligible for enrolment in this course, students must have completed all requirements of the WIL Office in preparation for placement, including allocation to an industry placement. Enquiries are to be directed to the Course Convenor.
title: Work Integrated Learning Placement
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course is conducted primarily as individual student placements. The course introduces the concept of industry-based training and experience, while assisting in the transition from university to the workplace. Students will consolidate their scientific training and knowledge by undertaking a practical placement in a professional workplace whilst simultaneously managing their learning and course assessment. The course emphasizes that competence in legal (OHS/WHS), ethical, scientific, academic and social responsibilities are essential and key components of the scientific profession.
title: Work Integrated Learning Special Topic
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course is an introduction to the law as it applies to synthetic biology (genetics and engineering ideas applied to genetics) and examines in detail the various regulatory schemes that control the exploitation of synthetic biology and its products. Following a basic introduction to genetics thinking and the knowledges of genetics (and science as a knowledge system more broadly), you will learn how the discipline of science interacts with the discipline of law and its engagement with the detail of regulatory decision making, and you will gain an understanding of the current and upcoming challenges facing our embrace of technology. This course can be taken as a free choice elective.
title: Law and Synthetic Biology
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: Cyber Security Governance, Policy, Ethics & Law is an exploration of the critical cyber-governance factors essential to an organisations' ability to proactively manage risk and respond appropriately to data breaches. It outlines the theoretical, ethical and practical aspects of managing data breaches, sufficient to equip cyber security practitioners with the latest 'best practice' knowledge. The course looks at an organisations' risk profile from the three important dimensions: systems, networks, and data. Business models are analysed with emphasis on their resilience to potential threats, their governance structure, and mitigation strategies. The course also covers legal and regulatory compliance and reporting requirements with consideration of short- and medium-term impacts on the business. Previously known as 7907ICT Managing Data Breaches: Cyber Risk, Compliance and Privacy and is incompatible with 7907ICT Managing Data Breaches: Cyber Risk, Compliance and Privacy. Over ten modules, you'll explore a wide range of topics essential for negotiating the complex terrain of modern cybersecurity and digital ethics. From foundational IT governance frameworks to cutting-edge issues in artificial intelligence and smart cities, this course provides a holistic view of the challenges and opportunities in our increasingly connected world. We begin by laying a foundation in IT governance and compliance, ensuring you understand the regulatory landscape that shapes cybersecurity practices. You'll then delve into practical aspects of cybersecurity and data protection, including ethical hacking and breach response strategies. Real-world case studies, such as the Equifax data breach, will help you apply theoretical knowledge to actual scenarios. You'll gain insights into advanced concepts like the Cybersecurity Incident Management Maturity Model and the Cybersecurity Capability Maturity Model (C2M2). These frameworks will equip you with the tools to assess and improve organizational cybersecurity postures. A major aspect of the course are the ethical considerations in the digital age. We'll explore meta-cognition, ethical decision-making models, and theories of ethical behavior. You'll also tackle emerging ethical challenges in AI and algorithmic bias, preparing you for the moral complexities of tomorrow's technologies. Intellectual property, copyright, and digital rights management form another crucial component of the curriculum. You'll learn about open-source software licensing and the legal aspects of cyber risk at state, national, and international levels. The course also covers the broader societal impact of IT, including social media behavior, technology for social good, and the importance of accessibility and inclusion in the digital realm. We'll examine the growing field of cyber insurance and explore how e-government initiatives and digital transformation are reshaping citizen engagement and urban development. Throughout the course, you'll engage with
title: IT and Cyber Security Governance, Policy, Ethics and Law
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: Using the life cycle of a company the operation of the Australian corporate regulatory framework is illustrated. Thus, the subject examines: company registration; corporate governance issues arising from the company's daily operations, and the external administration of a company on its insolvency.
title: Company Law
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This subject explains the laws introduced by the Australian government in response to terrorism, from those enacted in response to the 9/11 attacks to those recently passed in response to Islamic State. It focuses on theories of prevention, the impact of these laws on Australia's criminal justice system, and questions of accountability and human rights. The course also considers policy strategies for countering radicalisation and violent extremism.
title: Counter-Terrorism Law
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course presents the principles of fluid mechanics and the application of these principles to practical, engineering problems. Topics covered in the course will include fluid properties, fluid statics, fluid flow in closed conduits, fluid viscosity and turbulence, forces developed by fluids in motion, introduction to flow around submerged objects, lift and drag, open channel flow, pumps and turbines. Applications relevant to environmental engineering fields such as water and wastewater treatment, fluid storage and distribution systems and open channel flow are investigated. In addition, the study of energy processes for turbines and pumps provides an introduction to fluid power analysis. Design examples for renewable energy applications are undertaken. Incompatible: 2002ENG Fluid Mechanics and Hydraulics
title: Fluid Mechanics
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This clinically-based course expands on 7031DOH_Y1/Y2 in the major selected by the candidate. It is based on case presentations and advanced clinical practice. Learning activities are presented by staff with expertise in the specific major.
title: Advanced Clinical Dentistry 4
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: Clinical practicum forms a key component of work-integrated learning activities that integrates theoretical learning with its application in the workplace. Exercise Physiology Practicum will require students to undertake a minimum of 360 hours of clinical practicum across a diverse range of relevant practice domains. This course will provide students with opportunities to practice and further develop their vocational skills in professional practice settings. Prerequisites: 4601AHS Exercise for Clinical Populations I, 4602AHS Exercise for Clinical Populations II, 4603AHS Professional Practice in Exercise Physiology I, 4604AHS Professional Practice in Exercise Physiology II Co-requisites: 4605AHS Professional Practice in Exercise Physiology III
title: Exercise Physiology Practicum
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: In the context of an introduction to civil obligations, this course provides a broad introduction to legal processes, the legal system and legal theory. The emphasis in this course is on contract law, but it also introduces related areas of civil obligations, particularly negligence and restitution. THIS COURSE IS ONLY OPEN TO LAW STUDENTS.
title: Contracts 2
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course covers the laws that govern the creation and operation of government institutions within their political, social and economic contexts, especially the powers and limits on powers of parliaments to make laws under Australia's federal Constitution. THIS COURSE IS ONLY OPEN TO LAW STUDENTS.
title: Constitutional Law
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: Child and youth mental health care is a developing specialty in Queensland and this course may appeal to students planning to seek work in mental health services. The course introduces students to theories and models for interventions with children and youth with mental health problems. Drawing on recent research, clinical practice examples and policy documents, this course will provide students with the knowledge, attributes and skills needed for reflective child and youth mental health practice. This course is available to undergraduate students in nursing and related areas of study.
title: Child and Youth Mental Health
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: Students will continue to develop their midwifery knowledge to ensure that they are prepared to work within the full scope of midwifery practice across the normal-complex continuum of childbirth including the complex care of a woman with a pre-existing condition.
title: Complex Maternal Care
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: This course explores issues relating to the health and wellbeing of Australian children and young people. In this course students will learn to promote youth health and wellbeing. The course will focus on a range of health issues and concepts relevant to the contemporary Australian context. Students will also engage with contemporary approaches to health promotion in school settings.
title: Youth Health and Wellbeing
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course aims to provide pre-service special needs educators with foundational skills for their work in a range of specialist and regular settings. The course will have two modules. The first module will assist special educators to understand, develop and to intentionally apply helping skills based on counselling micro-skills. This module provides core skills for the 3316EDN Collaboration and Co-teaching that concentrates more on team and group processes for teachers. The second module will introduce a range of evidence-based instructional practices essential for teaching students with special needs and disability within a tiered approach to intervention involving instructional decisions that are data-based. Taken together these modules will be foundational for intervention courses in the program.
title: Foundation Skills for Special Needs Educators
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course is the first of two courses in which students plan and execute a substantial piece of research, which is reported in the form of a dissertation. The dissertation will investigate a topic that is relevant to the student and would normally be approximately 30,000 words. The dissertation builds on previously studied courses that have developed the student's understanding of research foundations, design and methodologies.
title: Dissertation Part 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course is one of a series of courses in which students plan and execute a substantial piece of research, which is reported in the form of a dissertation. The dissertation will investigate a topic that is relevant to the student and would normally be expected to be approximately 60,000 - 80,000 words. The dissertation builds on previously studied research courses that have developed the student's understandings of research planning, research methodologies and research design.
title: Research Project - Part 2
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course includes in-depth teaching of the Senior Physical Education and Senior Health syllabuses. Pre-service teachers will develop a deeper understanding and skills required to plan, teach and assess Health and Physical Education Senior Secondary syllabuses (QCAA as base syllabus). This course prepares students for HPE professional experience.
title: Health and Physical Education Curriculum - Senior Secondary
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course explores both historical and current understandings of the biological and social constructions of 'adolescence'. It also investigates the physical, cognitive, social and emotional development during this stage and the implications for what are best pedagogical practices to meet the changing needs of these students.
title: Understanding Adolescence and Adolescents
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: The Independent Research Project gives students the opportunity to choose a practice based topic to initiate, develop and produce a research project at an advanced level, from the point of conceptualising a research question to writing a scholarly paper reporting the results of research which the student has undertaken. This 10 credit point course requires progress towards a thesis/dissertation. It is the second course of three (totalling 30 credit points) and a grade/credit will not be awarded unless all the thesis courses are completed and the thesis is submitted.
title: Independent Research Project
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course is focused on preparing for and demonstrating the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (APST) at the graduate stage, where there is a focus on collecting, synthesising, reflecting and appraising evidence of impact on student learning. Please be aware that this course may not follow the standard academic calendar. Please check your timetable on myGriffith for details of when classes commence and the duration of the Professional Experience Placement.
title: The Griffith Graduate Teacher
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course introduces students to the tax consequences of operating a business in Australia, and considers how the tax outcomes can be influenced by the business structure adopted (such as a sole trader, partnership, trust or corporation). The course also considers the employment related taxes that a business will need to consider when employing staff, such as fringe benefits tax, as well as the tax concessions available for small businesses, including on the sale of their business.
title: Taxation Planning for Advisors
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course provides students with the opportunity to respond to industry client projects. Students will work in teams to design innovative solutions that considers client and stakeholder needs to contribute to solving the real-world crises. Student teams will be guided by industry mentors as they explore solutions-based opportunities and engage in design thinking. Through this course, students will develop their problem solving capabilities and understanding of how organisations can be responsive to the concept of sustainability. While also reflecting on their own professional capabilities and the impact they can make as professionals and as a member of the global community.
title: Co-Design Incubator
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

description: Online technology has changed the way businesses interact with consumers and business-to-business. Peer to peer platforms have become powerful tools that even the largest traditional Online Travel Organizations (OTAs e.g., booking.com and Expedia group) are adapting their business models. This course examines E Commerce platforms for tourism and hospitality businesses, with a focus on future consumer and product development.
title: E Commerce Platforms for T and H Business
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This course aims to prepare students to teach Digital Technologies in the junior secondary years in alignment with the Australian Curriculum in Queensland. It assumes prior familiarity with foundational concepts in computer education, particularly programming and information systems, and builds these into pedagogical practice for school settings. Students examine how Digital Technologies teaching is shaped by the interplay of learners, school context, curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, and professional judgement. The course introduces specialised teaching approaches, resources, and tools for designing learning that develops students' computational, design, and systems thinking. It also addresses curriculum planning, sequencing, inclusive participation, assessment, feedback, and the effective use of digital tools to support meaningful learning in junior secondary classrooms.
title: Digital Technologies Curriculum - Junior Secondary
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course provides students with historical, theoretical, and skills-based knowledge on the use of restorative justice practices as a response to criminal offences and other forms of wrongdoing and harms, in Australia and globally. The first part of the course provides students with in-depth knowledge of the history and theoretical foundations of restorative justice, including examination of empirical research on the impact and outcomes of restorative justice processes for participants. The second part of the course is aimed at helping students learn and demonstrate fundamental aspects of restorative justice facilitation, including knowledge of best-practice guidelines, facilitation skills, and common problems in facilitation. The third part of the course considers existing challenges in the use of restorative justice in relation in cases of gendered violence, and in its use for Indigenous and culturally diverse peoples. The course concludes with examination of the growing use of restorative practices beyond the criminal justice system.
title: Restorative Justice Practices
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course explores different perspectives on crime prevention, assisting students to develop an understanding of situational, developmental, community, and criminal justice approaches to the prevention of crime and anti-social behaviour, and an understanding about their effectiveness. The course will encourage students to think critically about the consequences of each approach for diverse groups and communities and for their own practice. In particular, students will develop skills in applying these approaches to particular problems. This course is designed for students in their second year of studying criminology and criminal justice.
title: Crime Prevention
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course deepens students' understanding of qualitative social science research, with a focus on methods commonly used in criminology. It focuses on the qualitative methods commonly applied within criminology and social science more generally. Students will further explore qualitative research design and critically reflect on the ethical and social implications of conducting research in diverse communities. The course covers key concepts in qualitative research, along with methods for qualitative data collection and analysis, equipping students with a solid theoretical foundation in this area.
title: Qualitative Methods for Social Research
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course examines the role wrongful convictions play in shaping, facilitating, or impeding justice within the Australian legal framework. By dissecting real-life cases and analysing the systemic flaws contributing to wrongful convictions, students develop a nuanced understanding of the legal system's vulnerabilities and their far-reaching consequences and how these can be prevented. This fosters critical thinking skills, empathy, and a profound appreciation for the imperative of fairness and equity within the justice system.
title: Wrongfully Convicted
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course will introduce you to the most common method used by social researchers, that is, the interview. You will learn about different modes of qualitative interviewing and have the opportunity to apply your knowledge to a project of your choice. You will undertake interviews, analyse the data from these interviews and produce a research report on your findings.
title: Qualitative Interviewing for Social Research
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Transportation is an integral component of the tourism industry serving both a functional and an experiential role. This course will analyse how tourists interact with various modes of transportation and the strategic and sustainability challenges associated with these complex networks.
title: Tourism Transportation Management
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This course aims to develop students' knowledge of psychopathology and advanced therapeutic skills across the lifespan. Students will learn advanced therapeutic skills, such as working with complex clinical presentations (e.g. bipolar disorder), systems (e.g. couples), diverse client groups (e.g., LGBTIQ, cross-cultural approaches to therapy), and clinical approaches/frameworks (e.g., solution focused therapy).
title: Lifespan Psychopathology and Therapy 3
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This course introduces some commonly used tools for sourcing, accessing, presenting and analysing digital data, focusing on Geographical Information Systems (GIS) for spatial data and Excel for other data types. Basic statistical methods will also be introduced for data interpretation. Students will critically explore data and information sources and carry out some basic data analysis. Incompatible 1108ENG Digital and Data Skills.
title: Spatial and Digital Data Skills
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: Developing Professionally II is a core course that prepares students for professional practice across the diverse workplaces within the fields of criminology and criminal justice. The course focuses on developing the skills required to engage effectively respectfully, and inclusively in collaborative professional contexts, apply ethical reasoning and professional judgement to complex and evolving situations, and clearly articulate personal strengths and potential contributions to the discipline. Through reflective practice and applied professional activities, students will connect theory and evidence to a wide range of workplace environments and build confidence in communicating their professional identity. The skills developed in this course are relevant across varied career pathways, including government, community, policy, research, and justice-related professions.
title: Developing Professionally 2
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This postgraduate course is designed to provide students with advanced knowledge and practical skills in operating and managing a Cyber Security Operations Center (CSOC) and responding effectively to cybersecurity incidents. Participants will gain expertise in utilizing critical cybersecurity technologies such as Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems, firewalls, and various incident response strategies to protect organizations from cyber threats. On completing the course, Students will have a comprehensive understanding of CSOC operations, advanced knowledge of SIEM and firewall technologies, and the skills required to effectively respond to and manage cybersecurity incidents. Graduates will be prepared for roles such as CSOC analyst, incident responder, or cybersecurity manager in various industries and organizations.
title: Cyber Security Operations Centres
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: This course emphasises real-world applications and the development of employability skills. It provides an opportunity to thoroughly analyse how real-world companies engage with international business. Students will work in interdisciplinary and culturally diverse teams, where they will have autonomy in team collaboration, undertake research and analysis using relevant frameworks to write reports, and hone their pitching skills through hands-on experience.
title: Engaging with International Business
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: Through a series of case studies and expert presentations, students in this course will develop a broad understanding of the evolving digital landscape and how digital technologies are shaping competitive dynamics and global value creation. Emphasis is placed on developing the skills and understanding required for tech savvy, socially responsible leadership in an age of ongoing digital transformation.
title: The Digital Economy
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: The course introduces students to procurement methods and the practice of construction contract management. Students will learn about: (a) different options for project delivery and the options for contract price; (b) the common matters covered in the general conditions of a major construction contract, including (but not limited to) practical completion, extension of time, liquidated damages, latent conditions, delay costs, bonus and variation clauses; (c) the relevance of legal concepts, including unjust enrichment, frustration, waiver, estoppel, and specific performance to contract administration; (d) alternative dispute resolution methods; and (e) the purpose and application of security of payment legislation for the construction industry.
title: Construction Procurement
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course introduces students to advancements in criminological theories to better understand crime and criminal behavior at the situational, individual, and societal levels. Students will learn how criminologists engage with new research to improve our understanding of how and why people engage in criminal activity and why certain types of crime are more prevalent than others.
title: Advanced Criminological Theories
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: Information derived from data is important to the management, productivity and competitive advantage of an organisation. Data must be efficiently collected, organised, retrieved and managed to make it meaningful to the organisation. It is the role of the IT professional to develop, deploy, manage and integrate data and information systems to support the organisation. This course includes the organisation, modeling, transformation and presentation of data.
title: Data Management
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: This is the second course which contributes to the major in Performance and is designed for students with serious performance aspirations. It builds out from the previous focus on live performance to develop also some foundational skills for recording and presenting performative outcomes in digital form. The focus continues also to develop foundational skillsets, knowledge bases, attitudes and awareness relevant to the instrument(s) of the student's expertise (including voice).
title: Performance 2
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course uses weekly workshops to explore and inspire collaborative creative processes within a community of practice. Workshops present a range of creative exemplars for critical listening and analysis, alongside a broad range of creative prompts, inspiring students to expand their creative process beyond their current habits and workflows. Students will engage in multiple peer-feedback sessions throughout the course, thereby growing their artistic vocabulary and ability to work within an artistic community.
title: Music Creation Perspectives 2
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This course builds on the learning outcomes of 1420QCM Music Making 1 to enable students to further explore performative and creative pursuits that align with their emerging musical aspirations. It aims to develop students' potential through a range of learning activities, including modules, specialist focus groups, individual tuition, workshops and ensembles encompassing a range of collaborative activities.
title: Music Making 2
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: This subject examines the origins and development of corrective services in Australia. The correctional system is studied in terms of custodial and non-custodial sanctions, and considers special client populations including men, women, juveniles and Indigenous offenders. The issues of privatisation and deaths in custody are examined.
title: Introduction to Corrections
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course considers the theory and processes of negotiation and conflict resolution in various settings. It provides an analytic understanding of negotiation and conflict resolutions, including issues of strategy and tactics, as well as development of skills necessary for implementation of this knowledge.
title: Negotiation
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: We all communicate. Communication plays a major role in all human activity. It is part of our culture. Within the business community, in both public and private sectors, communication is often associated with specific activities such as interacting, informing, instructing and persuading. People who possess demonstrable skills in these activities are employed, prized and promoted. If businesses are to survive in an increasingly competitive and information-oriented environment they will need trained communicators who can speak, write and interact with others efficiently, effectively and professionally. This course is intended to provide participants with advanced understanding of the concepts and principles of professional business communication and to support the development of their skills in interpersonal, spoken and business related communications through practice and feedback. Course participants will be encouraged to participate actively in the course. Prerequisites: NIL. Co-requisites: NIL. Incompatible: 2088EHR Business Communication/ EHR208 Business Communication/ 1008HSV Interpersonal Skills. Incompatible and co-taught: GBS212 Business Communication.
title: Business Communication
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

description: In this course, students conduct an industry-based placement within a commercial or industrial environment under professional supervision while managing their learning and course assessment. The placement provides students with the opportunity to undertake a substantial body of work that has an industry application and brings together the wide range of knowledge and skills already developed in earlier courses within their degree program. The aim is for students to develop the necessary attributes, skills and competencies expected in a graduate/postgraduate professional while working within a relevant workplace while under the guidance and direction of an Industry Partner. To be eligible for this course, students must have registered online with the Griffith Sciences Partnership Office in the trimester prior to enrolment. Please contact wil-gs@griffith.edu.au to register. If your registration is successful, you will be given permission to enrol prior to the start of the trimester. Prerequisites: must have completed 160 credit points which define the program with at least 20 credit points from the major and have a cumulative GPA of 5.0 at the time of registration.
title: Work Integrated Learning - Placement
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: This course is designed to introduce students to fundamental knowledge and the business implications of trade and strategy in an international context. A number of themes are prominent, including the globalisation of business and trade, strategy and its application to global business in its many forms, the multiple reasons why nations trade, commodity composition of trade, foreign exchange rates, trade and development strategy, investment across borders and global environmental issues. The application of trade and capital flow knowledge between countries will support student understanding of the global business environment.
title: Trade and Global Strategy
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: Australian Screen explores the increasingly intertwined histories of Australian cinema and television from their beginnings to the present day. A central concern is how these screen industries have balanced the pressures of a global media marketplace with the need to tell Australian stories in a distinctive voice, with growing emphasis on the nation's diversity. Through an examination of industrial and social transformations, alongside close analysis of key films and television programs, students will discover how Australia's screen media has evolved and what its stories reveal about Australian culture and society.
title: Australian Screen
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course provides you with an in-depth understanding of how to develop viable novel business ideas through empathetic design and customer discovery and validation. This course focuses on creativity, problem solving and critical thinking tools to create these novel solutions.
title: Innovation, Creativity and Entrepreneurship
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: In Year 3 of the Doctor of Medicine (MD) program, students enroll in Medicine 3 twice annually. This course encompasses four key domains of medical education: 1. Science and scholarship 2. Clinical practice 3. Professionalism and leadership 4. Health and Society Students are assigned to designated hospital(s) for the full academic year, rotating through six 6-week clinical blocks: 1.Medicine 2.Aged/Cancer Care 3.Mental Health 4.Surgery 5.Women's Health 6.Children's Health. Learning experiences occur in diverse clinical settings, including ward rounds, out-patient clinics, procedural and specialist clinics, theatre sessions, multidisciplinary team meetings, liaison rounds, community clinics (both medical and nonmedical), and on-call with junior medical staff. There is an emphasis on learning in clinical and small group environments. A variety of delivery methods are used in relation to educational resources (additional to clinical teaching), including seminars, Case-Based Learning (CBL) tutorials with an online case presentation system (OSCAR), an online lecture series covering the common conditions, and relevant journal articles/ guidelines /textbooks linked to learning items on Learning@Griffith. Students will be assessed throughout the year with a variety of assessment modalities including oral and written presentation of cases (OSCAR), mini-clinical evaluation exercises (mini-CEX), in-block training assessments (ITA), written assessments including multiple choice questions, assignments, competency-based clinical assessments, and an OSCE. A satisfactory summative ITA is required to pass each rotation.
title: Clinical Medicine Year 3
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: In Year 4, MD students enrol twice a year in a single course, Medicine Year 4. Students rotate through five six-week clinical placements, alongside a pre-internship preparedness block over the year. This consists of three core rotations - critical care/orthopaedics, emergency medicine and general practice - and a selective and elective rotation. The students attend their core rotations of critical care/orthopaedics and emergency medicine in a designated zone, and general practice in a practice in Southeast Queensland. Students also complete a selective placement which is usually locally based chosen from a list organised by the School of Medicine, and an elective placement which is usually student-organised and may be local, interstate or international. After the end of year exams, students then complete a four week pre-internship preparedness block. The settings for learning experiences will vary from discipline to discipline but include ward rounds, outpatient clinics, general practice surgeries, emergency departments, procedural and specialist clinics, theatre sessions, multidisciplinary team meetings, liaison rounds, community clinics (both medical and non-medical) and on-call with junior medical staff. There is an emphasis on learning in clinical and small group environments. A variety of delivery methods are used in relation to educational resources, including seminars, and case-based learning (CBL) tutorials with an online presentation system (OSCARS). There are workplace based assessments in each block, assignments and written examinations through the year and an OSCE at the end of year. A satisfactory summative ITA is required to pass each rotation.
title: Clinical Medicine Year 4
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course introduces the key skills of Computer Aided Design (CAD), and Digital 3D parametric modelling. It does this through the lens of manufacturing and students are instructed in industry ready modelling methodologies through projects that directly link to manufacturing processes. Upon completing this course students will be ready to tackle projects alone within or outside of university. CAD methodology is also accompanied by professional file management strategies, the importance of managing data professionally and design for various manufacturing processes.
title: Digital Design and Modelling
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course introduces students to the principles of programming intelligent robots through simulation. Students will learn how to control actuators, process data from sensors, implement path planning and obstacle avoidance, and design decision-making systems. Concepts from computer vision and machine learning will be introduced to show how artificial intelligence can enhance robotic perception and behaviour. Through a mix of lectures and simulator-based workshops, students will gain practical experience in developing and testing robotic systems in a safe virtual environment. Ethical and safety considerations in robotics and AI will also be discussed. The course concludes with a project in which students design and present an AI-enabled robotic application.
title: Programming for Robotics
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: This course advances students' understanding of global filmmaking using the popular concept of film genre. Students explore a diverse range of world cinema, from Hollywood blockbusters to international arthouse films, analyzing their cultural, social, and political contexts and impacts. Through screenings, readings, and in-class discussions, students develop a nuanced understanding of global cinema, its history, influence and significance in shaping collective narratives and impacting on contemporary social, cultural, political or environmental issues and debates.
title: World Screens Through Global Genres
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Film School

description: This course deepens students understanding and practical experience in digital cinematography, with a focus on storytelling through lighting, shadow and colour. Through hands-on exercises, analysis and reflective practice, students will develop the knowledge, skills and attitudes to work across a variety of disciplines and platforms as a professional cinematographer.

description: The course focuses on the transnational 'organised crime' enterprise. We begin with introducing all the relevant concepts before moving on to exploring the 'entrepreneurs' or actors of organised crime, their origins and structures. The course then delves into 'market' of organised crime, exploring the different crime types with a deep dive into drug trafficking, wildlife trafficking and human trafficking and modern slavery and the intersection with financial crime. We will then touch on the convergence of transnational crime types and nexus with terrorist activities and how the proceeds of these crimes are laundered. The final part of this course dives into techniques and regulations that assist with investigating, preventing and controlling these crimes.

description: Sexuality saturates modern life. Our sexual and gender identities signal our selfhood to others and define who we are, whether straight, queer, trans or gender diverse, or one of many other possibilities. Sex is everywhere, from the sheets to the streets, to the internet. How we present ourselves, who we are intimate with, what we do and how often we do it is the subject of commentary, intervention, and regulation. But who has determined what's 'unnatural' and what's 'normal' and when? What have historical actors, experts and institutions said in the past about sex? And have ordinary people always followed the rules? This unit explores histories of sexuality from antiquity to the present. Taking a chronological approach to private practices and erotic lives, we will investigate diverse topics, including prostitution, marriage, crossdressing, birth control, war, chastity, queer lives, and the internet, to identify historical change and continuity. The course focuses on practices, identities and attitudes in Europe, the US, and Australia to consider how gender, class and ethnicity inflect public narratives and intimate lives. Using primary sources and historical objects, you will investigate the meanings people and institutions attach to desire, bodies, and sexuality at different times and places and interrogate our contemporary sexual lives and their possibilities.
title: Histories of Sexuality
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

The course aims to relate to the 'real-life' environment of a dental laboratory. Providing an 'in context' atmosphere requires professional behaviour, critical evaluation of work practices, communication with health professionals and the application of teamwork. Practical artistic skills are developed, improved and built on throughout this course. The course allows students to develop their time management and technical skills, while communicating with clinicians at the same time understanding the financial and operational nature of a dental laboratory. Real life real time learning maximises the learning opportunity to prepare the student beyond graduation. Students will have the opportunity to learn in the team environment. In conjunction to this a research project will be conducted. The research component to the course develops students' ability to prepare, conduct and evaluate research related to their practice. description: This course covers the theory and algorithms of statistical digital signal processing, estimation and modelling together with their applications in the electrical and electronic engineering disciplines. The first half of the course covers the mathematical preliminaries in deterministic digital signal processing, such as z-transform theory, discrete-time Fourier transform, FIR and IIR filter design. The second half covers the core of the course, which examines the modelling and estimation of random signals and processes using spectral estimation, optimal filtering, linear MMSE estimation (Wiener and Kalman filtering), and adaptive filters. Emphasis is placed on electrical and electronic engineering applications, such as signal enhancement, signal estimation in noise, adaptive noise cancellation, and time-series prediction. Students will also learn how to implement signal processing algorithms in the C and Python programming languages on PCs and embedded DSP hardware. Incompatible: 3303ENG Digital Signal Processing and 6321ENG Discrete Time Signal Processing and 6307ENG Advanced Digital Signal Processing.

description: This course offers a comprehensive and accessible introduction to Public International Law, focusing on its foundational principles, core sources, and main actors. It examines how international legal rules and norms are created, interpreted, applied, and enforced, and how they operate in practice in a rapidly changing global environment. Students will explore the dynamic interplay between sovereignty, state responsibility, and global governance, with particular attention to the role of states, international organisations, and selected non-state actors. Key topics include the sources of international law (treaties, customary international law, and general principles), international legal personality, jurisdiction, state responsibility, and mechanisms for the peaceful settlement of disputes. The course is designed to be accessible to students with no prior background in law, including undergraduate students taking the course as an elective and students from related disciplines such as international relations or politics. Core legal concepts and methods are introduced progressively, with an emphasis on understanding how international law differs from domestic legal systems. Workshops are closely connected to current events and contemporary legal controversies, enabling students to analyse how public international law is interpreted, applied, and sometimes contested in real-world situations through cases, legal texts, and developments in the news. This course functions as a foundational course in Public International Law, while also being suitable and recommended for students who have not previously completed an equivalent undergraduate course in the field.
title: Principles of Public International Law
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: The subject examines the concept of 'employment relations strategy' and revisits core concepts central to employment relations that have been introduced in other units. Drawing from a number of disciplines, including Management, Strategic HRM and Industrial (now 'Employment') Relations, the unit encourages students to think in a holistic way about strategic employment relations planning in an organisation. Is it merely reactive, via adjustments to new legislation and via incremental changes through enterprise bargaining and/or in management policies? Or can employment relations be seen as 'strategic', affecting the bottom line of the organisation? To what extent are there multiple solutions to a particular problem or issue, and what kinds of decision making are necessary to ensure the optimal solution is chosen? What is the boundary between 'HR' and 'employment relations' and, in a day-to-day sense, are the two separable?
title: HRM and Employment Relations Strategy

academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This is one of two Studio courses within the Master of Cinematic Arts. Simulating the experience of working in a professional studio environment, the MoCA Studio focuses on the application of knowledge, skills and experience in cinematic arts practice, including experimentation and innovation, in the production of creative work. In this course, students work as reflective practitioners, applying their specific skills in collaborative projects while critically examining and developing their own practice. At the end of the MoCA Studio courses, students will have produced high-quality creative works in the cinematic arts, accelerated their professional skills and identity, and demonstrated their ability to work collaboratively as informed practitioners and key creative contributors.
title: MoCA Studio 1
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Film School

description: This course contains the competencies required to obtain identifiable recordings from deceased persons and to apply workplace health and safety policies applicable when working with deceased persons. This competency will be implemented by police staff involved in forensic fingerprint investigation. These competencies should be demonstrated and applied within a mortuary, crime incident scene or mass fatality (Disaster Victim Identification) context.
title: Undertake Fingerprinting of Deceased Persons
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course builds the academic and practical skills you need to succeed at university. You'll strengthen your critical thinking and problem-solving abilities while developing academic literacy skills such as research, referencing and writing. You'll also gain confidence with digital tools and everyday maths, giving you a strong foundation for further study and your future career.
title: Foundations for University Success
academicOrgDescription: EmpowerED

description: As a Bachelor of Musical Theatre graduate, you will have gone through many facets of training to become highly skilled, musically adaptable and equipped to enter professional life as a creative and flexible 21st century musical theatre performer. This course helps you prepare for connection with the industry.
title: Building Your Musical Theatre Profile
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: As a Bachelor of Musical Theatre graduate, you will have gone through many facets of training to become highly skilled, musically adaptable and equipped to enter professional life as a creative and flexible 21st century musical theatre performer. This course helps you prepare for connection with the industry.
title: Musical Theatre Industry Showcase
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: In this course, students will examine a particular issue in the criminal justice system: the role of the victim. To do this, students will gain an understanding of the role and characteristics of crime victims, how victims interact (or not) with the criminal justice system, and the differential impacts of victimisation experiences. Students will then apply this knowledge to assessing initiatives to recognise victim suffering and enhance victim support. Issues of inequality and rights will be central themes to understanding victims and their experiences.
title: Victims and Justice
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This course provides a critical reflection on issues currently facing First Nations peoples, in Australia and globally, in achieving justice. Students will be exposed to Indigenous perspectives on justice through Indigenous-authored research that allows the lived experiences of First Nations people to be heard. Using a strengths-based approach, the course provides students to consider the intersections of history, culture and justice in the ways we have responded and should respond to crime.
title: First Nations and Justice
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: Building on knowledge of human behaviour, basic counselling skills and processes, as well as case conceptualisation, students will be introduced to the processes and techniques of cognitive and behavioural approaches to therapy including CBT (Cognitive-Behaviour Therapy) and ACT (pronounced "act"; Acceptance and Commitment Therapy). Students will participate in activities that will prepare them for counselling work with people experiencing a variety of life issues and personal difficulties, and will develop skills in developing client intervention plans. Corequisite: Students must be enrolled in corequisite 3014PSY
title: Counselling Development 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This foundational block supports the transition to university study and future professional contexts. Learners develop the essential literacies, learning strategies, and self-reflection skills needed to thrive in business education and beyond.
title: Academic and Professional Foundations: Identity in Practice
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

description: This block builds evaluative judgement, ethical reasoning, and cultural competence. Learners explore business as a values-driven and culturally situated practice, gaining tools to make informed and inclusive decisions.
title: Business Purpose, Regional Engagement, and Decision-Making
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

description: This course introduces students to Islam as a religious tradition, civilisation and way of life, examining its origins, historical development and diverse expressions in the modern world. Students explore the message and major themes of the Qur'an, the life and legacy of the Prophet Muhammad, the development of Islamic civilisation, law and theology, and the emergence of diverse Muslim traditions and political communities. The course then considers how Muslims and Muslim-majority societies have responded to the challenges of the modern world, including colonialism, nation-states, political change, sectarianism, jihad and militancy, questions of peace and coexistence, and relations between Muslims and other communities. Particular attention is given to contemporary Muslim societies and to the experiences, identities and contributions of Muslims in Australia. Throughout the course, students are encouraged to distinguish Islamic teachings from their varied historical, political and cultural manifestations and to develop an informed and critical understanding of Islam and Muslims in the contemporary world.
title: Islam in the Modern World
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course introduces students to key political, social, and cultural events, issues, and questions that have shaped Australian history and identity. Sometimes seen as a distant and isolated continent, Australia's history and identity has always been shaped by global forces. From the geological break up of Gondwanaland 180 million years ago, to the technological cosmopolitanism of the 21st century, this course helps students understand and analyse the origins, narratives and consequences of events in Australian history, and their place in national and international contexts. Prerequisites: NIL; Co-requisites: NIL; Incompatible: 2063EDN Australian Studies; 2101ART / 2101HUM / AUS211 / 2101LHS Australia and the World; AUS21 Australia and the World (OUA Course Equivalent).
title: Australia: A Global History
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course equips students with advanced proficiency in studio-specific animation tools and techniques. Focused on 2D puppet animation, the course includes rig development towards nuanced character performances, integrating detailed gesture and facial animation. Through technical instruction, hands-on practice, and critical reflection students elevate their animation skills to industry-standard levels, preparing for dynamic careers in character animation.
title: Character Animation: Processes and Tools
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Film School

description: This course explores the intersection of game design and the evolving landscape of contemporary issues. As video games continue to gain prominence as a powerful medium for storytelling and interactive experiences, it becomes crucial for game designers to engage with and consider complex social, cultural, ethical, and technological issues. In this course, students will learn to critically analyse and examine the relationship between contemporary issues and game design. Students will explore how games can address and engage with social justice, climate change, identity and representation, politics, mental health, globalisation, and more. By completing this course, students will develop the ability to assess and articulate the strengths, weaknesses, and societal impact of games that address contemporary issues and design solutions.
title: Contemporary Issues and Game Design
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Film School

description: This course is designed to introduce students to fundamental directing skills across film and television. Students will learn how to analyse scripts, direct performances, and use the camera to convey meaning. Students will also explore the director's relationship with complementary crew roles such as the producer, director of photography, production designer and sound designer.
title: Directing Fundamentals
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Film School

description: Outbound Griffith Exchange students who are studying at a partner university must enroll in exchange courses for the trimester(s) they will be studying overseas. The tuition fees for each trimester will be determined by the course code(s), which considers the credit points and field of study. These factors are set by the Australian Government. This course is specifically tailored for both undergraduate and postgraduate students who are pursuing fields of study that include Social Studies or Behavioural Science.
title: Exchange Studies
academicOrgDescription: Griffith International

description: Outbound Griffith Exchange students who are studying at a partner university must enroll in exchange courses for the trimester(s) they will be studying overseas. The tuition fees for each trimester will be determined by the course code(s), which considers the credit points and field of study. These factors are set by the Australian Government. This course is specifically tailored for both undergraduate and postgraduate students who are pursuing fields of study that include Visual and Performing Arts.
title: Exchange Studies
academicOrgDescription: Griffith International

description: Outbound Griffith Exchange students who are studying at a partner university must enroll in exchange courses for the trimester(s) they will be studying overseas. The tuition fees for each trimester will be determined by the course code(s), which considers the credit points and field of study. These factors are set by the Australian Government. This course is specifically tailored for both undergraduate and postgraduate students who are pursuing fields of study that include Law, Accounting, Administration, Economics, Commerce, and Communications.
title: Exchange Studies
academicOrgDescription: Griffith International

description: Outbound Griffith Exchange students who are studying at a partner university must enroll in exchange courses for the trimester(s) they will be studying overseas. The tuition fees for each trimester will be determined by the course code(s), which considers the credit points and field of study. These factors are set by the Australian Government. This course is specifically tailored for both undergraduate and postgraduate students who are pursuing fields of study that include Education, Clinical Psychology, English, Mathematics, and Statistics.
title: Exchange Studies
academicOrgDescription: Griffith International

description: Outbound Griffith Exchange students who are studying at a partner university must enroll in exchange courses for the trimester(s) they will be studying overseas. The tuition fees for each trimester will be determined by the course code(s), which considers the credit points and field of study. These factors are set by the Australian Government. This course is specifically tailored for both undergraduate and postgraduate students who are pursuing fields of study in Society and Culture, including History, Archaeology, Indigenous Studies, Justice and Law Enforcement, and Philosophy and Religious Studies.
title: Exchange Studies
academicOrgDescription: Griffith International

description: This course focuses on developing students' skills in creative writing through the study of fiction, non-fiction, poetry and other forms of writing. Students will explore a range of approaches that authors take to developing and refining a sustainable creative writing practice, discuss avenues for generating original ideas and problem-solving during the writing and editing process, and develop an understanding how the writing and publishing industry works. Students read and discuss a series of classic and contemporary works of creative writing, and learn to exchange considered interpretations with their peers as well as developing critical analysis skills to apply to their own writing and the work of other writers. The course takes a scaffolded approach to introducing key creative writing skills and techniques, which students are then invited to apply across a range of different forms and styles of writing, drawing on themes and ideas that are relevant to their own interests. The course introduces students to the rich and vibrant world of contemporary creative writing, and offers students opportunities to experiment with a range of established and new creative writing forms and approaches.
title: An Introduction to Creative Writing: Forms and Techniques
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course focuses on techniques used in the writing of contemporary short fiction. Students will develop technical skills in writing short fiction alongside an understanding of the wider literary contexts and traditions of the form. The course engages students in exploring a range of genres, styles and perspectives in writing short fiction, offering examples of contemporary, experimental and classic short stories to frame the development of students' own writing practice. Students will have opportunity to develop skills and knowledge applicable to a range of publishing outcomes and will be provided with a supportive environment for producing original pieces of short fiction reflecting their development during the trimester.
title: Writing Short Fiction
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course explores the preparation, planning and delivery of communication strategies and activities for major events and entertainment industries. It builds on students' knowledge of strategic communication while applying that knowledge and skills in practice to events and entertainment contexts.
title: Event and Entertainment Communication
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course will equip students with essential, practical skills for communicating information about health and science issues and will help them to critically evaluate and interpret health and science information and adapt that for a range of purposes.
title: Health, Science and Risk Communication
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Discover how to harness the power of data to make smarter business decisions. This hands-on course is designed for business students who want to build practical skills in data processing, analysis, visualisation, and predictive modelling. You'll work with real-world tools and datasets to explore business challenges, uncover insights, and communicate your findings through clear, compelling visual stories. Whether you're interested in marketing, finance, operations, or strategy, this course will show you how to turn data into a competitive advantage. By the end of the course, you'll be confident in using data to support ethical, evidence-based decision-making in a business context.
title: Business Analytics and Decision Intelligence
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: How do we determine the terms by which we live together? This course examines how human societies have sought to establish just and peaceful coexistence through sacred and temporal covenants, treaties, social contracts, law and citizenship. It explores diverse frameworks of social order, including Indigenous Australian concepts such as Makarrata, concerned with truth-telling, agreement-making and reconciliation, and Tjukurpa, encompassing sacred law, order and ways of life; Islamic covenantal principles (ahd and mithaq) concerning human responsibility, justice and coexistence; Western social contract traditions; and contemporary international covenants governing human rights, peace and security. Through comparative study, the course develops critical understanding of the cultural, religious, ethical and political foundations of coexistence, reconciliation, social order and global justice. It is particularly relevant to further study in Islam-West Relations, Indigenous Studies, Sociology, Law, Government and International Relations, and related fields.
title: Human Existence and Coexistence
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course equips students with foundational skills in criminological research and introduces them to the role of evidence in shaping policy and practice. Students will learn the principles of qualitative and quantitative research design, data collection, analysis, and ethical inquiry. Through applied examples, including evidence-based policing and justice policy, students will develop the capacity to critically assess research and understand its relevance in real-world justice contexts. The course also lays the groundwork for advanced research learning, preparing students to become informed producers and users of evidence in criminology and criminal justice.
title: Evidence-Based Practice and Research
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: This intermediate-level course will advance your ability to design meaningful user experiences through considered interactive projects. Through studio-based projects, you will draw upon research into historical, contemporary, and future-focused narratives to evaluate how designers engage users through carefully curated experiences. From packaging design, wayfinding, the use of sustainable materials, human intuition, and sensorial experiences, you are given the opportunity to explore the connection between tangible and intangible design elements. Understand how colour, materials, finishes, form, and functionality in combination can educate, amuse, instruct and elevate the relationship between people and products through an experience. By the end of the course, you will have the ability to test and evaluate approaches to user experience design across various creative media and how it shapes our experience of everyday things.
title: User Experience Design
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course focuses on the style and principles of Indigenous art, fostering experimentation, exploration and work across a range of media. The course encourages individual and collective engagement with Indigenous media. Students will begin to establish a consistent and self-directed practice. This course is restricted to Bachelor of Contemporary Australian Indigenous Art students ONLY. Prerequisites: NIL
title: Indigenous Media 1
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: The reality of work has changed radically, and human resource management practices have evolved with these changes. The rise of the knowledge economy means intellectual capital management is crucial. In this course you will apply theoretical perspectives to interpret and critically evaluate the changing nature of work and work arrangements and the implications these changes pose for managers. Critical issues revolving around the impact of technological augmentation and disruptions will also be examined. With thorough knowledge of policies and strategies to manage organizations human, social and structural intellectual resources in a dynamic working environment, you will be able to create frameworks for building relevant future-focused competencies and innovations in the workplace.
title: The Purpose and Future of Work
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: In this course, students will utilize advanced techniques rooted in the MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) framework to understand, simulate, and defend against sophisticated cyber threats. On completing the course students will possess advanced knowledge and practical skills in ethical hacking techniques aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Graduates will be well-equipped to identify, exploit, and defend against cyber threats, making them valuable assets in organizations seeking to bolster their cybersecurity defence and resilience. Prerequisites: 7611ICT
title: Offensive Cyber Security
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: Organisations typically use many disparate technologies to achieve their business objectives. This course first gives an overview of low-level technologies such as programming with a focus on code reuse, scripting techniques and software configuration tools. This is followed by a practical presentation of software packages commonly used for handling data and producing reports and presentations.
