The aim of this course is to provide students with practical legal experience outside Australia and with global and international perspectives and opportunities. Students will explore and compare legal systems and the strengths and weaknesses of different models. The course enables students to practice their technical and practical skills in an international legal workplace, and aims to build: -cross cultural awareness and skills -global perspectives and a professional identity as a global legal practitioner -capacity to make informed decisions, both personally and professionally -capacity to reflect on the impact of the law on individuals and society -ethical awareness, sense of social justice and professional responsibility -multi-disciplinary awareness and competence -graduate skills, professional identity, career direction, confidence, and employability -practical and technical skills, including dealing with unstructured situations, written and oral communication, collaboration, teamwork and time management. Griffith sourced opportunities are advertised by student email each Trimester for the following Trimester. Each opportunity sets out the partner's requirements for each internship. Students must apply and be selected. Students sourcing their own international legal placement of at least two weeks duration can submit the placement for convenor approval to enrol in this course. The course is a law elective available to all JD and LLB students who have: -completed at least 120 CP in law subjects -have a minimum GPA of 4, although some partners require a higher GPA, which will be stated For further information please contact the course convenor.
title: International Experience Clinic
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This placement course introduces students to the practice field of medical nutrition therapy, applying the nutrition care process to patients and clients. Students spend a minimum of 50 working days in a hospital and/or other health care setting, delivering nutritional care to individuals and small groups. Students are placed under the supervision of field Accredited Practising Dietitians with a minimum of two years' experience. During the placement, students observe, practice and are evaluated on the delivery of dietetic care to individuals. Students will be evaluated against the Dietitians Australia National Competency Standards for Dietitians in Australia.
title: Nutrition Care Process Placement
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course explores disease processes and their evolution, assessment and treatment, and develops problem-solving skills to enable the development of competent practitioners who can solve real life problems in nursing care. The primary focus is on infectious diseases, microbiology and medical disorders that are generated at the cellular level.
title: Human Pathophysiology and Pharmacology 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Nursing and Midwifery

description: This course involves the execution of the research proposal, including experimentation, and analysis of research results under the guidance of two or more supervisors. It also involves the preparation and presentation of the completed Master of Medical Research thesis, including research aims, hypotheses, significance, rationale, literature background, experimental design, methods, results, discussions and conclusions. The thesis would normally be expected to be approximately 40,000 words. Enrolment depends on availability of research topic and supervisors.6001HLS Dissertation preparation, research proposal and ethical application (needs to be completed during 6001HLS course) and availability of a supervisor. Prerequisite: 6001HLS Dissertation preparation, research proposal and ethical application (needs to be completed during 6001HLS course) and availability of a supervisor.
title: Research Thesis
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: This course focuses on contemporary information systems and demonstrates how these systems are used throughout the international tourism, hospitality, sport and event service sectors. It will emphasise the key information systems that include people, software, hardware, data and communication technologies. The course will explore the important role of information and knowledge management within service sectors. It will provide students with an understanding of the types of information systems relevant to the service sector and how these systems are useful for improving efficiency and effectiveness for management and organisations. This course will also provide students with an understanding of how information systems can assist in improving service to, and developing stronger relationships with, sport, event, tourism, and hospitality consumers.
title: Tourism Product Design, Innovation and Digitization
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: This course focuses on the operational processes that create successful special events. The content builds on a planning and project management framework and considers elements of event logistics and transport, site planning and design, management of subcontractors and volunteer labour.
title: Event Coordination and Logistics
academicOrgDescription: Department of Tourism and Marketing

description: Students enrolled in the Honours program will undertake an Honours Dissertation relevant to their study of urban and environmental planning under the guidance of one or more supervisors appointed by the Honours Convenor. The topic and nature of the Dissertation will be determined through consultation and mutual agreement of the student and supervisor and must be approved by the Honours Convenor. Students in 1658 and 1660 will be required to align the topic of their Honours Research Project to that of their major if they have chosen a major. The Dissertation will involve original research but this can include the collection and analysis of primary data, the analysis of secondary data, or the development of new theoretical or conceptual models. Assessment will comprise a written report of the work, prepared in the form of a thesis and submitted for independent examination by at least two assessors. Students will also be required to make two presentations: one of their research proposals and one describing their work and provisional conclusions. The quality of these presentations will contribute to the overall assessment of the Project. Pre-requisite: Students must have passed 4029ENV Project Proposal in Honours and must have completed 4030ENV_P1 or have the permission of the course convenor before enrolling in this course.
title: Honours Dissertation
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: The course develops students' knowledge, skills and application for buildings classification under the building code of Australia (BCA). The course provides students with an overview of regulations and construction techniques on the low-rise residential buildings in Australia. The course covers construction processes including building regulations; environmental issue, footing systems, flooring and timber, wall framing and roof designing systems, waterproofing and first fix and fit-out. Students will be taught how to read plans and build a house by studying construction theory and legislation, visiting building sites and sketching construction details.
title: Domestic Construction
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course delves into the theory and practical applications of big data, guiding students through the journey from raw data to informed decision-making. Students will gain comprehensive knowledge of big data formats, data processing platforms, and advanced analytics tools. The curriculum emphasises the skills needed to transform, visualise, model, and effectively communicate the insights derived from data, equipping students with the expertise to harness big data for strategic advantage.
title: Big Data Analysis
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: This course examines how business is changing and how, as a result, there are a growing number of businesses that are focused on responding to major social, environmental, and economic challenges both in Australia and internationally. Businesses are changing the way we approach issues like poverty, homelessness, climate change, and unemployment and alongside these changes we are seeing the growth of social enterprises, impact investment, social innovation, and market-based approaches to creating positive outcomes for people, place and planet.
title: The Business of Changing the World
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: This course provides experience in performing a complete mini-research project, incorporating standard biochemical techniques and molecular biology techniques, particularly those involved with molecular cloning, protein purification and characterisation, recombinant protein expression and protein engineering, electrophoresis and Western blotting. Students will also be taught how to become more effective scientific writers and communicators through practical examples and exercises. This course will be delivered in an intensive mode, comprising two weeks of daily intensive lab sessions and workshops, followed by six weeks of writing tutorials. Pre-requisite: 2019ESC Biotechniques Laboratory (or similar lab-based course if approved by course convenor). Note: pre-req is not applicable for students enrolled in Program 1540.
title: Biomolecular Sciences Laboratory
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: We live in a VUCA (volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous) world today. The grand challenges facing humanity are urgent, systemic, complicated, and evolving faster than ever before. That is why the World Economic Forum has listed complex problem-solving as one of the top ten skills for the 21st century. Complex problem-solving requires critical and lateral thinking, reasoning, analysis, interpretation, synthesising information, research skills, reflection, creativity, curiosity, imagination, innovation, perseverance, self-direction, planning, self-discipline, adaptability, initiative, teamwork, and collaboration. In this course, you will be exposed to concepts and frameworks associated with grand challenges and problem-solving techniques. Through interactive course materials and weekly workshops, you will learn by doing, looking at problems from different perspectives, applying (where possible) solutions to problems and grand challenges in a proper context, and learn how to effectively present your solutions.
title: Grand Challenges for Business
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

description: This course comprises a period of program-approved industry-based work placement relevant to your discipline - for students enrolled in the following programs, Master of Architecture 5558 and Bachelor of Architectural Design/Master of Architecture 5759; the supervisor at the host organisation must be a registered architect. The unit requires you to complete a minimum of 130 hours of workplace experience during the trimester, plus approximately 20 hours to complete the assessments. The course provides students with valuable professional experience and the opportunity to apply and further develop the knowledge, skills, and principles of their discipline within a real-world professional environment. Students may be involved in a range of activities such as project work, design and planning processes, client and stakeholder engagement, teamwork, communication, and professional practice. The type of experience will vary according to the student's discipline, skills, academic level, and host organisation. The student will engage in work and projects agreed upon and negotiated between the host organisation and the course convenor. For students enrolled in the following programs, Master of Architecture 5558 and Bachelor of Architectural Design/Master of Architecture 5759, an emphasis on understanding the application of the 2021 NSCA performance criteria in a practice environment is a key learning opportunity How to Enrol (Departmental Consent Required): · Students must independently secure a suitable placement relevant to their discipline before requesting enrolment in this course. · Email: wil-gs@griffith.edu.au (WIL Office) · The WIL Office will send you some paperwork to complete. · Once you have completed the paperwork, the WIL Office will contact the course convenor to confirm departmental consent. · After consent is confirmed, you will be able to enrol in the class.
title: Work Integrated Learning
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

description: This course offers students the opportunity to explore the materials, processes and language of painting. A major emphasis of the course will be the development of conceptual and thematic responses to set projects that are designed to provide a focus for creative investigation in the first year Visual Art studio courses. Prerequisites: Nil
title: Introduction to Painting
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course offers students the opportunity of exploring the materials, processes and language of sculpture, performance and installation. A major emphasis of the course will be the development of conceptual and thematic responses to set projects that are designed to provide a focus for creative investigation in the first year Visual Art studio courses. Prerequisites: Nil
title: Introduction to Sculpture, Performance and Installation
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course explores the diversity and development of Indigenous Australian art and Design. It aims to introduce students to critical and contemporary understandings of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander culture, and the foundational knowledge required to engage with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, communities and organisations. Prerequisites: Nil
title: Contemporary Australian Indigenous Art Foundations
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: This course provides you with an in-depth understanding of how to develop viable novel business ideas through empathetic design and customer discovery and validation. This course focuses on creativity, problem solving and critical thinking tools to create these novel solutions.
title: Innovation, Creativity and Entrepreneurship
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: The aim of this course is to understand the complex workings of businesses that are family-owned and run. The course explores the unique personal and interpersonal issues, as well as the business issues associated with the family-owned and managed firm.
title: Family Business Management
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: This subject focuses on the application of prior knowledge to the development of the necessary capacity to assess clients' needs; prepare, present, evaluate and implement tailored, comprehensive financial plans. Students will also be able to recognise the implications of legal and ethical codes that relate to financial planners and to apply them to their own work activities.
title: Financial Planning, Construction and Review
academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics

description: This course represents the second part of your placement components of the Master of Pharmacy program. In this placement course, you will be undertaking special interest placements that build on the knowledge and skills you gained through the earlier placements. The placement opportunities will be sought based on your specific areas of interest (as indicated by an expression of interest process at the end of your first year) and may include a broad range of pharmacy practice settings including hospital pharmacy, community pharmacy, rural placements, community-based health services, and aged care facilities. There may also be opportunities for you to undertake your placement at organisations that are involved with medicines regulation (e.g. the TGA), funding (e.g. PBS), professional bodies (e.g. the PSA, PGA), and in settings that deliver pharmacists' broadening roles (e.g. pharmacists in GP clinics). These placements will help you to understand, and further envision, current and future roles for pharmacists within the continuum of care.
title: Experiential Rotations II
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: In General Dental Practice 1 students develop knowledge and skills of principles, techniques and materials applied to the practice of endodontics, periodontics and removable and fixed prosthodontics. Students will attend professional practice sessions to enable them to reach a level of clinical competence to operate safely in a clinical environment. Pre-requisite: Students must have successfully completed all preceding years courses to progress to year 3 and students must have successfully completed 3060DOH_Y1 in the current year to progress to 3060DOH_Y2.
title: General Dental Practice 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: Positive psychology has powerful implications for learning, teaching and professional development. But what is positive psychology, and why is it so important for education and learning, for professional learning, and for leadership and coaching? This course identifies and unpacks the science of positive psychology, with a focus on areas of research that have high applicability to education and professional learning settings. We explore the implications of this research for fostering knowledge and skills integral to effective learning and leading learning, such as: positivity and positive mindset, positive communication and relations, social intelligence, emotional intelligence, strengths-based approaches to learning and development, adaptability, empathy, resilience, creativity, cognitive flexibility, psychological flexibility, motivation and self-determination, social connectedness, self-regulation, discipline, and wellbeing. You will gain a strong conceptual overview of positive psychology research as it applies to enabling the learning of others, understand the science behind the most efficacious interventions and practices, and confidently apply these understandings to your current or future professional aspirations, whether that be teaching, school leadership, professional development, professional coaching and mentoring, and/or people focused leadership and communication roles. The materials, learning experiences and assessment requirements provide scaffolded opportunities to consider specific areas of positive psychology and education research and apply them to the development of authentic practices and potential interventions that are of most relevance to your current or future professional setting.
title: Positive Psychology and Education
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: This course involves development of a research project under supervision, analysis of literature and execution of experimentation. Results and conclusions are presented in oral and written forms.
title: Dissertation 1
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: A sound understanding of the institutions of public policy is essential for effective practice in a range of human services professions. This knowledge allows practitioners to better navigate the system as they use their initiative to influence, advocate and improve social policy and legislation and contribute toward social change. This course is designed to ensure you can do those things by becoming an effective practitioner advocate with planning, problem solving, critical thinking, teamwork, communication, cooperation and engagement skills. It covers the Australian system of government and the Australian legal system, and the processes by which social policies are developed, it will empower you to participate in and influence the social policy development process. The course is broken into two parts: the first half of the trimester examines the Australian system of government and aspects of the Australian legal system that impact on both practitioners and their future clients; the second half examines the policy making process with a particular focus on influencing change from outside the policy making system. As a graduate, you will be equipped to be a front-line human services worker with the tools needed to engage in effective advocacy that achieves change.
title: Human Services : Law and Social Policy
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course continues to develop students' competence as a practising psychologist within the second part of the practical internship in the Psychology Clinic (an extension of 8181PSY). Students continue to work as a provisionally registered clinical psychologists under close clinical supervision. The applied focus of this internship is designed to develop further student competence in managing a therapeutic caseload and working with clients across the lifespan, individually and in groups. This course is a non-graded course and students who pass the course will receive a non-graded pass (NGP) on their transcript. You must have satisfactory performance on all assessment tasks to receive a non-graded pass in the course.
title: Practicum 2A
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: This is the third of three practicum courses which students must complete as part of their internship. Students complete the internship (8181PSY, 8180PSY_P1 and 8180PSY_P2) over a one-year period. Practicum training is an essential and compulsory requirement for post graduate training in Clinical Psychology. Students will undertake a practical internship in the Griffith University Psychology Clinic under close supervision. They will manage a therapeutic caseload and work with clients across the lifespan, individually and in groups. Students must hold provisional registration with the Psychology Board of Australia before commencing their internship.
title: Practicum 2B
academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

description: The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Moot is an annual competition involving teams from Law Schools in Southeast Queensland. It is intended to develop students' skills in writing, oral advocacy and team work, and giving students the opportunity to network with other students and legal practitioners. Students who participate in this Moot will attend seminars at Griffith and at various law firms, complete written outlines of argument, and prepare and deliver oral submissions. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students who have completed their first year of the Law program are eligible to apply.
title: First Peoples Moot - Written
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: Social Data Analytics is designed for students from a range of disciplines who want to make sense of data - without needing to love mathematics. Delivered by the School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science, and created by people who understand that statistics can feel intimidating, this course takes a supportive, accessible, and hands-on approach to exploring what data can reveal about society. You will learn the foundations of data analysis and descriptive statistics with minimal jargon, using real-world survey data to investigate meaningful questions about society, values, and social change. Through guided weekly demonstrations, you will learn how apply statistical and data visualisation techniques, use industry-relevant software, and interpret findings in clear and useful ways. The course is structured so that weekly learning activities directly contribute to your assessment project, allowing you to progressively build confidence, skills, and independence throughout the trimester. Tutorials provide opportunities to check your progress, receive personalised support, and work directly on course assessments in a collaborative environment. By the end of the course, you will gain transferable, industry-relevant skills in data analysis and software use that are valued across a wide range of careers - not only in specialist statistical roles, but also in policy, research, business, marketing, and community development.
title: Social Data Analytics
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: This course introduces students to common programming software and develops their computing skills. The course introduces students to data manipulation, analysis and numerical techniques. It prepares students to analyse and use a range of data types to develop solutions to catchment science problems using programming.

description: Pharmacy Practice IV is the culminating capstone practice course that emphasises pharmacists' professional roles as primary health care providers and medication managers in Australian society and within multidisciplinary health care teams. Expected course outcomes include legal and ethical practice in dispensing, counselling and medicines management, and readiness for intern practice.
title: Pharmacy Practice IV
academicOrgDescription: School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences

description: This course is the second of two courses in which students enrol to complete a research dissertation. The dissertation will investigate a topic that is relevant to the program. The enrolled student would normally be expected to complete approximately 20 000 words and take 600 hours work. The dissertation builds on previously studied research course/s that have developed students' understandings of methodology and design. The main objective of the dissertation is to provide students with the opportunity to engage in a major piece of research in education. By doing this they will come to understand better the nature and dynamics of education, and gain practice in a formal research method, as well as investigating a significant area of knowledge, question or problem in the field that is relevant to the student's specific program. Students should discuss both topic and supervisor with the program director before enrolment is approved.
title: Research Dissertation 2
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

description: In this course, students will engage in a comprehensive examination of the substantive law, rules, and policies governing criminal justice in Queensland. The course covers a series of related criminal procedural issues and the sentencing process in the context of criminal investigations, trials, and appeals. Each week, legal, ethical, and policy issues relevant to substantive and procedural matters will be studied, discussed, and critically reflected upon. You will be encouraged to consider the effectiveness and fairness of Australia's adversarial criminal justice system. You will learn to interpret and apply the general principles and statutory laws governing criminal procedure. THIS COURSE IS ONLY OPEN TO LAW STUDENTS.
title: Crime 2
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: In this course students participate in a project-based engagement with a real client. Projects are sought from a range of industry and university partners (project sponsors) that require significant development, communication and documentation effort. A project problem is addressed by a number of students working in a group to form a student project team. Significant importance is placed on effective project management and excellent communication strategies between team members, the project manager, and with the client. Students work in close liaison with their client and academic assessor throughout the project and are expected to demonstrate a good understanding of their project. To be eligible for this course, students must have registered online with the Griffith Sciences Partnership Office in the trimester prior to enrolment. Please contact wil-gs@griffith.edu.au to register. If your registration is successful, you will be given permission to enrol prior to the start of the trimester. Pre-requisite: Must have completed 160CP with at least 20CP from the major subjects which define the program.

academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: The course will provide the basis for an understanding of the principles that underpin rehabilitation (including prevention and management) of selected clinical conditions and how a detailed understanding of those principles and mechanisms may improve clinical outcomes. Clinical conditions examined in this course will include musculoskeletal and neurological conditions.
title: Exercise for Clinical Populations II
academicOrgDescription: School of Allied Health, Sport and Social Work

description: This course introduces students to fundamental elements of the law of property providing the basis for further study in the core course 7715LAW Property 2. This course critically assesses the justifications for property and considers the delineation of property using a variety of examples such as land, chattels and intangibles (intellectual property), illustrating how property is defined and limited through the legal concepts of "ownership", "title" and "possession". A significant focus of this course is a critical assessment of the legal justifications for property and the manner in which particular groups have used conceptual tools to secure their property rights. THIS COURSE IS ONLY OPEN TO LAW STUDENTS.
title: Property 1
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Law School

description: This course is centred on the observational traditions of Still-life, Landscape and Portrait painting. Since the mid-twentieth century the use of painting as a means by which to directly observe and interpret the material world has fallen out of favour. Painters, until recently, have preferred instead to focus on questions of abstract form, photographic representation or digital technologies. While this course by no means argues for a nostalgic return to traditional representational painting, we will reflect on how these traditional genres can be (and are being) redeployed in a contemporary context for a more nuanced engagement with the material world. Painting 'from life' demands a highly conscious and extended negotiation between the painter's body, material objects (including the painting) and other bodies. In this way, painting continues to offer a particularly acute mode of visual observation, engagement and understanding. Within the tradition of painting more broadly, Still-Life, Landscape and Portraiture differ in approach and emphasis. The differences between these ways of seeing and representing the material world form the foundation Painting and Observation. Prerequisites: Nil
title: Painting and Observation
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

You will develop core skills in financial literacy for business and an understanding of the key principles of accounting, finance and economics. Sound accounting, finance and economics skills are sought by employers in any business graduate, as they enable a solid understanding of the principles that drive enterprise toward success. Students will synthesise this information to inform design decisions which encompass the conceptual and compositional aspects of their proposals with clear ties to its urban scale. Prerequisites for this course are 1901ENG (or 1911ENV) and 1902ENG (or 1912ENV). Incompatible with 2901ENV.
title: Studio 3 - Contextual Response
academicOrgDescription: School of Engineering and Built Environment

The course develops the critical skills required to analyse an area of finance specialisation that is topical and of interest to the postgraduate student. The objective of the course is to extend the student's expertise beyond the foundations of finance. This course should be taken in the last year of study.

Through a series of exercises, students will look at what design is and dispel any pre-concepts. Students will investigate the experiential dimensions of space, its materiality and qualities in relation to the human body. The course introduces modes of observation, cognition, experimentation and representation as they relate to the design process. The course encourages students to build skills across a range of manual media in order to document observed and cognitive conditions (diagrams/graphic/written) and plan/design small-scale proposals. description: Bioinformatics has become an essential field in biological and medical research. The "Applied Bioinformatics" course offers an introduction to the computational analysis of biological data, integrating key principles from molecular biology, biotechnology, chemistry, environmental sciences, and biomedical sciences. The curriculum blends theoretical lectures with hands-on, computer-based laboratory sessions, providing a balanced approach to learning theory and application. Students will explore a variety of bioinformatics algorithms, tools, and databases, gaining practical experience in their applications. A solid foundation in genetics, molecular biology, and biochemistry is required to fully benefit from the course content.
title: Applied Bioinformatics
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

description: This course aims to develop students' identity as a clinical psychologist and registered health practitioner. Students will gain familiarity with the processes of working in a professional Psychology Clinic, including appropriate professional and ethical conduct.

academicOrgDescription: School of Applied Psychology

Students will get an understanding of the various components of experience design including user research, user testing, user/customer journeys, user flows, prototyping, personas and qualitative data gathering. The course will also delve into the historical and contemporary placing of Experience Design in global emerging practice.
title: Experience Design
academicOrgDescription: Queensland College of Art and Design

description: Effective communication requires more than strong writing and storytelling skills, it also requires an understanding of the legal boundaries that govern what can be published, shared and reported. This subject provides an introduction to the legal environment surrounding journalism, public relations and professional communication in Australia. You'll examine the laws, regulations and principles that influence how information is gathered, created and distributed across traditional media, social media and emerging digital platforms. Through real scenarios, you'll investigate issues including freedom of expression, defamation, privacy, confidentiality, copyright and access to information. You'll also explore the legal constraints surrounding court reporting, publication of sensitive material and the balance between public interest and individual rights. Gain insight into the challenges facing communicators in a digital and socially connected media landscape, where information can be published and shared instantly across multiple channels. You'll learn how legal obligations apply to online publishing, social media content, public relations practice and independent media ventures. You'll gain a practical understanding of the legal considerations that affect professional communication and the confidence to make informed publishing decisions while reducing the risk of legal disputes. PLEASE NOTE: Media Law is taught in a 12-week teaching mode in Study Session 1 each year. In Study Session 3, the subject is delivered in an intensive six-week teaching mode, with the remaining six weeks dedicated to completion of the final assessment.
title: Media Law
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

Topics move from the very origins of humanity, through the earliest Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, and Neolithic societies, through the ancient Mediterranean world, and through to the complex societies of the Americas.
title: Topics in Archaeology
academicOrgDescription: School of Environment and Science

The course will also look at the relationship of Indigenous Peoples to the Canadian state.
title: Foundations of Canadian Law

description: Police, Courts and Corrections explains the processes that govern the way crimes are investigated, tried, and punished. The course begins with an overview of the aims and functions of the criminal justice system with consideration for the laws and justice principles that underpin it. It then examines the roles and functions of the police, courts and corrective services and the process through which a criminal case progresses through the system, concluding with some reflections on alternatives to traditional practice. Throughout this course, consideration is given to understanding the powers, responsibilities and accountabilities of key criminal justice actors as well as the application of justice principles within the system. The course particularly references the Queensland criminal justice system, however general principles are common to all Australian systems.
title: Police, Courts and Corrections
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

description: The term social problem is usually taken to refer to social conditions that affect a significant number of people within society in a negative way. Social problems are seen as being disruptive or damaging to society, as social injustices that we should be striving to solve. For example, crime and safety, violence, alcohol, and drug use are often constructed as significant social problems for many people in Australia while others are more concerned with inequality and discrimination. In fact, social problems like crime are often the consequence of factors extending beyond the individual's control, such as inequality, discrimination, prejudice, oppression, and concomitant social injustice. Sociology provides us with the critical thinking skills to understand the connection between social problems and the social structure including how social problems come to be 'problems' in the first place. In this course, you will develop frameworks for critical sociological thought by exploring multiple intersectional axes of power, oppression, inequality, and social injustice including classism, racism and colonialism, sexism, heterosexism and transmisia, ableism, adultism, and ageism. You will learn how oppression and power within these spheres (and the intersections between them) are vital to understanding the social problems of most concern to the discipline of criminology and reflect on how (in)justice might be mitigated. The knowledge gained will equip you with the tools to do criminology in a socially just way.
title: Social Problems - (In)equality and (In)justice
academicOrgDescription: School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

You will beome accomplished in using cultural strength-based approaches and frameworks in education and ways of seeing, being and doing that strongly align with the knowledges and philosophy of Indigenous peoples. You will strong connection between the role and value of language and culture, with positive experiences and academic achievements in schooling. This course provides an immersive experience that models classroom practices to support of academic achievements and foster intercultural respect and understanding. You will learn through developing culturall responsive community informed pedagogical planning and developing a relationship with a community service.

academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

Students explore and critically examine the educational systems, cultural practices, and social contexts of a country other than their own. The course includes a school-based placement and builds an important foundation for the future global teacher.
title: International Experience
academicOrgDescription: School of Education and Professional Studies

title: Mathematics for Computer Science
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

description: In Year 4, MD students enrol twice a year in a single course, Medicine Year 4. Students rotate through five six-week clinical placements, alongside a pre-internship preparedness block over the year. This consists of three core rotations - critical care/orthopaedics, emergency medicine and general practice - and a selective and elective rotation. The students attend their core rotations of critical care/orthopaedics and emergency medicine in a designated zone, and general practice in a practice in Southeast Queensland. Students also complete a selective placement which is usually locally based chosen from a list organised by the School of Medicine, and an elective placement which is usually student-organised and may be local, interstate or international. After the end of year exams, students then complete a four week pre-internship preparedness block. The settings for learning experiences will vary from discipline to discipline but may include ward rounds, outpatient clinics, general practice surgeries, emergency departments, procedural and specialist clinics, theatre sessions, multidisciplinary team meetings, liaison rounds, community clinics (both medical and non-medical) and on-call with junior medical staff. There is an emphasis on learning in clinical and small group environments. A variety of delivery methods are used in relation to educational resources, including seminars, and case-based learning (CBL) tutorials with an online presentation system (OSCARS). There are workplace based assessments in each block, assignments and written examinations through the year and an OSCE at the end of year. A satisfactory summative ITA is required to pass each rotation.
title: Clinical Medicine Year 4
academicOrgDescription: School of Medicine and Dentistry

description: Devising Theatre is an advanced course drawing on social justice themes and experiences to inform developmental and production processes. Students work with an experienced director in 6 hr blocks of intensive collaborative explorations of theatre processes to devise theatre performance/production based in socio-cultural justice issues, challenges or agenda's. The advanced theatre investigation requires students to transform and integrate research into theatrical production and develop a production that will speak to an external audience about a specific contemporary experience. This course is offered in intensive mode - weeks 1-6 (6hrs studio workshop + 3 hrs CTM per week) and the production is showcased in week 7 (of an evening).
title: Devising Theatre
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

Whether you are a beginning (honours student) or a bit further along your journey, this course is designed to give you the technical knowledge of where to start with translating your research into outputs. It will cover how to translate your work to industry, media, conferences, and journal publications as well as address the difference between predatory and quality outlets to publish your work. At the end of the course, students will have a strong understanding of how and where to translate their research into outputs beyond their dissertation.
title: Translating Research into Academic Outputs
academicOrgDescription: Griffith Business School

The course provides opportunities to develop project and cyber security management capabilities as students manage the full project lifecycle, evaluate security and privacy requirements, and build resilient systems aligned with best practices and ethical principles. Students also engage in reflective practice by finalising a portfolio that captures their learning journey and showcases technical proficiency and strategic thinking developed throughout the program.
title: Cyber Security Capstone Project
academicOrgDescription: School of Information and Communication Technology

title: Lyric Diction
academicOrgDescription: Queensland Conservatorium

description: Simulated placement and ethics in counselling will prepare counselling students by engaging in realistic, yet controlled, scenarios designed to mimic the challenges and situations they may encounter in their future professional practice. These simulations are conducted in a safe and supportive environment, allowing students to practice and refine their counselling skills before working with actual clients. Simulated placement learning will include various forms, such as role-playing exercises, case studies, or virtual simulations. Ethical considerations are integral to both simulated and real counselling settings, emphasizing principles such as confidentiality, informed consent, cultural sensitivity, competence, and maintaining professional boundaries. These ethical principles ensure that counselling students are well-prepared for the complexities of real-world practice while upholding the well-being and rights of their future client. This course is not available for credit based on prior studies or external activities. Prerequisites: Must have completed at least 60CP of the Bachelor of Counselling courses including 1018PSY and 3005PSY.

description: This course is an introduction to the academic conventions and practices of communicating at a postgraduate level. It focuses on conventions associated with accepted practice in researching and writing essays, reports and case studies as well as the presentation and delivery of academic material. There is a focus throughout on the use of methods, technologies and strategies to develop an academic voice integrated with other viewpoints for effective expression and communication at the postgraduate level. The course scaffolds students' navigation through research and use of existing knowledge sources without incurring the risk of plagiarism.

description: This course provides students with an opportunity to improve their academic and communication skills in an Australian university and societal context. The course focuses on the concept of cultural competence, emphasising communication across cultures to ensure students are equipped to respond appropriately in varied multicultural and social environments. The course aims to develop students' personal awareness, allow them to gain insight into diverse cultural backgrounds, develop their skills in verbal, non-verbal, and written communication, and use of 'inclusive language' in everyday interactions, while they also identify and overcome barriers to effective intercultural communication.
title: Intercultural Issues for Postgraduate Students
academicOrgDescription: Department of Management

description: Experimental Writing takes what you thought you knew about creative writing and turns it upside down. As a third-year course in the Creative Writing major, Experimental Writing is an opportunity for Creative Writing students to spread their wings and explore far-off and hitherto forbidden (and forbidding) regions of creative practice. The course examines experimental theory and technique, and draws on literary histories of innovative poetry and prose. In the first half of the course, students are introduced to a rich field of experimental possibilities, and are encouraged to utilise these in the development of their own projects. Then, through ongoing discussions with their tutor and peers, students are supported to produce the boldest, most original and most unusual project of their degrees.
title: Experimental Writing
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

description: Students need high level audio and video production skills for a range of communication professions. This course develops literacy in these styles of production and understandings on how they are used to best communicate with stakeholders and publics.

description: This course travels through different cultures of writing, and writing from different cultures. Award-winning and highly influential works of fiction, poetry and non-fiction will provide us with opportunities to study a diverse range of writing techniques, as well as a platform for critical engagement with contemporary cultures and their literatures.
title: Writing Across Cultures
academicOrgDescription: School of Humanities, Languages and Social Science

A greater knowledge of these principles and techniques equip students with relevant foundational skills to analyse the general economy in a dynamic manner with particular relation to the implications, opportunities and challenges an ever changing economic landscape presents. The application of concepts provides for a better understanding of business decision-making at firm level and policy making and governmental level. Students completing this course as part of the Accounting (Extended) major will have assumed knowledge of 1006GBS Why Money Matters.

academicOrgDescription: Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics
